children.title: Fixed-Point Representations
children.top_down_role: Computational representations through which acceleration mechanisms access a problem.

children.title: Iterate–Map Representation
children.top_down_role: The direct operator-iteration representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate–Map Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct representation of a stationary fixed-point process on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subseteq H\), and let \(T:D\to D\). Given \(x^0\in D\), the direct iterate–map representation is
\[
x^{k+1}=T(x^k),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots .
\]
A point \(x^\star\in D\) solves the associated fixed-point problem precisely when \(T(x^\star)=x^\star\). Thus the generated sequence consists of successive compositions \(x^k=T^k(x^0)\), where \(T^0=I\) and \(T^{k+1}=T\circ T^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary fixed-point method repeatedly applies one self-map. Its solutions are exactly the points left unchanged by that map.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(D\subseteq H\).

notation.meaning: k-fold composition of the iteration map, with zeroth power equal to the identity

children.title: Residual Mapping
children.top_down_role: Residual objects used by extrapolation and multisecant accelerators.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual associated with a fixed-point map under the identity-minus-map convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subseteq H\), and let \(T:D\to H\). The residual mapping associated with \(T\) is the map \(R_T:D\to H\) defined by
\[
R_T(x)=(I-T)(x)=x-T(x).
\]
Its norm \(\lVert R_T(x)\rVert\) measures failure of \(x\) to satisfy the fixed-point equation. This record uses the identity-minus-map convention; the alternative sign convention \(T-I\) has the same zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the identity-minus-map convention, the residual is the point minus its image, and its zeros are exactly the fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to H\).

notation.meaning: identity mapping on the ambient space

children.title: Root-Finding Form
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point problems viewed through associated root problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Root-Finding Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root formulation induced by the residual of a fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subseteq H\), and let \(T:D\to H\). With residual \(R_T=I-T\), the fixed-point problem for \(T\) is represented as the root-finding problem
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in D\text{ such that }R_T(x^\star)=0.
\]
Equivalently, the solution set in root form is \(R_T^{-1}(\{0\})\). The formulation is algebraic and does not by itself require continuity, monotonicity, or differentiability of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point problem can be written as finding a zero of the identity-minus-map residual.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to H\).

notation.meaning: zero set of the residual mapping

children.title: Residual–Root Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between residual evaluations and root-oriented acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Root Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic correspondence between fixed points and residual zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subseteq H\), and let \(T:D\to H\). Define \(R_T=I-T\). For every \(x\in D\),
\[
R_T(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x-T(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
T(x)=x.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=R_T^{-1}(\{0\}),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{x\in D:T(x)=x\}\). Hence a fixed-point solver for \(T\) and a root solver for its residual target exactly the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zeros of the identity-minus-map residual are exactly the fixed points of the underlying map.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to H\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of T in D

children.title: Resolvent Representation
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point maps expressed through resolvent operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent of a set-valued operator on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). The resolvent of \(A\) with parameter \(\gamma\) is the set-valued inverse
\[
J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}.
\]
Thus \(p\in J_{\gamma A}(x)\) exactly when
\[
x\in p+\gamma A(p),
\]
or equivalently \((x-p)/\gamma\in A(p)\). If \(A\) is maximally monotone, then \(J_{\gamma A}:H\to H\) is everywhere defined and single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent inverts the identity plus a scaled operator; maximal monotonicity makes it an everywhere-defined single-valued map.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\) and \(p\in J_{\gamma A}(x)\iff (x-p)/\gamma\in A(p)\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of the scaled operator gamma A

children.title: Monotone-Inclusion Representation
children.top_down_role: Operator-inclusion forms underlying accelerated fixed-point iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Inclusion Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point representation of a zero of a monotone set-valued operator through its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be monotone, and let \(\gamma>0\). The monotone-inclusion problem
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in H\text{ such that }0\in A(x^\star)
\]
has the resolvent fixed-point representation
\[
x^\star=J_{\gamma A}(x^\star),
\qquad J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}.
\]
This equivalence is algebraic whenever the displayed resolvent value is defined. Maximal monotonicity of \(A\) ensures that the resolvent is a single-valued self-map on all of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero of a monotone operator is exactly a fixed point of any positive-parameter resolvent of that operator; maximal monotonicity makes the resolvent an everywhere-defined self-map.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone.

notation.meaning: set of points x satisfying zero in A(x)

children.title: Proximal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections from resolvent fixed points to proximal method families.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex subdifferential resolvents coincide with proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\gamma>0\). Then
\[
J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)
=(I+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}(x)
=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)
=\mathop{\arg\min}_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
0\in\partial f(x^\star)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x^\star),
\]
so minimizers of \(f\) are precisely fixed points of its proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, the subdifferential resolvent equals the proximal map, whose fixed points are exactly the minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled function gamma f

children.title: Splitting-Operator Representation
children.top_down_role: Composite fixed-point representations produced by operator splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Splitting-Operator Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point encoding produced by composing explicitly evaluable component operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and consider an inclusion \(0\in A_1(x)+\cdots+A_m(x)\). An operator splitting supplies a self-map \(T:H\to H\), constructed from separately evaluable component operations such as resolvents, forward evaluations, reflections, affine combinations, or compositions, together with a recovery map \(P:H\to H\), such that
\[
z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
0\in A_1(Pz^\star)+\cdots+A_m(Pz^\star).
\]
When the representation is exact, every solution is recoverable: \(\operatorname{zer}(A_1+\cdots+A_m)=P(\operatorname{Fix}T)\). The baseline iteration is \(z^{k+1}=T(z^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator splitting encodes a composite inclusion as a fixed-point map assembled from separately computable component operations, with a map recovering primal solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A_i:H\rightrightarrows H\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
\(T:H\to H\) and \(P:H\to H\) define an exact splitting representation.

notation.meaning: fixed-point operator assembled by the splitting scheme
map recovering an inclusion solution from a fixed point
zero set of a set-valued operator A

children.title: Picard Iteration
children.top_down_role: Direct fixed-point iteration used as a baseline in contractive regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Picard Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed fixed-point iteration, with contraction stopping control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a complete metric space \((X,d)\), a map \(T:X\to X\), an initial point \(x^0\in X\), and a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), compute
\[
x^{k+1}=T(x^k).
\]
Stop and output \(x^{k+1}\) when \(d(x^{k+1},x^k)\leq\varepsilon\). If \(T\) is a contraction with modulus \(q\in[0,1)\), then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^\star\), the iterates converge to it, and
\[
d(x^k,x^\star)\leq q^k d(x^0,x^\star).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration repeatedly applies the map. Under a contraction, it converges geometrically to the unique fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a complete metric space and \(T:X\to X\).
For the convergence claim, \(d(Tx,Ty)\leq qd(x,y)\) for some \(q\in[0,1)\).

children.title: Krasnosel'skii–Mann Iterations
children.top_down_role: Averaged baseline iterations central to nonexpansive fixed-point theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Krasnosel'skii–Mann Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed fixed-point iteration for a nonexpansive self-map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a real Hilbert space \(H\), a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq H\), a nonexpansive map \(T:C\to C\), an initial point \(x^0\in C\), relaxation parameters \((\lambda_k)_{k\geq0}\subseteq[0,1]\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Compute
\[
x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)x^k+\lambda_kT(x^k).
\]
Stop and output \(x^k\) when \(\lVert x^k-T(x^k)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). If \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda_k(1-\lambda_k)=+\infty\), then \((x^k)\) converges weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Krasnosel'skii–Mann iteration averages each iterate with its image. Standard relaxation and nonexpansiveness conditions yield weak convergence to a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space and \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive.

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Hilbert space

children.title: Perturbed Baseline Iterations
children.top_down_role: Reference trajectories subject to deterministic additive perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Baseline Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively perturbed relaxed fixed-point iteration with deterministic errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a normed space \(X\), a convex set \(C\subseteq X\), a map \(T:C\to X\), an initial point \(x^0\in C\), relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k\in[0,1]\), deterministic perturbations \(e^k\in X\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Generate
\[
x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)x^k+\lambda_kT(x^k)+e^k,
\]
provided the right-hand side belongs to \(C\). Stop and output \(x^k\) when \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). The error-free Krasnosel'skii–Mann baseline is recovered by setting \(e^k=0\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed baseline iteration adds a prescribed deterministic error to each relaxed fixed-point update; zero perturbations recover the exact method.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(C\subseteq X\) is convex, and \(T:C\to X\).
Each computed right-hand side lies in \(C\).

notation.meaning: additive deterministic perturbation at iteration k

children.title: Inexact Baseline Iterations
children.top_down_role: Reference trajectories using approximate map evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Baseline Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed iteration using deterministic approximations to map evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a normed space \(X\), a convex set \(C\subseteq X\), a map \(T:C\to X\), an initial point \(x^0\in C\), relaxation parameters \(\lambda_k\in[0,1]\), error tolerances \(\eta_k\geq0\), and stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), obtain an approximate evaluation \(y^k\in X\) satisfying
\[
\lVert y^k-T(x^k)\rVert\leq\eta_k,
\]
and set
\[
x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)x^k+\lambda_ky^k,
\]
provided \(x^{k+1}\in C\). Stop and output \(x^k\) when \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). Exact evaluation is recovered when \(\eta_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact baseline iteration replaces each exact map value by an approximation satisfying a deterministic error tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(C\subseteq X\) is convex, and \(T:C\to X\).

notation.meaning: inexact evaluation of T at the current iterate

children.title: Deterministic Error Regimes
children.top_down_role: Error behaviors relevant to stability of the baseline trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Error Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies deterministic perturbations of a baseline fixed-point iteration by their magnitude or decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(T:H\to H\), and consider \(x_{k+1}=T x_k+e_k\), where \((e_k)_{k\geq 0}\subset H\) is deterministic. Given nonnegative bounds \(\eta_k\) satisfying \(\lVert e_k\rVert\leq\eta_k\), the errors are bounded if \(\sup_k\eta_k<\infty\), vanishing if \(\eta_k\to0\), and absolutely summable if \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty\). They are relatively controlled with parameter \(c\geq0\) if \(\lVert e_k\rVert\leq c\lVert T x_k-x_k\rVert\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic iteration errors may be bounded, vanish asymptotically, be absolutely summable, or be controlled relative to the current fixed-point residual.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a normed space and \(T:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((e_k)\) belongs to the stated regime exactly when its displayed bound, decay, summability, or relative-residual condition holds.

notation.meaning: deterministic evaluation error at iteration k
fixed-point residual at the current iterate

review_flags: Exact multi-regime classification requires a source explicitly treating deterministic perturbations of fixed-point iterations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definitions are plausible, but the combined taxonomy of bounded, vanishing, summable, and relatively controlled deterministic errors requires a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Linear Maps

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear operator model for fixed-point dynamics on a normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed vector space. A map \(T:X\to X\) is a bounded linear map if there exists \(L<\infty\) such that, for all \(x,y\in X\) and scalars \(a,b\), \(T(ax+by)=aT(x)+bT(y)\) and \(\lVert Tx\rVert\leq L\lVert x\rVert\). Its fixed points form \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\ker(I-T)\), and the unperturbed fixed-point iteration satisfies \(x_k=T^k x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded linear fixed-point map preserves linear combinations; its fixed points form the kernel of the identity-minus-operator, and its iterates are operator powers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is bounded linear precisely under the displayed linearity and boundedness conditions, with \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\ker(I-T)\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of T

review_flags: A source locator specifically supporting the bounded-linear fixed-point formulation is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-linear definition and fixed-point identities are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Matrix Map and Induced Spectral-Radius Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear combinations of prescribed real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given $A_1,\ldots,A_p\in\mathbb S^n$, define $A:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb S^n$ and $f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R$ by
\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x^{(i)}A_i,
\qquad
f(x)=\rho(A(x)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given symmetric matrices A_i, their coefficient map sends x to the linear combination of the A_i, and the induced objective is the spectral radius of that combination.

children.title: Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Shifted linear fixed-point dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine extension of linear fixed-point dynamics, including the associated linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed vector space, let \(A:X\to X\) be bounded linear, and let \(b\in X\). The map \(T:X\to X\) defined by \(T(x)=Ax+b\) is affine. Its fixed-point equation is equivalent to \((I-A)x=b\). For the iteration \(x_{k+1}=Ax_k+b\), one has \(x_k=A^k x_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}A^j b\) for every integer \(k\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map is a linear map plus a constant; its fixed points solve a linear system, and its iterates admit a finite power-series formula.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to X\) is bounded linear and \(b\in X\).

notation.meaning: linear part of the affine map

review_flags: A source locator specifically supporting affine fixed-point dynamics is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine fixed-point equation and iterate formula are correct and appropriately classified as a definition, but the record has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov-Compatible Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial subspace structure generated by affine fixed-point iteration and affine residual recombination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and \(T(x)=Ax+b\). For \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), define \(r_k=T(x_k)-x_k\) and \(\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Ar_0,\ldots,A^{k-1}r_0\}\). Then \(r_k=A^k r_0\) and \(x_k-x_0\in\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)=\mathcal K_k(I-A,r_0)\). Moreover, if \(y=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_i x_i\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_i=1\), then \(T(y)-y=p(A)r_0\), where \(p(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_i z^i\) and \(p(1)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine fixed-point residuals are operator polynomials of the initial residual, so affine combinations of iterates perform constrained polynomial residual transformations in a Krylov subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_k=A^k r_0\), \(x_k-x_0\in\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)\), and every affine recombination has residual \(p(A)r_0\) with \(p(1)=1\).

notation.meaning: order-k Krylov subspace generated by A and r_0
residual polynomial induced by affine recombination coefficients

review_flags: The precise Krylov residual-polynomial formulation requires a dedicated acceleration or numerical linear algebra source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Krylov identities and residual-polynomial formulation are internally consistent and fit a property leaf, but this nontrivial formulation needs a dedicated source and locator.

children.title: Contractive Maps
children.top_down_role: The regime supporting direct global or local rate comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global contraction regime yielding a unique fixed point and direct linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space. A map \(T:X\to X\) is a contraction with modulus \(q\in[0,1)\) if \(d(Tx,Ty)\leq qd(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in X\). Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x_\star\), and the iteration \(x_{k+1}=T x_k\) satisfies \(d(x_k,x_\star)\leq q^k d(x_0,x_\star)\) for every \(k\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction shrinks every pairwise distance by a uniform factor below one; on a complete space it has one fixed point and Picard iteration converges linearly.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) satisfies the contraction inequality with \(q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(x_\star\in X\) with \(T x_\star=x_\star\), and \(d(x_k,x_\star)\leq q^k d(x_0,x_\star)\).

children.title: Nonexpansive Maps
children.top_down_role: Nonexpansive operator regimes for accelerated fixed-point iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric nonexpansion in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty. A map \(T:C\to H\) is nonexpansive if \(\lVert Tx-Ty\rVert\leq\lVert x-y\rVert\) for every \(x,y\in C\). Equivalently, its Lipschitz modulus on \(C\) is at most one. This definition alone does not assert that \(T(C)\subseteq C\), that a fixed point exists, or that the Picard iterates converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive map never increases distances. This property alone neither guarantees an invariant domain nor ensures existence or convergence to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive exactly when \(\lVert Tx-Ty\rVert\leq\lVert x-y\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

children.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Maps
children.top_down_role: Firmly nonexpansive regimes associated with resolvent-style maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space operator class equivalent to one-half averagedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty. A map \(T:C\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive if, for every \(x,y\in C\), \(\lVert Tx-Ty\rVert^2\leq\langle Tx-Ty,x-y\rangle\). Equivalently, \(2T-I\) is nonexpansive on \(C\); hence \(T=\tfrac12 I+\tfrac12 R\) for some nonexpansive map \(R:C\to H\). In particular, every firmly nonexpansive map is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A firmly nonexpansive map satisfies a strengthened Hilbert-space distance inequality; equivalently, it is one-half averaged and therefore nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Firm nonexpansiveness is equivalent to nonexpansiveness of \(2T-I\), and it implies nonexpansiveness of \(T\).

notation.meaning: nonexpansive map in the averaged representation

children.title: Averaged Maps
children.top_down_role: Averaged-operator regimes supporting Mann and splitting iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-combination representation between the identity and a nonexpansive map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A map \(T:C\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged if there exists a nonexpansive map \(R:C\to H\) such that \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\). Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\), \(\lVert Tx-Ty\rVert^2\leq\lVert x-y\rVert^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\lVert(I-T)x-(I-T)y\rVert^2\). Every averaged map is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged map is a strict convex combination of the identity and a nonexpansive map; it obeys a strengthened nonexpansive inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged exactly when it has the displayed representation, equivalently the displayed norm inequality.

children.title: Operator-Class Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Structural nesting among the three nonexpansive operator classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Class Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion relations among firmly nonexpansive, averaged, and nonexpansive Hilbert-space maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let all maps have a common nonempty domain \(C\subseteq H\). Every firmly nonexpansive map is \(\tfrac12\)-averaged. If \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and \(\alpha\leq\beta<1\), then \(T\) is also \(\beta\)-averaged. Every \(\alpha\)-averaged map with \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) is nonexpansive. Consequently, writing \(\mathcal F\), \(\mathcal A_\alpha\), and \(\mathcal N\) for these classes, \(\mathcal F=\mathcal A_{1/2}\subseteq\mathcal A_\beta\subseteq\mathcal N\) whenever \(\beta\in[1/2,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Firmly nonexpansive maps are exactly one-half averaged; increasing the averaging parameter preserves averagedness, and every averaged map is nonexpansive.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
All operator classes use the common domain \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\mathcal A_{1/2}\subseteq\mathcal A_\beta\subseteq\mathcal N\) for every \(\beta\in[1/2,1)\).

children.title: Nonsmooth Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes requiring alternatives to smooth local linearization analyses.

children.title: Nonsmooth Maps
children.top_down_role: Operator regimes lacking ordinary smooth local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz fixed-point maps lacking classical differentiability at some points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. A map \(T:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz if every \(x\in U\) has a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) and a constant \(L_V<\infty\) such that \(\lVert T(y)-T(z)\rVert\leq L_V\lVert y-z\rVert\) for all \(y,z\in V\). In this regime, \(T\) is called nonsmooth when it fails to be Fréchet differentiable at at least one point of interest, so no classical Jacobian is available there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz map is nonsmooth at a point when it lacks a Fréchet derivative there, even though it retains local distance control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a nonsmooth point \(x\), no linear map \(J\) satisfies \(T(x+h)=T(x)+Jh+o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant on a neighborhood V
remainder negligible relative to the step norm

review_flags: The inventory provides no precise nonsmooth-analysis definition locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local Lipschitz and pointwise nondifferentiability conditions are plausible, but calling a map globally nonsmooth because it fails differentiability at a 'point of interest' is context-dependent and requires a precise nonsmooth-analysis source.

children.title: Semismooth Maps
children.top_down_role: Structured nonsmooth regimes admitting semismooth local analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-Jacobian approximation property for locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(T:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x\in U\). The map \(T\) is semismooth at \(x\) if it is directionally differentiable at \(x\) and, as \(h\to0\), \(\sup_{V\in\partial_C T(x+h)}\lVert T(x+h)-T(x)-Vh\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert)\). It is strongly semismooth at \(x\) if the final remainder is \(O(\lVert h\rVert^2)\). Semismoothness on a set means semismoothness at every point of that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semismooth map is directionally differentiable and is approximated to first order by every nearby Clarke generalized Jacobian; strong semismoothness gives a quadratic remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semismoothness and strong semismoothness are characterized by the respective \(o(\lVert h\rVert)\) and \(O(\lVert h\rVert^2)\) generalized-Jacobian remainders.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of T at y

review_flags: A nonsmooth-analysis source supporting the selected Clarke generalized-Jacobian definition is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Clarke-generalized-Jacobian formulation is plausible, but the exact uniform remainder condition and strong-semismoothness convention require an authoritative source with a definition or page locator.

children.title: Smooth-Linearization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of acceleration analyses based on smooth local linearization.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Linearization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks when a single Jacobian accurately models local fixed-point errors and when that model fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(T:U\to\mathbb R^n\), and let \(x_\star\in U\) satisfy \(T(x_\star)=x_\star\). If \(T\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x_\star\) with Jacobian \(J\), then for \(e=x-x_\star\), \(T(x)-x_\star=Je+o(\lVert e\rVert)\). The smooth linearization boundary is crossed when no single linear map \(J\) gives this remainder relation. Mere local Lipschitz continuity does not suffice: \(T(x)=|x|\) at \(x_\star=0\) is Lipschitz but admits no such scalar derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiability yields a single-Jacobian local error model. Local Lipschitz continuity alone does not: the absolute-value fixed-point map has no linearization at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A classical first-order model exists exactly when some \(J\) satisfies \(T(x_\star+e)-x_\star-Je=o(\lVert e\rVert)\); \(T(x)=|x|\) at zero violates this condition.

notation.meaning: fixed point about which the map is linearized

children.title: Nonconvexity-Nonmonotonicity Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Regimes where residual progress, stationarity, and globalization must be distinguished.

children.title: Nonconvex Map Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point acceleration in optimization settings with nonconvex structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Map Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite proximal-gradient maps generated by a nonconvex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, suppose \(f+g\) is nonconvex, and let \(\gamma>0\). The associated nonconvex proximal-gradient map is \[T_\gamma(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\bigl(x-\gamma\nabla f(x)\bigr).\] Its fixed points are precisely the composite stationary points: \[x=T_\gamma(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x).\] This is a nonconvex map regime because its generating composite objective is nonconvex; global averagedness or contractivity of \(T_\gamma\) is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconvex composite objective, the proximal-gradient map has fixed points exactly at composite stationary points, without any assumed global contractive or averaged behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma>0\), and the proximal map is evaluated exactly.

notation.meaning: proximal operator of the scaled function

children.title: Nonmonotone Map Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operator regimes without monotone progress behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Map Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonmonotonicity in the Hilbert-space inner-product sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(T:D\to H\). The map \(T\) is nonmonotone on \(D\) when monotonicity fails, equivalently when there exist \(x,y\in D\) such that \[\langle T(x)-T(y),x-y\rangle<0.\] A fixed-point iteration using such a map lies in a nonmonotone regime unless monotonicity is recovered for a related residual, restriction, metric, or local neighborhood; monotone-operator inequalities for \(T\) itself are then unavailable globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is in the nonmonotone regime when some pair of points violates the defining monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is nonmonotone exactly when \(\exists x,y\in D\) with \(\langle T(x)-T(y),x-y\rangle<0\).

children.title: Residual–Stationarity Separation
children.top_down_role: Regimes where residual progress does not directly settle stationarity behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Stationarity Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of residuals to certify optimization stationarity without a compatibility relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Residual smallness alone does not imply optimization stationarity. On \(\mathbb{R}\), take the differentiable objective \(f(x)=x\) and the fixed-point map \(T(x)=x\). The residual \(r(x)=x-T(x)\) satisfies \(r(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), while \(f'(x)=1\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence every point is an exact fixed point of \(T\), but no point is stationary for \(f\). A residual-to-stationarity conclusion therefore requires an explicit compatibility condition between \(T\) and the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An identity map has zero residual everywhere, yet for a linear objective none of those points is stationary; compatibility is indispensable.
assumptions_latex: The fixed-point map is not assumed to encode the stationarity condition of the objective.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Globalization Requirements
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions motivating safeguards or fallback mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Globalization Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A merit-decrease safeguard sufficient for global residual convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(D\subseteq H\), let \(T:D\to D\), define \(r(x)=x-T(x)\), and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subseteq D\). Suppose \(V:D\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(c>0\) satisfy \[V(x_{k+1})\le V(x_k)-c\lVert r(x_k)\rVert^2\] for every \(k\ge0\). In a safeguarded accelerated method, this condition may be enforced by accepting an accelerated candidate only when the inequality holds and otherwise using an always-available fallback step that also satisfies it. If \(\inf_{k\ge0}V(x_k)>-\infty\), then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert r(x_k)\rVert^2<\infty\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad\lVert r(x_k)\rVert\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform sufficient decrease of a lower-bounded merit function, enforced by an acceptance test and an always-available fallback, is sufficient to make the fixed-point residuals vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a normed space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to D\).
A step satisfying the decrease inequality is always available.

children.title: Stochastic-Inexact Evaluation Regimes

children.title: Stochastic Maps
children.top_down_role: Maps accessed through noisy or sampled evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditionally unbiased stochastic evaluation of a deterministic fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be a deterministic map on a real Hilbert space, and let \(\widehat T(x,\xi_k)\) be a random evaluation at iteration \(k\). Relative to a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)\), it is an unbiased stochastic map with variance bound \(\sigma_k^2\) when, for every \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable input \(x_k\), \[\mathbb E[\widehat T(x_k,\xi_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=T(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert\widehat T(x_k,\xi_k)-T(x_k)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\sigma_k^2.\] The stochastic residual evaluation is \(x_k-\widehat T(x_k,\xi_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic map is a random evaluation whose conditional mean equals the target map and whose conditional variance is controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat T(x_k,\xi_k)-T(x_k)\) is conditionally mean zero with conditional second moment at most \(\sigma_k^2\).

children.title: Inexact Maps
children.top_down_role: Maps evaluated through deterministic approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministically perturbed evaluation of a fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(D\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \(T:D\to H\). A deterministic inexact evaluation at iteration \(k\) has the form \[\widetilde T_k(x)=T(x)+e_k(x),\qquad x\in D,\] where \(e_k:D\to H\) is the evaluation error. An absolute-error model requires \(\lVert e_k(x)\rVert\le\eta_k\), whereas a relative-residual model requires \(\lVert e_k(x)\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert x-T(x)\rVert\), with \(\eta_k\ge0\). Defining \(r(x)=x-T(x)\), the inexact residual is \[\widetilde r_k(x)=x-\widetilde T_k(x)=r(x)-e_k(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic inexact map adds a controlled evaluation error to the exact map and therefore perturbs the fixed-point residual by the negative of that error.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a normed space, \(D\subseteq H\) is nonempty, and \(T:D\to H\).
At least one displayed error model is imposed with \(\eta_k\ge0\).

children.title: Mixed Evaluation Error
children.top_down_role: Operator evaluations combining sampling variability with approximation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Evaluation Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bias–noise decomposition for stochastic inexact map evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\), and let \((\mathcal F_k)\) be a filtration. For an \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable input \(x_k\), a mixed stochastic-inexact evaluation admits the representation \[\widetilde T_k(x_k)=T(x_k)+b_k+\zeta_k,\] where \(b_k\) is an integrable, \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable bias and \(\zeta_k\) is integrable with \(\mathbb E[\zeta_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\). Consequently, \[\mathbb E[\widetilde T_k(x_k)-T(x_k)\mid\mathcal F_k]=b_k.\] A controlled mixed-error model may additionally impose \(\lVert b_k\rVert\le\beta_k\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert\zeta_k\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\sigma_k^2\), thereby separating systematic conditional bias from zero-mean stochastic noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed evaluation error is represented as an integrable conditional bias plus integrable conditionally zero-mean noise, with separate optional bounds on bias magnitude and noise variance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\).
\((\mathcal F_k)\) is a filtration, and \(x_k\) and \(b_k\) are \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable.
\(b_k\) and \(\zeta_k\) are integrable, and \(\mathbb E[\zeta_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\).
For the variance bound, \(\zeta_k\) has finite conditional second moment.

children.title: Fixed-Point Residual Reduction
children.top_down_role: Approximate fixed-point quality as the performance target.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual norm as the performance target for approximate fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a map \(T:D\to H\) on a normed space, define the fixed-point residual by \(r(x)=x-T(x)\). A point \(x\in D\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate fixed point when \(\lVert r(x)\rVert\le\varepsilon\). Relative to an initial point \(x_0\) with \(r(x_0)\ne0\), an output \(x_N\) achieves residual-reduction factor \(\rho\ge0\) when \[\lVert r(x_N)\rVert\le\rho\lVert r(x_0)\rVert.\] For a nonmonotone residual sequence, the best-iterate criterion replaces the left side by \(\min_{0\le k\le N}\lVert r(x_k)\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual reduction measures approximate fixed-point quality by the norm of x minus T(x), either at the final or best iterate.
assumptions_latex: The chosen norm and output convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual performance is certified by \(\lVert r(x_N)\rVert\le\varepsilon\) or by a declared relative factor \(\rho\).

children.title: Iterate Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of the generated trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence of the generated iterates to an unspecified fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:D\to D\) act on a normed space, and let \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\subset D\) be generated by a fixed-point method. The method has strong iterate convergence for the initial point \(x_0\) when there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) such that \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert=0.\] This property is stronger than residual convergence alone: the condition \(\lVert x_k-T(x_k)\rVert\to0\) does not, without additional compactness or regularity assumptions, assert convergence of the sequence \((x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterate convergence means the complete sequence converges in norm to some fixed point, not merely that its residuals vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) lies in a normed space and \(T:D\to D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\) in norm.

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of T

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of a distinguished solution when the fixed-point set is non-singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(D\subseteq H\), let \(T:D\to D\) have a nonempty fixed-point set, and let \(A\subseteq D\) be the set of admissible initial points. A fixed-point selector is a mapping \(S:A\to\operatorname{Fix}(T)\). A fixed-point algorithm realizes \(S\) when, for every \(x_0\in A\), its generated iterates satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert x_k-S(x_0)\rVert=0.\] Selection is nontrivial when \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) contains more than one point. Possible uniquely defined selections include a metric projection of \(x_0\), a minimum-norm fixed point, or a fixed point minimizing an auxiliary criterion, whenever the required existence and uniqueness conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-point selection specifies which fixed point an algorithm approaches in norm from each admissible initial point when multiple fixed points may exist.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a normed space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to D\).
\(A\subseteq D\) is the admissible initial-point set, and \(S:A\to\operatorname{Fix}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm realizes \(S\) exactly when \(\lVert x_k-S(x_0)\rVert\to0\) for every \(x_0\in A\).

notation.meaning: set of fixed points of T

children.title: Selection-Sensitive Convergence
children.top_down_role: Interactions between trajectory limits and preferred fixed-point outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Sensitive Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantee that preserves the identity of the selected fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(D\subseteq H\), let \(T:D\to D\) have a nonempty fixed-point set, let \(A\subseteq D\) be the admissible initial-point set, and let \(S:A\to\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) be a prescribed selector. For each \(x_0\in A\), let \(x_k(x_0)\) denote the iterate generated from \(x_0\). Convergence is selection-sensitive with respect to \(S\) when \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\lVert x_k(x_0)-S(x_0)\rVert=0\] for every \(x_0\in A\). A residual bound or convergence to an unspecified member of \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) is not selection-sensitive. A quantitative selection-sensitive rate directly bounds \(\lVert x_k(x_0)-S(x_0)\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection-sensitive convergence guarantees norm convergence from every admissible initial point to the fixed point prescribed by the selector, rather than merely to some fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a normed space, \(D\subseteq H\), and \(T:D\to D\) has a nonempty fixed-point set.
\(A\subseteq D\) is the admissible initial-point set.
The iterates \(x_k(x_0)\) are defined for every \(x_0\in A\).

children.title: Optimization Progress Certificate Pair
children.top_down_role: Optimization-facing performance beyond operator residual reduction.

children.title: Objective Progress
children.top_down_role: Performance measured through changes in objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Progress
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable objective decrease and certified upper bound on suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(x_0,x_N\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and suppose \(\ell\) is a known lower bound satisfying \(\ell\le f^*:=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\). The pair \[\Delta_N=f(x_0)-f(x_N),\qquad G_N=f(x_N)-\ell\] is an objective-progress certificate. The value \(\Delta_N\) certifies realized objective decrease, while \(G_N\) gives the verifiable bound \[0\le f(x_N)-f^*\le G_N.\] Thus \(G_N\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-objective optimality; without a valid lower bound, decrease alone does not certify global suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective progress records achieved decrease and, when a valid lower bound is known, an upper bound on the final suboptimality gap.
assumptions_latex: The certified lower bound satisfies \(\ell\le f^*\).

notation.meaning: known lower bound on the optimum value

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(T:X\to X\), and define the residual \(r_T(x)=\|x-Tx\|\). Suppose \(\operatorname{Fix}T\) equals the stationary solution set \(S\) of the underlying optimization problem. Then \(r_T(x)=0\) certifies \(x\in S\). For iterates \((x_k)\), stationarity progress is measured by \(r_T(x_k)\), or by \(\min_{0\le j\le k}r_T(x_j)\). If additionally \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le \kappa r_T(x)\) on a set containing the iterates, where \(\kappa\ge0\), then for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(r_T(x_k)\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\le\kappa\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-point residual certifies exact stationarity, and under a residual error bound it quantitatively controls distance to the stationary set.

children.title: Residual–Objective Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Cases where operator-residual improvement does not track objective improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Objective Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small fixed-point residual need not imply a small objective gap without a calibration inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with minimizer \(x^\star=0\), and for \(0<\alpha<1\) let \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)=(1-\alpha)x\). At \(x=1\), the fixed-point residual is \(\|x-T_\alpha x\|=\alpha\), while the objective gap is \(f(x)-f(x^\star)=1/2\). Hence the residual can approach zero solely because the step scale approaches zero, although objective suboptimality remains fixed. An implication from residual accuracy to objective accuracy therefore requires fixed scaling and an inequality relating objective gap to residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual may become arbitrarily small through step-size scaling while the objective gap stays fixed; objective progress requires an additional calibration inequality.

notation.meaning: gradient fixed-point map with step scale alpha

children.title: Operator-Oracle Evaluation Cost Model
children.top_down_role: Accounting based on operator evaluations and oracle access.

children.title: Operator Evaluation Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost measured by applications of the fixed-point operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts evaluations of the fixed-point operator independently of internal primitive-oracle work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm producing \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_K\) using a fixed-point operator \(T:X\to X\), let \(q_k\) be the number of newly computed values of the form \(T(z)\) used to construct \(x_{k+1}\). The operator-evaluation cost through iteration \(K\) is \(N_T(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}q_k\). Reuse of a cached value incurs no new evaluation, whereas evaluations at distinct arguments are counted separately. This metric treats one evaluation of \(T\) as one unit even when \(T\) is composite; its internal calls are recorded by oracle-access or composite accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator cost is the number of newly computed fixed-point-map values, excluding cache reuse and leaving internal primitive calls to separate accounting.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) is the operator exposed to the acceleration method.

notation.meaning: new operator evaluations during iteration k

children.title: Oracle Access Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost measured by calls to problem-specific information oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Access Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts calls to primitive optimization oracles used directly or within operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{O}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{O}_s\) be primitive oracles, such as gradient, proximal, projection, or coordinate oracles. During a run through iteration \(K\), let \(n_{k,i}\) denote the number of calls to \(\mathcal{O}_i\) made while constructing \(x_{k+1}\), including calls internal to evaluations of \(T\). The oracle-access vector is \(N_{\mathcal O}(K)=(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}n_{k,1},\ldots,\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}n_{k,s})\). Given nonnegative unit prices \(c_i\), its scalarized cost is \(C_{\mathcal O}(K)=\sum_{i=1}^s c_iN_{\mathcal O,i}(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle access cost records every primitive oracle call, optionally scalarized by nonnegative per-oracle prices.
assumptions_latex: \(c_i\ge0\) is the unit price of oracle \(\mathcal{O}_i\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative unit price for oracle i

children.title: Composite Evaluation Accounting
children.top_down_role: Accounting for iterations that invoke multiple operator or oracle components.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Evaluation Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposes accelerated-iteration cost into operator, primitive-oracle, and algebraic components without double counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one evaluation of \(T\) invokes \(a_i\) calls to primitive oracle \(\mathcal O_i\), and iteration \(k\) also makes \(b_{k,i}\) calls outside \(T\). If \(q_k\) operator evaluations occur at iteration \(k\), then \(N_{\mathcal O,i}(K)=a_iN_T(K)+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}b_{k,i}\). With operator overhead price \(c_T\), oracle prices \(c_i\), and algebraic cost \(A_k\), the non-double-counting composite cost is \(C(K)=c_TN_T(K)+\sum_{i=1}^sc_iN_{\mathcal O,i}(K)+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}A_k\), where \(c_T\) excludes the already priced primitive calls internal to \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite accounting expands each operator evaluation into primitive calls and adds only unpriced operator overhead and acceleration algebra, avoiding double counting.
assumptions_latex: Each evaluation of \(T\) makes exactly \(a_i\) calls to \(\mathcal O_i\).
\(b_{k,i}\) counts calls to \(\mathcal O_i\) made outside \(T\).
\(c_T\) prices only overhead not included in primitive-oracle prices.

children.title: Linear-Algebra Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost of factorizations, least-squares solves, and auxiliary subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebra Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense arithmetic cost of a depth-limited residual-mixing acceleration step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times m_k}\), with \(m_k\le m\), contain the retained residual differences of a depth-\(m\) acceleration method. Computing coefficients by the constrained least-squares problem \(\min_{\alpha\in\mathbb R^{m_k}}\|R_k\alpha\|_2\) subject to \(\mathbf 1^\top\alpha=1\), using dense QR or an equivalent stable factorization, costs \(O(nm_k^2+m_k^3)\) arithmetic operations when recomputed from scratch. Forming the accelerated combination costs an additional \(O(nm_k)\). Thus the worst-case dense linear-algebra cost per accelerated step is \(O(nm^2+m^3)\), excluding operator and oracle evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense depth-m residual-mixing step costs at most order n m-squared plus m-cubed arithmetic when its constrained least-squares problem is rebuilt.
assumptions_latex: The constrained least-squares factorization is recomputed densely from scratch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The per-step algebraic cost is \(O(nm_k^2+m_k^3)\subseteq O(nm^2+m^3)\).

children.title: Memory Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage required by depth-limited residual mixing and its dense small-dimensional factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\), a depth-\(m\) acceleration method retaining at most \(m\) iterates and \(m\) residual or difference vectors requires \(O(nm)\) scalar storage for history. A dense Gram matrix, triangular factor, or equivalent coefficient-space factorization requires \(O(m^2)\) additional scalars. Current iterates, residuals, and temporary vectors require \(O(n)\) storage. Consequently, the total auxiliary memory is \(O(nm+m^2)\); it reduces to \(O(nm)\) when \(m\le n\). Operator-internal and distributed replication storage are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Depth-m acceleration stores order n m history scalars and, for dense coefficient algebra, order m-squared factorization scalars.
assumptions_latex: Iterates and residuals belong to \(\mathbb R^n\).
At most \(m\) history columns are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Auxiliary memory is \(O(nm+m^2)\), and is \(O(nm)\) when \(m\le n\).

children.title: Depth-Dependent Resource Scaling
children.top_down_role: Resource changes induced by acceleration depth or history length.

knowledge_statements.title: Depth-Dependent Resource Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint oracle-independent arithmetic and storage scaling with acceleration depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(K\) accelerated steps in \(\mathbb R^n\) with maximum retained depth \(m\). If each step evaluates the fixed-point operator once and recomputes a dense residual-mixing factorization, then operator cost is \(K\), total acceleration algebra is \(O(K(nm^2+m^3))\), and peak auxiliary memory is \(O(nm+m^2)\). If depth varies as \(m_k\le m\), the sharper algebraic accounting is \(O(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(nm_k^2+m_k^3))\), while peak memory is \(O(n\max_km_k+(\max_km_k)^2)\). These bounds exclude the internal cost of each operator evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dense recomputation, increasing depth raises history memory linearly in n m and algebra quadratically or cubically in depth.
assumptions_latex: The run has \(K\) accelerated steps in \(\mathbb R^n\).
Each step uses one operator evaluation and dense factorization from scratch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Operator, algebra, and peak-memory costs are respectively \(K\), \(O(K(nm^2+m^3))\), and \(O(nm+m^2)\).

children.title: Parallel Execution Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost accounting for concurrency and available parallel resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Execution Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work–span accounting for parallel execution of accelerated fixed-point iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the run by a directed acyclic task graph with total work \(W\) and span \(S\), measured in unit-time arithmetic or operator tasks. On \(p\) identical processors, every schedule has parallel execution time \(T_p\ge\max\{W/p,S\}\). Under an ideal greedy scheduler with negligible communication and scheduling overhead, \(T_p\le W/p+S\). Thus the attainable speedup \(W/T_p\) is at most \(\min\{p,W/S\}\). Operator evaluations that cannot overlap lie on the span; independent coordinate or block evaluations contribute parallel work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time is limited by both work per processor and critical-path span; ideal speedup cannot exceed processor count or available parallelism.
assumptions_latex: The computation is represented by a finite acyclic task graph.
The upper bound assumes a greedy scheduler and negligible communication overhead.

children.title: Communication Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost accounting for data movement and synchronization.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latency–bandwidth accounting for messages exchanged by a distributed acceleration run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed run, let \(M\) be the number of point-to-point messages and let \(B\) be the total number of transmitted scalar words. In the latency–bandwidth model with per-message latency \(\lambda\) and per-word transfer time \(\beta\), define communication cost by \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}=\lambda M+\beta B\). For synchronized rounds \(r=1,\ldots,R\), a critical-path refinement is \(T_{\mathrm{comm}}=\sum_{r=1}^R(\lambda M_r^{\mathrm{cp}}+\beta B_r^{\mathrm{cp}})\), where only messages and words on the round's communication critical path are counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication cost separates message latency from transferred volume, with critical-path accounting used for elapsed communication time.
assumptions_latex: For elapsed time, rounds and their communication critical paths are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}=\lambda M+\beta B\), with critical-path time \(T_{\mathrm{comm}}\) as displayed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path elapsed time including computation, communication, synchronization, and imbalance.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Synchronization Issues in Parallel and Distributed Algorithms p. 88

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition a distributed run into sequential phases \(r=1,\ldots,R\) executed on \(p\) processors. Let \(C_{r,j}\) be processor \(j\)'s computation time in phase \(r\), let \(D_r\) be critical-path communication time, and let \(H_r\) be synchronization or scheduling overhead. Define the wall-clock cost by \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\sum_{r=1}^R\left(\max_{1\le j\le p}C_{r,j}+D_r+H_r\right)\). Consequently, total processor work divided by \(p\) need not predict elapsed time because communication, serial dependencies, and load imbalance can dominate. The time to accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is this quantity evaluated at the first phase whose declared stopping certificate is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock cost sums each phase's slowest computation, critical-path communication, and synchronization overhead until the requested certificate accuracy is reached.

children.title: Concurrency–Synchronization Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between parallelism gains and synchronization overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Concurrency–Synchronization Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher concurrency reduces ideal compute time but may increase delay, communication, and synchronization overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) workers execute updates whose convergence guarantee permits delay at most \(\tau_{\max}\). For a concurrency policy with induced delay \(\tau(p)\), synchronization count \(N_{\mathrm{sync}}(p)\), and synchronization latency \(h\), admissibility requires \(\tau(p)\le\tau_{\max}\). Its wall-clock lower model is \(T(p)\ge\max\{W/p,S\}+hN_{\mathrm{sync}}(p)+T_{\mathrm{comm}}(p)\). Increasing \(p\) can decrease \(W/p\), but need not decrease \(T(p)\) because delay, communication, or synchronization may grow. An admissible concurrency level should therefore minimize the complete cost model, not merely maximize \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More workers reduce ideal compute time only while admissible delay, communication, and synchronization costs do not erase the gain.
assumptions_latex: Work, span, communication, and synchronization use compatible time units.

If \(s_n=s+c\lambda^n\) with \(c
eq0\) and \(\lambda
otin\{0,1\}\), then \(\mathcal A(s_n)=s\). For vectors, applying this formula coordinatewise is basis-dependent and requires nonzero coordinatewise denominators; vector extrapolation methods instead replace scalar division by a specified projection, least-squares, or inner-product rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aitken extrapolation exactly removes a single scalar geometric error mode. Coordinatewise application to vectors is basis-dependent, so genuine vector variants require an additional projection or least-squares convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(s_n)=s_n-(\Delta s_n)^2/\Delta^2s_n\), and a single nonconstant geometric error mode is eliminated exactly.

notation.meaning: Forward-difference operator on a scalar sequence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar formula and geometric-mode exactness are standard and internally consistent, but no inspectable source supports either them or the broader vector-facing interpretation.

children.title: Steffensen Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Derivative-free fixed-point acceleration derived from scalar extrapolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Steffensen Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical scalar derivative-free Steffensen iteration obtained by applying Aitken extrapolation to three fixed-point iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:D\to D\) for \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), and choose \(x_0\in D\). At iteration \(n\), compute \(y_n=g(x_n)\), \(z_n=g(y_n)\), and \(d_n=z_n-2y_n+x_n\). If \(d_n\neq0\), set
\[x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{(y_n-x_n)^2}{d_n}.\]
If \(d_n=0\), the classical step is undefined and the algorithm must stop or invoke a declared safeguard. Output an iterate when a prescribed residual test such as \(|g(x_n)-x_n|\leq\varepsilon\) holds. For a simple fixed point \(x_\star\), twice continuous differentiability near \(x_\star\), and \(g'(x_\star)\neq1\), locally well-defined iterates have at least quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steffensen’s method evaluates the fixed-point map twice and applies Aitken extrapolation, yielding derivative-free local quadratic convergence under standard smoothness and nondegeneracy conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is twice continuously differentiable near a fixed point \(x_\star\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated derivative-free update is locally quadratically convergent whenever its denominators remain nonzero.

notation.meaning: Second forward difference formed from two successive map evaluations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf and the update is coherent, but the stated local quadratic-convergence theorem requires an authoritative locator supporting its exact hypotheses and rate.

children.title: Shanks Transformations
children.top_down_role: Scalar sequence transformations underlying epsilon-type methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Shanks Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-k scalar Shanks transformation and its first-order identification with Aitken extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a scalar sequence \((s_n)\), integers \(k\geq1\), and admissible \(n\), define the order-\(k\) Shanks transform by
\[e_k(s_n)=\frac{\det\!\begin{pmatrix}s_n&\cdots&s_{n+k}\\ \Delta s_n&\cdots&\Delta s_{n+k}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ \Delta^k s_n&\cdots&\Delta^k s_{n+k}\end{pmatrix}}{\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&\cdots&1\\ \Delta s_n&\cdots&\Delta s_{n+k}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ \Delta^k s_n&\cdots&\Delta^k s_{n+k}\end{pmatrix}},\]
provided the denominator determinant is nonzero. If \(s_n=s+\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_j\lambda_j^n\) with distinct \(\lambda_j\notin\{0,1\}\), then \(e_k(s_n)=s\) wherever defined. In particular, \(e_1(s_n)\) is the Aitken delta-squared transform.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The order-k Shanks determinant ratio eliminates k distinct geometric error modes exactly when its denominator is nonzero; its first order is Aitken’s transformation.
assumptions_latex: \((s_n)\) is scalar and the displayed differences exist
For exactness, the error is a sum of \(k\) distinct nonconstant geometric modes
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k(s_n)=s\) for the stated finite exponential model, and \(e_1\) equals the Aitken transform.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both displayed determinant arrays have k+2 rows and k+1 columns, so they are not determinants. An authoritative source is needed to establish the intended Shanks determinant convention and exactness statement before revision.

children.title: Relaxation Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Acceleration and stabilization through scalar or scheduled mixing.

children.title: Scalar Relaxation Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Classical scalar relaxation regimes.

children.title: Underrelaxation
children.top_down_role: Conservative scalar relaxation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Underrelaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant scalar underrelaxation of a fixed-point map on a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real normed vector space and let \(T:C\to C\). For a constant parameter \(\omega\in(0,1)\), the underrelaxed map is
\[T_\omega=(1-\omega)I+\omega T,\]
and the underrelaxed fixed-point iteration is \(x_{n+1}=T_\omega x_n=x_n+\omega(Tx_n-x_n)\). Because \(C\) is convex, \(T_\omega x\in C\) for every \(x\in C\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\omega)=\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) for every \(\omega\neq0\); thus underrelaxation changes the trajectory but not the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Underrelaxation moves only a fraction between the current point and its image. On a convex domain it remains feasible and preserves all fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex in a real normed vector space
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\omega=(1-\omega)I+\omega T\) maps \(C\) into itself and satisfies \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\omega)=\operatorname{Fix}(T)\).

notation.meaning: Relaxed fixed-point map with scalar parameter omega.
Identity map on the ambient space.

children.title: Overrelaxation
children.top_down_role: Aggressive scalar relaxation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Overrelaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant scalar extrapolation beyond the unrelaxed fixed-point image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) lie in a real vector space, let \(T:C\to C\), and choose \(\omega>1\). The overrelaxed map and iteration are
\[T_\omega=(1-\omega)I+\omega T,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n+\omega(Tx_n-x_n).\]
Thus \(T_\omega x\) lies beyond \(Tx\) on the affine line through \(x\) and \(Tx\). Although \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\omega)=\operatorname{Fix}(T)\), convexity of \(C\) alone does not imply \(T_\omega(C)\subseteq C\); feasibility and convergence therefore require additional invariance or operator-specific restrictions on \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overrelaxation extrapolates beyond the fixed-point image. It preserves fixed points algebraically, but convexity alone no longer guarantees feasibility or convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(T:C\to C\) on a subset of a real vector space

notation.meaning: Overrelaxed affine combination of the identity and fixed-point map.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Relaxation-Regime Transition
children.top_down_role: Behavior across conservative, neutral, and aggressive relaxation choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Regime Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The scalar threshold separating interpolation from extrapolation in relaxed fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(T_\omega=(1-\omega)I+\omega T\), the parameter value \(\omega=1\) is the transition between relaxation regimes. If \(0<\omega<1\), then \(T_\omega x\) is a strict convex combination of \(x\) and \(Tx\); if \(\omega=1\), then \(T_\omega=T\); and if \(\omega>1\), then \(T_\omega x\) extrapolates beyond \(Tx\). For a differentiable map at a fixed point \(x_\star\), the local linearization changes continuously as
\[DT_\omega(x_\star)=(1-\omega)I+\omega DT(x_\star),\]
so an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(DT(x_\star)\) is transformed to \(1-\omega+\omega\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At omega one, relaxed iteration becomes the original map. Crossing this value changes interpolation into extrapolation and affinely transforms every local eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is differentiable at a fixed point \(x_\star\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometric regime changes at \(\omega=1\), and local eigenvalues obey \(\lambda\mapsto1-\omega+\omega\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Derivative of the map at the fixed point.

children.title: Adaptive Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Relaxation policies selected from observed iteration behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded residual-driven selection of a varying scalar relaxation parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(T:C\to C\), \(x_0\in C\), bounds \(0<\omega_{\min}\leq\omega_{\max}\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), define \(r_n=Tx_n-x_n\). Before step \(n\), choose \(\omega_n\in[\omega_{\min},\omega_{\max}]\) as a measurable function of the observed history \((x_0,r_0,\ldots,x_n,r_n)\), subject to any feasibility requirement \(x_n+\omega_nr_n\in C\), and set
\[x_{n+1}=x_n+\omega_nr_n.\]
Stop and output \(x_n\) when \(\lVert r_n\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). Adaptivity alone gives no convergence guarantee; a convergence theorem must additionally constrain \(T\), the admissible interval, and the selection policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive relaxation chooses each safeguarded step length from observed residual history. The update is explicit, but convergence requires operator-specific restrictions beyond adaptivity itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm produces \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\omega_n(Tx_n-x_n)\) and terminates at the declared residual tolerance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a valid abstract template for history-dependent relaxation, but it does not identify a standard adaptive policy and supplies no authoritative algorithmic locator.

children.title: Scheduled Relaxation Families
children.top_down_role: Scheduled families of relaxation parameters.

children.title: Cyclic Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Relaxation schedules that cycle through a prescribed finite pattern.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation obtained by repeatedly traversing a prescribed finite ordered list of parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(T:C\to C\), \(x_0\in C\), an ordered list \((\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_{p-1})\) with \(p\geq1\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), define \(r_n=Tx_n-x_n\) and update
\[x_{n+1}=x_n+\omega_{n\bmod p}r_n.\]
The order of the list is part of the algorithm. Every generated point must belong to \(C\); this is automatic for \(0<\omega_j\leq1\) when \(C\) is convex, but otherwise requires separate invariance. Stop and output \(x_n\) when \(\lVert r_n\rVert\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cyclic relaxation repeatedly applies an ordered finite list of relaxation parameters. The ordering, feasibility conditions, residual test, and cycle length are part of the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation parameter at iteration \(n\) is \(\omega_{n\bmod p}\), and the schedule repeats after every \(p\) steps.

notation.meaning: Length of the cyclic parameter list.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and cyclic update are internally coherent, but an authoritative source is required to confirm that this ordered periodic schedule is the intended meaning of cyclic relaxation in this context.

children.title: Periodic Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Relaxation schedules organized by recurring parameter behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed fixed-point iteration whose scalar parameter sequence has a fixed positive period.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:C\to C\) and let \((\omega_n)_{n\geq0}\) be a scalar sequence. The iteration
\[x_{n+1}=(1-\omega_n)x_n+\omega_nTx_n\]
is periodic relaxation of period \(p\geq1\) if \(\omega_{n+p}=\omega_n\) for every \(n\geq0\). Its fundamental period is the least positive integer satisfying this identity. A constant relaxation is the special case with fundamental period one. The definition specifies temporal repetition only; convergence additionally depends on \(T\), the parameter values, and preservation of the domain \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic relaxation uses a parameter sequence repeating every p iterations. Constant relaxation has period one, while convergence depends on the map and chosen parameter values.
assumptions_latex: The displayed update is well-defined in \(C\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation schedule repeats with period \(p\), with fundamental period equal to its least positive period.

notation.meaning: A positive period of the relaxation sequence.
Relaxation parameter used at iteration n.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly describes a periodic scalar schedule and distinguishes a fundamental period, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Schedule-Period Effects
children.top_down_role: Acceleration behavior associated with the length and structure of recurring schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Period Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-period error propagation for scalar-relaxed affine linear fixed-point iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(x)=Mx+c\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(x_\star=Mx_\star+c\), and use a period-\(p\) relaxation schedule \((\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_{p-1})\). With \(e_n=x_n-x_\star\), one complete period satisfies
\[e_{n+p}=P_p(M)e_n,\qquad P_p(z)=\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}\bigl(1-\omega_j+\omega_jz\bigr).\]
Consequently, asymptotic contraction sampled once per period requires \(\rho(P_p(M))<1\). If \(M\) is normal, then \(\lVert P_p(M)\rVert_2=\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(M)}|P_p(\lambda)|\), so period design is a polynomial minimax problem over the spectrum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For affine linear maps, one schedule period applies a polynomial in the iteration matrix. Its spectral radius determines contraction at period boundaries.
assumptions_latex: The scalar relaxation schedule has period \(p\)
For the norm identity, \(M\) is normal
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{n+p}=P_p(M)e_n\), and period-boundary convergence is governed by \(\rho(P_p(M))\).

notation.meaning: Spectrum of the linear iteration matrix.
