children.title: Least-Squares Realizations
children.top_down_role: Numerically distinct realizations of the Anderson fitting problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Realizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent constrained-coefficient and residual-difference realizations of the Anderson fitting problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given residuals \(f_{k-m},\ldots,f_k\), let \(F=[f_{k-m},\ldots,f_k]\) and \(Y=[f_{k-m+1}-f_{k-m},\ldots,f_k-f_{k-1}]\). The constrained Anderson fit
\[
\alpha^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\alpha=1}\|F\alpha\|_2
\]
is algebraically equivalent to the unconstrained difference fit
\[
\gamma^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\gamma}\|f_k-Y\gamma\|_2.
\]
The coefficients are related by \(\alpha_0=\gamma_1\), \(\alpha_j=\gamma_{j+1}-\gamma_j\) for \(1\le j<m\), and \(\alpha_m=1-\gamma_m\). QR, SVD, or normal-equation solvers realize the same exact problem, although their finite-precision stability differs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anderson’s constrained affine residual fit and its unconstrained residual-difference fit are equivalent; QR, SVD, and normal equations are numerical realizations.
assumptions_latex: At least two consecutive residuals are available.
Both formulations use the same Euclidean norm and unregularized objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed coefficient transformation maps the minimizers of one least-squares formulation to minimizers of the other.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: telescoping coefficient transformation between the two standard Anderson least-squares forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient transformation is algebraically consistent and representation is appropriate. An Anderson-specific source is still required, particularly for the claim grouping QR, SVD, and normal equations as realizations under potentially rank-deficient data.

children.title: History Governance Policy System
children.top_down_role: Policies governing retained and reused history information.

children.title: History Selection
children.top_down_role: Policies choosing which past information enters the acceleration subproblem.

knowledge_statements.title: History Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic selection of a bounded Anderson history before least-squares fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given candidate pairs \(\mathcal H_k=\{(s_i,y_i):0\le i<k\}\), memory budget \(m\), and a deterministic score \(q_k(i)\), choose
\[
I_k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{I\subseteq\{0,\ldots,k-1\},\ |I|\le m}\sum_{i\in I}q_k(i),
\]
with a fixed tie-breaking rule. Form \(S_k=[s_i]_{i\in I_k}\) and \(Y_k=[y_i]_{i\in I_k}\), solve the prescribed Anderson least-squares problem using only these columns, and output the resulting accelerated iterate. The common recency policy is recovered with \(q_k(i)=i+1\), which selects the newest \(\min\{m,k\}\) pairs. Selection precedes any rank or conditioning filter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history-selection policy chooses at most the memory budget's worth of secant pairs by a fixed score, then fits Anderson using only them; strictly positive increasing scores recover the usual newest-pairs policy.
assumptions_latex: A finite set of candidate secant pairs is available.
The score and tie-breaking rule are fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fitting matrices contain exactly the selected columns and have at most \(m\) columns.

notation.meaning: Candidate Anderson history at iteration k.
Selection score of history pair i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract bounded-memory selection policy stated as a deterministic optimization rule
source needed for canonical Anderson history-governance terminology

children.title: History Filtering
children.top_down_role: Policies excluding low-quality, redundant, or unstable history.

knowledge_statements.title: History Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential rejection of unusable or nearly dependent Anderson history columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given ordered candidate columns \((s_i,y_i)\), tolerance \(\tau>0\), and an initially empty accepted matrix \(Q\), inspect candidates in the policy order. Reject \((s_i,y_i)\) if \(\|y_i\|_2=0\). Otherwise compute
\[
z_i=y_i-Q(Q^{\mathsf T}y_i).
\]
Accept the pair only if \(\|z_i\|_2\ge\tau\|y_i\|_2\); upon acceptance append \(z_i/\|z_i\|_2\) to \(Q\) and append \((s_i,y_i)\) to the filtered history. Stop after reaching the memory budget or exhausting candidates. The Anderson least-squares problem is then formed from the accepted pairs only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: History filtering rejects zero or nearly dependent residual-difference columns before forming the Anderson least-squares problem.
assumptions_latex: Candidates are processed in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted \(y_i\) has relative orthogonal component at least \(\tau\), while rejected pairs are excluded from the fit.

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis for accepted residual differences.
Component of the candidate orthogonal to accepted columns.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relative linear-independence filter for least-squares histories

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically well specified in exact arithmetic and fits History Filtering, but no Anderson-specific source supports this particular relative-independence filter as the intended method.

children.title: History Recycling
children.top_down_role: Policies reusing retained information across acceleration windows or restarts.

knowledge_statements.title: History Recycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse of accepted secant pairs across restarts or related fixed-point solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal R\) be a stored set of pairs \((s_i,y_i)\) from an earlier phase, and let \(f\) be the residual map in the current phase. For each stored step \(s_i\), recompute or validate the current secant image
\[
\widehat y_i=f(x_{\mathrm{ref}}+s_i)-f(x_{\mathrm{ref}}).
\]
Retain the recycled pair only if it passes the current compatibility, rank, and conditioning tests. Merge accepted recycled pairs with newly generated pairs, apply the current memory budget and selection order, solve the resulting Anderson least-squares problem, and output the accelerated iterate. A pair whose old residual difference is not valid for the current residual map must not be reused without recomputation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: History recycling reuses earlier step directions only after their residual differences are validated or recomputed for the current fixed-point problem.
assumptions_latex: Stored step directions and a current reference point are available.
The current residual map can be evaluated at the required points.
Current selection, rank, and conditioning tests are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only pairs valid for the current residual map enter the recycled Anderson fitting matrices.

notation.meaning: Current reference point for secant validation.
Residual difference recomputed in the current phase.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: secant information is transferable only when compatible with the current residual map
recycling semantics and validation criterion require a dedicated source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the leaf, but the proposed recomputation at a current reference point defines a new secant pair rather than automatically validating the old one. A dedicated source and explicit compatibility criterion are needed.

children.title: History-Policy Interactions
children.top_down_role: Interactions among retention, exclusion, and reuse policies.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Policy Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-sensitive interaction among selection, filtering, recycling, and memory constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C_k\) be the union of newly generated and validated recycled pairs. A history-governance policy is the ordered composition
\[
\mathcal C_k\xrightarrow{\text{compatibility}}\mathcal V_k
\xrightarrow{\text{selection}}\mathcal S_k
\xrightarrow{\text{rank/conditioning filter}}\mathcal A_k,
\qquad |\mathcal A_k|\le m.
\]
Because selection scores and rank tests depend on the current candidate set, these operations generally do not commute: filtering before selection may produce a different accepted span from selecting before filtering, and recycled columns may displace recent columns under a shared budget. Therefore the operation order, tie-breaking rules, and whether rejected slots are refilled are part of the mathematical specification of the Anderson method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: History governance is order-sensitive: selection, filtering, recycling, and budget enforcement can produce different accepted subspaces when reordered.
assumptions_latex: Every policy stage is deterministic, including tie breaking.
Selection or filtering depends on the candidates presented to that stage.
A finite memory budget \(m\) is enforced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted history \(\mathcal A_k\), and hence the Anderson update, can depend on the ordering of policy stages.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set-dependent selection and rank filtering are generally noncommutative
source needed for Anderson-specific policy interaction claims

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle is an appropriate kind and the claim is plausibly stated as a possible order dependence, but the particular governance pipeline and Anderson-specific interaction claims have no inspectable support.

children.title: Rank-Conditioning Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms for dependent, ill-conditioned, or noisy histories.

children.title: Rank Control
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms managing dependent or nearly dependent history.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical-rank truncation of the Anderson residual-difference matrix before fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an Anderson residual-difference matrix \(Y_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), let \(q=\min\{n,p\}\) and compute a compact singular value decomposition
\[
Y_k=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_q)V^{\mathsf T},
\qquad \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q\ge0,
\]
where the columns of \(V\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\) are right singular vectors. For an absolute tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm a}\ge0\) and relative tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm r}\ge0\), set
\[
r=\max\{j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:\sigma_j>\max(\tau_{\mathrm a},\tau_{\mathrm r}\sigma_1)\},
\]
with \(r=0\) if the set is empty. Solve the Anderson least-squares problem in the retained right-singular subspace \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\), and output the corresponding update. This caps the effective history rank at \(r\) and discards numerically unresolved directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank control uses a compact singular value decomposition to discard residual-difference directions below absolute or relative singular-value tolerances.
assumptions_latex: At least one of \(\tau_{\mathrm a}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm r}\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Anderson fit is restricted to a subspace of numerical rank \(r\), containing only singular directions above the prescribed threshold.

notation.meaning: Singular values of the residual-difference matrix.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard truncated-SVD numerical-rank rule applied to Anderson least squares

children.title: Regularization
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms stabilizing ill-conditioned or noisy acceleration subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tikhonov stabilization of the Anderson least-squares coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the current residual \(f_k=G(x_k)-x_k\), history matrices \(\Delta X_k,\Delta F_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times m_k}\), and \(\lambda>0\), compute
\[\gamma_k=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{m_k}}\bigl\|f_k-\Delta F_k\gamma\bigr\|_2^2+\lambda\|\gamma\|_2^2=(\Delta F_k^{\mathsf T}\Delta F_k+\lambda I)^{-1}\Delta F_k^{\mathsf T}f_k.\]
Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+f_k-(\Delta X_k+\Delta F_k)\gamma_k\), append the new iterate and residual, discard data exceeding the prescribed history depth, and repeat until the chosen residual or step tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each step, solve the ridge-regularized Anderson coefficient problem, use its unique coefficients in the difference-form Anderson update, refresh the bounded history, and continue until the selected stopping tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is evaluable at every generated iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta F_k^{\mathsf T}\Delta F_k+\lambda I\succ0\), so \(\gamma_k\) is uniquely defined.

notation.meaning: fixed-point residual at the current iterate
stored iterate and residual difference matrices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard ridge-regularized type-II Anderson realization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Rank–Conditioning Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between retained numerical rank and subproblem conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Conditioning Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tradeoff induced by truncated-SVD rank selection in Anderson least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Delta F=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_q)V^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q>0\), and let \(V_r\) contain the first \(r\) right singular vectors. Define
\[\phi_r=\min_{z\in\mathbb R^r}\|f-\Delta F V_rz\|_2,\qquad \kappa_r=\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_r}.\]
For \(1\le r<q\), one has \(\phi_{r+1}\le\phi_r\) and \(\kappa_{r+1}\ge\kappa_r\). Thus retaining more history directions cannot worsen the fitted residual but can worsen coefficient sensitivity; truncation reverses these effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing retained rank improves or preserves residual fitting but admits smaller singular directions and therefore worsens or preserves conditioning.

notation.meaning: positive singular values of the residual-difference matrix
best residual fit using the leading r singular directions
condition number of the retained singular spectrum

children.title: Metric-Conditioning Interface
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for residual scaling and preconditioned acceleration.

children.title: Residual Scaling
children.top_down_role: Scaling choices for residual components and least-squares geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left scaling of Anderson residuals and residual differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a nonsingular scaling matrix \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). At iteration \(k\), form \(\widehat f_k=Sf_k\) and \(\Delta\widehat F_k=S\Delta F_k\), then solve
\[\gamma_k\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{m_k}}\|\widehat f_k-\Delta\widehat F_k\gamma\|_2.
\]
Use these coefficients in the original-coordinate update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+f_k-(\Delta X_k+\Delta F_k)\gamma_k\). Equivalently, the coefficient problem minimizes \(\|f_k-\Delta F_k\gamma\|_M\) for \(M=S^{\mathsf T}S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual scaling changes the metric used to select Anderson coefficients while leaving the fixed-point equation and original-coordinate update unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(f_k=G(x_k)-x_k\) and the history matrices have compatible dimensions.

children.title: Acceleration Preconditioning
children.top_down_role: Preconditioned interfaces for fixed-point acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anderson acceleration under an invertible linear change of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, set \(y=Px\), and define \(\widetilde G(y)=PG(P^{-1}y)\). Then
\[\widetilde f(y)=\widetilde G(y)-y=P\bigl(G(P^{-1}y)-P^{-1}y\bigr)=Pf(P^{-1}y).
\]
Applying Anderson acceleration to \(\widetilde G\) in Euclidean residual norm and mapping back by \(x=P^{-1}y\) produces the original-coordinate Anderson update whose coefficients minimize \(\|f_k-\Delta F_k\gamma\|_{P^{\mathsf T}P}\). Fixed points correspond bijectively under \(y=Px\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible coordinate preconditioner preserves fixed points and converts Euclidean Anderson acceleration into weighted-residual Anderson acceleration in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=G(x)\iff Px=\widetilde G(Px)\), with residual metric \(P^{\mathsf T}P\).

children.title: Metric-Sensitive Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Conditioning behavior induced by scaling or preconditioned metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Sensitive Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning of Anderson history measured in a weighted residual metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(D=\Delta F_k\) have full column rank. The weighted least-squares normal matrix is \(H_M=D^{\mathsf T}MD\), and
\[\kappa_M(D)=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(H_M)}{\lambda_{\min}(H_M)}}=\kappa_2(M^{1/2}D).
\]
Moreover,
\[\sqrt{\kappa_2(M)^{-1}}\,\kappa_2(D)\le\kappa_M(D)\le\sqrt{\kappa_2(M)}\,\kappa_2(D).
\]
Hence a metric may improve or degrade history conditioning according to its alignment with the residual-difference subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Anderson conditioning equals the Euclidean conditioning of scaled residual differences and can improve or degrade according to metric alignment.
assumptions_latex: \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_M(D)=\kappa_2(M^{1/2}D)\), subject to the displayed metric-dependent bounds.

notation.meaning: history condition number in metric M

children.title: History Resource Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Cost comparisons across depth, storage, factorization, and operator-evaluation regimes.

children.title: History Memory Requirements
children.top_down_role: Storage consumed by retained iterates, residuals, and factors.

knowledge_statements.title: History Memory Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense storage cost for depth-limited Anderson history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For iterates in \(\mathbb R^n\) and maximum history depth \(m\), a difference-form Anderson implementation stores the current iterate and residual together with at most \(m\) columns of each of \(\Delta X_k\) and \(\Delta F_k\). When the history is stored or allocated at full depth, these arrays require \(2nm+2n\) scalars. Retaining a dense \(m\)-dimensional factorization or Gram matrix adds \(O(m^2)\) scalars; if coefficients are recomputed without retaining it, that auxiliary term is omitted. Thus the worst-case history storage is
\[O(nm+m^2),\]
excluding storage internal to evaluating \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-m dense Anderson implementation uses at most two n-by-m history matrices and two current vectors, plus optional quadratic storage for a small dense factorization, giving worst-case storage O(nm+m²).
assumptions_latex: Iterates and residuals belong to \(\mathbb R^n\).
At most \(m\) history differences are retained.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct dense-array worst-case storage count
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Acceleration Work Requirements
children.top_down_role: Computational work from subproblem formation, factorization, and operator evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Work Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense arithmetic cost of one Anderson acceleration step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With residual-difference matrix \(\Delta F_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times m_k}\), a fresh dense QR solution of the Anderson least-squares problem costs \(O(nm_k^2+m_k^3)\) arithmetic operations, while forming the accelerated combination costs \(O(nm_k)\). A rank-one QR update for a sliding history reduces the linear-algebra overhead to \(O(nm_k+m_k^2)\) per iteration. These counts exclude the application of \(G\), whose cost is denoted \(C_G(n)\). Consequently the total per-step cost is \(C_G(n)\) plus the selected history-maintenance cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fresh dense least-squares solve costs O(nm²+m³); updated factorizations can reduce the per-step acceleration overhead to O(nm+m²).
assumptions_latex: Dense arithmetic is used with \(m_k\le m\ll n\).

notation.meaning: active history depth at iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dense QR and rank-one update operation counts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fresh dense bound is a valid upper bound, but the sliding-history rank-one QR update cost depends on the precise update/downdate implementation. An inspectable implementation-specific source is needed before accepting the combined complexity claim.

children.title: Memory–Work Exchange
children.top_down_role: Resource tradeoffs created by history depth and numerical realization.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory–Work Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource effect of changing the retained Anderson history depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\) be the maximum retained history depth in a dense Anderson implementation. Increasing \(m\) enlarges the coefficient search space, so the unregularized least-squares residual minimum cannot increase when the stored subspaces are nested. Simultaneously, difference-form storage grows as \(O(nm+m^2)\); a fresh QR solve grows as \(O(nm^2+m^3)\), whereas updated factors require \(O(nm+m^2)\) work per step. Restarting or truncating the history lowers both resources but may discard directions responsible for residual reduction. No monotone improvement of the actual nonlinear iteration count follows from increasing \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Longer nested histories improve least-squares fitting but consume more storage and algebra; they need not monotonically reduce nonlinear iteration counts.
assumptions_latex: The compared history subspaces are nested.
Dense storage and dense least-squares arithmetic are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\uparrow\) gives a nonincreasing fitted residual but increasing memory and linear-algebra bounds.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nested least-squares spaces and dense resource counts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested-subspace fitting claim is correct, but the record incorporates the unverified updated-factor work bound. That implementation-dependent component requires a specific source.

children.title: Anderson Convergence Theory
children.top_down_role: Convergence and improvement results organized by linearity, smoothness, contractivity, and globalization.

children.title: Affine-Linear Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Krylov-compatible convergence and stagnation regimes.

children.title: Linear Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Anderson convergence and stagnation behavior for linear maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Anderson Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-memory Anderson correspondence for a homogeneous linear fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x)=Ax\), \(B=I-A\), and \(r_0=-Bx_0\). At step \(k\), full-memory Anderson acceleration chooses coefficients \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^k\alpha_i=1\) minimizing \(\|\sum_{i=0}^k\alpha_i(G(x_i)-x_i)\|_2\), defines \(\bar x_k=\sum_{i=0}^k\alpha_i x_i\), and sets \(x_{k+1}=G(\bar x_k)\). If the associated GMRES process for \(Bx=0\) does not stagnate through step \(k\), then \(\bar x_k\) is its step-\(k\) residual-minimizing iterate in \(x_0+\mathcal K_k(B,r_0)\), and \(x_{k+1}=A\bar x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without Krylov stagnation, full-memory Anderson extrapolates to the corresponding GMRES iterate and then applies the linear fixed-point map.
assumptions_latex: Full history is retained and the coefficient problem is solved exactly.
GMRES for \((I-A)x=0\) does not stagnate through step \(k\).

notation.meaning: affine Anderson extrapolate before applying G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed full-memory Anderson–GMRES correspondence is convention- and index-sensitive. An authoritative theorem locator is required to verify that the stated nonstagnation hypothesis and indexing yield exactly these identities.

children.title: Affine Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Anderson behavior for shifted linear fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Anderson Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-memory Anderson correspondence for an affine fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x)=Ax+b\), \(B=I-A\), and \(r_0=b-Bx_0\). Apply full-memory Anderson acceleration by minimizing the Euclidean norm of an affine combination of all available fixed-point residuals, forming the corresponding extrapolate \(\bar x_k\), and setting \(x_{k+1}=G(\bar x_k)\). If GMRES applied to \(Bx=b\) from \(x_0\) does not stagnate through step \(k\), then
\[\bar x_k=x_k^{\mathrm{GMRES}}\in x_0+\mathcal K_k(B,r_0),\qquad x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{AA}}=Ax_k^{\mathrm{GMRES}}+b.
\]
Thus Anderson inherits GMRES residual minimization at its extrapolation stage under the nonstagnation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For affine maps, nonstagnating full-memory Anderson extrapolates to the GMRES iterate for the associated linear system, then applies the affine map.
assumptions_latex: Full history is retained and coefficient minimizations are exact.
GMRES for \((I-A)x=b\) does not stagnate through step \(k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine correspondence is plausible but inherits the indexing and nonstagnation subtleties of the Anderson–GMRES theorem. A specific authoritative theorem locator is required.

children.title: Affine-Shift Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Transfer of linear Anderson insights to affine fixed-point dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Shift Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of affine Anderson iteration to its homogeneous error dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x)=Ax+b\) and suppose \(x_\star=Ax_\star+b\). Under the translation \(e=x-x_\star\),
\[G(x)-x=(A-I)e,\qquad G(x)-x_\star=Ae.
\]
For any affine coefficients satisfying \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), one has \(\sum_i\alpha_i x_i-x_\star=\sum_i\alpha_i e_i\), and the residual combination equals \((A-I)\sum_i\alpha_i e_i\). Hence unregularized Anderson coefficients are translation invariant, and Anderson acceleration of \(G\) is exactly Anderson acceleration of the homogeneous error map \(e\mapsto Ae\), translated by \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifting an affine fixed-point problem by any fixed point converts it to homogeneous linear error dynamics without changing Anderson coefficients.
assumptions_latex: Anderson coefficients satisfy the affine constraint \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\).

notation.meaning: a fixed point of the affine map
error coordinate x minus the fixed point

children.title: Krylov Stagnation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Linear or affine regimes associated with Krylov-compatible stagnation.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Stagnation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvable affine problem where Krylov and Anderson histories stagnate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad G(x)=(I-B)x+b,
\]
and start from \(x_0=0\). The fixed-point equation is the solvable system \(Bx=b\), whose solutions satisfy \(x_2=1\). However, \(r_0=b\) and \(Br_0=0\), so every Krylov space \(\mathcal K_k(B,r_0)\) equals \(\operatorname{span}\{r_0\}\), on which the residual cannot be reduced. The generated fixed-point residuals remain equal to \(b\), hence every residual-difference column vanishes. Unregularized Anderson acceleration therefore has rank-zero history and cannot obtain a reducing direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solvable two-dimensional affine problem can have a one-dimensional stagnant Krylov space and zero Anderson residual differences, preventing acceleration.
assumptions_latex: GMRES and Anderson acceleration start from \(x_0=0\).
Anderson uses differences of generated fixed-point residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta F_k=0\) and the Anderson least-squares history supplies no residual-reducing direction for every \(k\ge1\).

notation.meaning: Krylov space generated by B and r_0

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: concrete example is directly algebraically checkable

children.title: Smooth Contractive Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Local and global analyses for smooth contractive maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Contractive Anderson Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local model of bounded-coefficient Anderson mixing near a smooth contractive fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:U\to\mathbb R^n\) have a fixed point \(x_\star\), be Fréchet differentiable at \(x_\star\), and satisfy \(\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\) on \(U\), where \(0\le q<1\). For nearby iterates \(x_{k-i}\), choose coefficients satisfying \(\sum_{i=0}^{m}\alpha_i=1\) and \(\sum_{i=0}^{m}|\alpha_i|\le M\), and set \(y_k=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\alpha_iT(x_{k-i})\). With \(J=T'(x_\star)\) and \(e_j=x_j-x_\star\), \[y_k-x_\star=J\sum_{i=0}^{m}\alpha_i e_{k-i}+o\!\left(\max_{0\le i\le m}\|e_{k-i}\|\right).\] Thus local acceleration is governed by the Anderson polynomial acting on \(J\), while the nonlinear modeling defect is higher order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a smooth contractive fixed point, bounded Anderson mixing follows the corresponding affine-linear iteration up to a higher-order error.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is contractive and Fréchet differentiable at \(x_\star\).
\(x_{k-i}\to x_\star\) for every retained history index.

notation.meaning: derivative of T at the fixed point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order expansion with uniformly bounded affine coefficients

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-coefficient first-order expansion is plausible, but no inspectable source supports the Anderson-specific interpretation, and the stated update alone does not establish a polynomial iteration in J.

children.title: Nonsmooth Contractive Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes without differentiable local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Contractive Anderson Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantee using contraction and coefficient control, without derivatives or local Taylor models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to X\) be a contraction on a Banach space with modulus \(q<1\) and fixed point \(x_\star\). Given retained iterates \(x_{k-i}\), form \(y_k=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\alpha_iT(x_{k-i})\), where \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\) and \(\sum_i|\alpha_i|\le M\). Then \[\|y_k-x_\star\|\le qM\max_{0\le i\le m}\|x_{k-i}-x_\star\|.\] Consequently, if every update uses this form and \(qM<1\), the sliding-window maximum error contracts geometrically. This conclusion requires no differentiability of \(T\); coefficient boundedness replaces control obtained from a smooth local model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsmooth contraction, Anderson mixing converges under a uniform coefficient bound strong enough that the product of contraction and coefficient bounds is below one.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(T\) is a \(q\)-contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|y_k-x_\star\|\le qM\max_i\|x_{k-i}-x_\star\|\), yielding geometric window contraction when \(qM<1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contraction inequality and bounded affine mixing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed contraction bound is correct, but the geometric rate occurs over history-length blocks rather than necessarily at every iteration. An Anderson-specific source should confirm the intended convergence formulation.

children.title: Globalized Nonexpansive Anderson Theory
children.top_down_role: Safeguarded convergence beyond strict contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Globalized Nonexpansive Anderson Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of Anderson candidates globalized by a uniform Fejér-decrease safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be averaged, and suppose \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\). At iteration \(k\), either accept an Anderson candidate \(z_k\) satisfying \[\|z_k-p\|^2\le\|x_k-p\|^2-c\|x_k-Tx_k\|^2\quad\text{for every }p\in F,\] with a constant \(c>0\), or take a relaxed fixed-point step whose averaged-operator inequality satisfies the same bound; set \(x_{k+1}\) to the selected point. Then \((x_k)\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(F\), \(\sum_k\|x_k-Tx_k\|^2<\infty\), and \(x_k\) converges weakly to a point of \(F\). In finite dimensions the convergence is strong.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive Anderson scheme converges globally when every accepted candidate or fallback step satisfies one uniform Fejér decrease inequality.
assumptions_latex: Every selected update satisfies the displayed Fejér decrease with one \(c>0\).
The standard demiclosedness property holds for \(I-T\).

children.title: Fast Base-Rate Acceleration Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary at which Anderson acceleration may fail to improve an already fast base method.

children.title: Superlinear Base-Rate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on useful acceleration when the baseline already converges superlinearly.

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Base-Rate Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-complexity boundary under explicit superlinear recurrence models of the same order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the base and accelerated error models satisfy \(e_{k+1}=C e_k^p\) and \(\widehat e_{k+1}=\widehat C\widehat e_k^p\), where \(p>1\), \(C,\widehat C>0\), \(C^{1/(p-1)}e_0<1\), and \(\widehat C^{1/(p-1)}\widehat e_0<1\). Their iteration counts for reaching error at most \(\varepsilon\) satisfy \[k(\varepsilon),\widehat k(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\log_p\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0,\] and \(\widehat k(\varepsilon)-k(\varepsilon)=O(1)\). Thus changing constants while preserving the superlinear order does not improve the leading iteration-complexity order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under explicit superlinear recurrence models with the same order, changing only constants alters the asymptotic iteration count by at most a bounded additive amount.
assumptions_latex: \(e_{k+1}=C e_k^p\) and \(\widehat e_{k+1}=\widehat C\widehat e_k^p\) with \(p>1\).
Both recurrence models use the same convergence order \(p\).

children.title: Quadratic Base-Rate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on useful acceleration when the baseline already has quadratic local behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Base-Rate Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No asymptotic order gain when acceleration changes constants in an explicit quadratic recurrence model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the base and accelerated errors satisfy \(e_{k+1}=C e_k^2\) and \(\widehat e_{k+1}=\widehat C\widehat e_k^2\), where \(C,\widehat C>0\), \(Ce_0<1\), and \(\widehat C\widehat e_0<1\). Then their iteration counts for reaching error at most \(\varepsilon\) satisfy \[k(\varepsilon),\widehat k(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\log_2\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right),\qquad \widehat k(\varepsilon)-k(\varepsilon)=O(1).\] Thus changing the quadratic recurrence constant does not change the leading iteration-complexity order. If each accelerated step costs a fixed factor \(\gamma>1\) more than a base step, any cost advantage must arise from finite-accuracy constants rather than an improved asymptotic order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicit quadratic recurrence models, changing only the recurrence constant saves at most a bounded number of iterations and gives no asymptotic order improvement.
assumptions_latex: The accelerated-to-base per-step cost ratio \(\gamma>1\) is fixed when cost is compared.

children.title: Acceleration Benefit Crossover
children.top_down_role: Regimes where acceleration overhead or perturbation outweighs rate improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Benefit Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-aware crossover between conservative iteration budgets derived from linear error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the base and accelerated methods satisfy \(e_k^{\mathrm b}\le C_{\mathrm b}\rho_{\mathrm b}^k\) and \(e_k^{\mathrm a}\le C_{\mathrm a}\rho_{\mathrm a}^k\), where \(0<\rho_{\mathrm a}<\rho_{\mathrm b}<1\), and have positive per-step costs \(c_{\mathrm b}\) and \(c_{\mathrm a}\). For \(0<\varepsilon<\min\{C_{\mathrm a},C_{\mathrm b}\}\), define the sufficient step budgets \[N_j(\varepsilon)=\left\lceil\frac{\log(C_j/\varepsilon)}{-\log\rho_j}\right\rceil,\qquad j\in\{\mathrm a,\mathrm b\}.\] The error-bound cost model favors acceleration exactly when \[c_{\mathrm a}N_{\mathrm a}(\varepsilon)<c_{\mathrm b}N_{\mathrm b}(\varepsilon).\] Equality marks a crossover in these conservative cost bounds; the bounds alone do not determine the methods' actual stopping costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the linear error-bound cost model, acceleration is favored when its conservative iteration budget times its per-step cost is smaller than the corresponding base-method bound.
assumptions_latex: Both methods obey the displayed linear error bounds.
\(c_{\mathrm a}>0\) and \(c_{\mathrm b}>0\) are tolerance-independent per-step costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound-based model favors acceleration precisely when \(c_{\mathrm a}N_{\mathrm a}(\varepsilon)<c_{\mathrm b}N_{\mathrm b}(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: sufficient base and accelerated step budgets

children.title: Progress-Based Acceptance Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Acceptance families based on observable progress measures.

children.title: Residual Acceptance Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Candidate acceptance based on observed fixed-point residual progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Acceptance Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguard accepting an Anderson proposal only after prescribed fixed-point residual reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T:X\to X\), define \(r(x)=x-Tx\). Given \(x_k\), compute a base candidate \(b_k=Tx_k\) and an Anderson candidate \(z_k\) from the retained history. Fix \(\eta_k>0\), and update by \[x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}z_k,&\|r(z_k)\|\le\eta_k\|r(x_k)\|,\\ b_k,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Optionally restart the Anderson history after rejection. Stop when \(\|r(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon\), and return \(x_k\). A global convergence claim additionally requires the accepted and fallback steps to satisfy assumptions linking residual decrease to boundedness and fixed-point convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an Anderson proposal only when it reduces the fixed-point residual by the required factor; otherwise take the base step and optionally restart.
assumptions_latex: The residual \(r(x)=x-Tx\) is evaluable at trial points.
A base candidate and an Anderson candidate are available.
The tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) and thresholds \(\eta_k>0\) are specified.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and residual-test algorithm fit the leaf, but no inspectable source establishes this particular Anderson safeguard or its relationship to globalization assumptions.

children.title: Merit Acceptance Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Candidate acceptance based on problem-specific merit progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Merit Acceptance Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguard based on sufficient decrease of a merit function rather than residual norm alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:X\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below, let \(r(x)=x-Tx\), and let \(z_k\) be an Anderson trial point at \(x_k\). Choose \(\sigma>0\), compute a globally admissible base point \(b_k\), and set \[x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}z_k,&\Phi(z_k)\le\Phi(x_k)-\sigma\|r(x_k)\|^2,\\ b_k,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Stop when \(\|r(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon\). If the fallback step obeys the same sufficient-decrease inequality and every accepted step uses the displayed test, then \(\sum_k\|r(x_k)\|^2<\infty\), hence \(\|r(x_k)\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an Anderson trial only if it gives sufficient merit decrease; otherwise use a globally admissible base step.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is bounded below along the generated sequence.
Accepted and fallback steps satisfy the stated decrease with \(\sigma>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient-decrease telescoping claim is mathematically coherent and the algorithm fits the leaf, but the Anderson-specific merit safeguard has no cited source.

children.title: Acceptance-Criterion Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Cases where residual and merit assessments favor different candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceptance-Criterion Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual and merit acceptance can disagree when the merit function is not calibrated to fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) given by \(T(x)=0\), so the unique fixed point is \(0\) and \(|r(x)|=|x|\). Let \(\Phi(x)=(x-1)^2\). From \(x=1/2\), the trial \(z=1\) satisfies \(\Phi(z)=0<1/4=\Phi(x)\), yet \(|r(z)|=1>1/2=|r(x)|\); merit acceptance permits residual deterioration. Conversely, from \(x=1\), the trial \(z=1/2\) satisfies \(|r(z)|<|r(x)|\), yet \(\Phi(z)=1/4>0=\Phi(x)\). Thus neither criterion implies the other without a quantitative error-bound relation between \(\Phi\) and \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A merit function unrelated to the residual can accept residual deterioration or reject residual improvement, so the two safeguards are not interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Merit decrease and residual decrease imply neither one another for the displayed map and merit function.

children.title: History Reset Rank-Control Safeguards
children.top_down_role: History reset and rank-control families.

children.title: Restart Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Safeguards that reset accumulated acceleration history.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History reset triggered by rejection, excessive coefficients, or ill-conditioned residual differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a history \(\mathcal H_k\) of at most \(m\) iterate-residual pairs. Compute Anderson coefficients and a trial \(z_k\) from \(\mathcal H_k\). Given bounds \(M>0\) and \(\kappa_{\max}>0\), declare failure if the trial is rejected, if \(\|\alpha_k\|_1>M\), or if the retained residual-difference matrix \(F_k\) has \(\kappa(F_k)>\kappa_{\max}\). On failure set \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\) and \(\mathcal H_{k+1}=\{(x_{k+1},r(x_{k+1}))\}\); otherwise accept \(z_k\), append its pair, and discard the oldest pair when necessary. Stop when \(\|r(x_k)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart from a base step whenever an Anderson trial fails acceptance, its coefficients become excessive, or its residual-difference system becomes ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: A finite memory bound \(m\) is fixed.
Coefficient and conditioning thresholds \(M\) and \(\kappa_{\max}\) are specified.
The residual and base step are evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every detected instability replaces the Anderson update by \(Tx_k\) and resets the stored history to one current pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restart specification fits the leaf, but its combined rejection, coefficient, and conditioning triggers require an Anderson-specific source. The treatment of rank-deficient F_k through its condition number should also be sourced or explicitly defined.

children.title: Rank-Control Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Safeguards that restrict dependent or ill-conditioned history.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Control Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical-rank selection for the Anderson least-squares history matrix before computing mixing coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_k=U\Sigma V^\top\) be a singular value decomposition of the Anderson residual-difference matrix, with singular values \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_s\ge0\). Given \(\tau\in(0,1)\) and a memory cap \(m\ge1\), set \(r_k=0\) when \(s=0\) or \(\sigma_1=0\); otherwise choose \[r_k=\max\bigl\{j\in\{1,\ldots,\min(m,s)\}:\sigma_j\ge\tau\sigma_1\bigr\}.\] Solve the Anderson least-squares problem only in the span of the first \(r_k\) right singular vectors. If \(r_k=0\), take the base update \(x_{k+1}=T x_k\). When \(r_k>0\), the retained matrix has spectral condition number at most \(1/\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain only available singular directions above a relative threshold, solve Anderson mixing in that numerical-rank subspace, and use the base update when no direction remains.
assumptions_latex: The base fixed-point update \(x_{k+1}=T x_k\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r_k>0\), the retained spectral condition number is at most \(1/\tau\); if \(r_k=0\), the base update is taken.

children.title: Reset–Truncation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between discarding all history and retaining a controlled subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Reset–Truncation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic tradeoff between preserving Anderson history and controlling least-squares conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=[f_1,\ldots,f_m]\) be a full-column-rank residual-difference matrix and let \(F_S\) contain a nonempty subset of its columns. Then \(\operatorname{range}(F_S)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(F)\), so truncation reduces the correction subspace, while Cauchy interlacing for the principal Gram matrix gives \[\sigma_{\min}(F_S)\ge\sigma_{\min}(F).\] A complete reset discards every correction direction and therefore maximizes loss of multisecant information; selective truncation preserves a smaller correction space while potentially improving conditioning. Neither operation alone guarantees a better trial, because approximation quality depends on whether discarded directions contain useful residual information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resetting removes all multisecant information; truncation preserves part of it and cannot reduce the smallest singular value, but may discard useful correction directions.
assumptions_latex: \(F_S\) is formed by deleting columns of \(F\).
Conditioning is measured with Euclidean singular values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: column-subspace inclusion and Gram-matrix interlacing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The column-space inclusion and singular-value inequality are standard and correct under full column rank, but the Anderson-specific multisecant interpretation and reset–truncation tradeoff lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Baseline Globalization Interface
children.top_down_role: Globalization through reliable unaccelerated iterations.

children.title: Baseline Fallback
children.top_down_role: Use of an unaccelerated candidate when acceleration is rejected or unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Fallback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic safeguard reverting a rejected Anderson proposal to one step of a globally reliable baseline map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:D\to D\) be a baseline fixed-point map, let \(x_k\in D\), and let \(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}}\) be an Anderson proposal. Compute the baseline candidate \(b_k=G(x_k)\). Given an admissibility predicate \(\mathcal A_k:D\to\{0,1\}\) and a progress predicate \(\mathcal P_k:D\to\{0,1\}\), set
\[
x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}y_k^{\mathrm{AA}},&\mathcal A_k(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}})=1\text{ and }\mathcal P_k(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}})=1,\\ b_k,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
The algorithm outputs the first iterate satisfying a prescribed stopping test; every rejected, undefined, or inadmissible accelerated proposal therefore produces exactly the baseline update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an Anderson proposal only when it is admissible and passes the progress test; otherwise take the globally reliable baseline fixed-point step.
assumptions_latex: The baseline iteration is defined at every accepted iterate.
The predicates are computable before updating the iterate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Baseline Fallback leaf and is internally coherent, but no source identifies this predicate-based fallback as the intended safeguarded Anderson variant.

children.title: Baseline Interleaving
children.top_down_role: Scheduled insertion of unaccelerated iterations into an accelerated trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Interleaving
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic globalization that inserts baseline steps independently of accelerated-step acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:D\to D\), choose an integer period \(q\geq1\), and let \(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}}\) denote an available safeguarded Anderson candidate. Starting from \(x_0\in D\), update
\[
x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}G(x_k),&k+1\equiv0\pmod q,\\ y_k^{\mathrm{AA}},&k+1\not\equiv0\pmod q\text{ and the safeguard accepts }y_k^{\mathrm{AA}},\\ G(x_k),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
Stop when the prescribed residual or iteration-limit test holds. Thus every block of \(q\) updates contains a baseline step, while additional baseline steps may occur after rejected accelerated proposals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force a baseline update at least once every fixed number of iterations, using further baseline steps whenever the accelerated candidate is rejected.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted accelerated candidate lies in \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Among any \(q\) consecutive updates, at least one satisfies \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the fixed-period interleaving rule is one particular policy and has no supporting citation.

children.title: Fallback-Trigger Regimes
children.top_down_role: Observable regimes motivating a return to the baseline map.

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback-Trigger Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable regimes in which a safeguarded Anderson step must be replaced by the baseline update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}}\) be the Anderson proposal, \(r(x)=G(x)-x\), \(c_k\) its mixing-coefficient vector, and \(M_k\) a finite reference merit value. For fixed \(C_k<\infty\), \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\), trigger fallback whenever at least one predicate holds:
\[
y_k^{\mathrm{AA}}\notin D,\qquad \|c_k\|>C_k,\qquad \|r(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}})\|>\sigma M_k+\varepsilon_k,
\]
or whenever the proposal, coefficients, or residual are undefined or nonfinite. If no trigger holds, the proposal is eligible for any remaining acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fallback is triggered by infeasibility, nonfinite computations, excessive mixing coefficients, or failure of a prescribed residual-progress inequality.
assumptions_latex: The norm and thresholds are fixed before testing the proposal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any listed trigger forces the baseline candidate \(G(x_k)\) to replace \(y_k^{\mathrm{AA}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but the thresholds and residual test are an uncited template. Moreover, r(y_k^{AA}) is not defined when the preceding infeasibility trigger y_k^{AA} notin D holds unless the tests are explicitly ordered.

children.title: Nonmonotone Globalization
children.top_down_role: Globalization permitting controlled temporary deterioration.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Globalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed residual safeguard allowing temporary deterioration relative to the latest iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r(x)=G(x)-x\), choose a window length \(m\geq1\), \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), and errors \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\). Define
\[
R_k=\max_{\max\{0,k-m+1\}\leq j\leq k}\|r(x_j)\|.
\]
Given an admissible accelerated candidate \(y_k\), accept it when \(\|r(y_k)\|\leq\sigma R_k+\varepsilon_k\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\). On acceptance set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\). Stop under the prescribed residual or iteration-limit criterion. The comparison with \(R_k\), rather than only \(\|r(x_k)\|\), permits controlled temporary residual increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the accelerated candidate with the largest recent residual, permitting bounded temporary deterioration while rejecting candidates that exceed the windowed threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(G:D\to D\) and all accepted candidates belong to \(D\).
The residual norm is finite at stored iterates.
The error allowance is prescribed independently of the candidate.

notation.meaning: maximum residual norm over the current window

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The windowed rule correctly represents a possible nonmonotone globalization algorithm, but its precise maximum-residual acceptance formula and hypotheses require a specific source.

children.title: Halpern Anchoring Families
children.top_down_role: Classical and regularized ways of anchoring a fixed-point iteration.

children.title: Fixed-Anchor Halpern Iteration
children.top_down_role: The classical anchored fixed-point family.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Anchor Halpern Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Halpern iteration for a nonexpansive map with one fixed anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive, choose an anchor \(u\in C\), an initial point \(x_0\in C\), and weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\). The fixed-anchor Halpern iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)T x_k,
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots .
\]
After each update, stop if the prescribed residual test, such as \(\|x_{k+1}-Tx_{k+1}\|\leq\epsilon\), holds; otherwise continue. The returned point is the last computed iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iterate is a convex combination of one fixed anchor and the image of the current iterate under the nonexpansive map.

children.title: Robust Variable-Anchor Halpern Family
children.top_down_role: Anchor-sequence and perturbation-stable variants.

children.title: Variable-Anchor Halpern Iterations
children.top_down_role: Halpern variants using an evolving anchor sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Anchor Halpern Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern iteration whose anchor may vary with the iteration index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive, choose \(x_0\in C\), an anchor sequence \((u_k)_{k\geq0}\subset C\), and weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\). Compute
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u_k+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k,
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots .
\]
Stop when a prescribed fixed-point residual or iteration-limit test holds and return the latest iterate. Taking \(u_k=u\) for every \(k\) recovers the fixed-anchor Halpern iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the fixed Halpern anchor by a prescribed anchor sequence, forming a convex combination with the current mapped iterate at every step.

children.title: Perturbed Halpern Iterations
children.top_down_role: Halpern variants subject to deterministic iteration perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Halpern Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern updates with additive evaluation errors in the mapped component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a normed space, let \(T:C\to C\), choose \(x_0,u	del C\), weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\), and perturbations \(e_k\) such that \(Tx_k+e_k\in C\). The perturbed Halpern iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k),
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots .
\]
A variable-anchor version replaces \(u\) by \(u_k\in C\). Stop under the prescribed residual, perturbation-budget, or iteration-limit test, and return the latest iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed Halpern step uses an inexact map evaluation, optionally together with a varying anchor, while retaining a convex-combination update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update has the form \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k)\in C\).

notation.meaning: anchor, replaceable by a variable anchor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement contains the invalid command \tdel where \in is intended. More importantly, the placement and admissibility model for the perturbation are variant-dependent and uncited, so a reliable replacement cannot be selected without a source.

children.title: Anchor-Sequence Stability
children.top_down_role: Stability behavior associated with variation in the anchor sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Anchor-Sequence Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted summability condition controlling displacement from a limiting anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((u_k)_{k\geq0}\) be anchors in a normed space, let \(u\) be a reference anchor, and let \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\). The anchor sequence is stable relative to \((\alpha_k)\) and \(u\) when
\[
u_k\to u
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k\|u_k-u\|<\infty.
\]
For the variable-anchor Halpern update, the difference from the fixed-anchor update at the same point is exactly \(\alpha_k(u_k-u)\); hence stability makes these anchor-induced update deviations absolutely summable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anchors converge to a reference anchor and their weighted deviations are summable, so the cumulative change relative to fixed anchoring is finite.
assumptions_latex: The anchors and reference anchor lie in one normed space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted summability implication is correct from the displayed condition and the condition kind fits, but calling this particular conjunction the anchor-sequence stability regime requires source support.

children.title: Perturbation-Robust Anchoring
children.top_down_role: Anchoring regimes designed to tolerate controlled evaluation errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Robust Anchoring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence under summable evaluation errors and a stable variable anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and let \(u_k\to u\in C\). Define
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u_k+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k).
\]
If \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), \(\sum_k|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k\|u_k-u\|<\infty\), and \(\sum_k\|e_k\|<\infty\), with every update in \(C\), then \(x_k\to P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u\) strongly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable evaluation errors and weighted anchor deviations preserve strong Halpern convergence to the fixed point nearest the limiting anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive with a fixed point.
The displayed control sequence, anchor, and error conditions hold.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the fixed-point set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind matches the convergence leaf, but the exact strong-convergence result for simultaneous variable anchors and additive map errors is nontrivial. Its hypotheses and conclusion require an authoritative theorem-level citation.

children.title: Viscosity Approximation Families
children.top_down_role: Contractive anchoring mechanisms for strong convergence and solution selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Viscosity Approximation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contractive anchoring iteration selecting a distinguished fixed point of a nonexpansive map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive, and let \(f:C\to C\) be a contraction. Given \(x_0\in C\) and \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\), the explicit viscosity iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k f(x_k)+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k,
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots .
\]
Stop when a prescribed residual or iteration-limit test holds and return the latest iterate. The contractive term supplies a state-dependent anchor; replacing \(f(x_k)\) by a constant anchor recovers fixed-anchor Halpern iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Blend the nonexpansive fixed-point step with a contractive, state-dependent anchor that can select a distinguished fixed point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit viscosity update is a standard-looking algorithm and fits the container, but no source supports this selected member of the broader viscosity approximation family.

children.title: Tikhonov-Regularized Anchoring
children.top_down_role: Regularized anchoring mechanisms related to minimum-norm selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Tikhonov-Regularized Anchoring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing regularization toward the origin for minimum-norm fixed-point selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space containing \(0\), let \(T:C\to C\), choose \(x_0\in C\), and let \(\lambda_k\in(0,1)\). The zero-anchor Tikhonov-Halpern iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=(1-\lambda_k)Tx_k.
\]
Equivalently, \(x_{k+1}=\lambda_k0+(1-\lambda_k)Tx_k\), so the vanishing parameter regularizes the iteration toward the minimum-norm reference point. Stop when the prescribed residual or iteration-limit test holds and return the latest iterate. Nonzero reference regularization replaces \(0\) by a fixed \(u\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a vanishing zero-anchor regularization to the fixed-point step; this is the Halpern form associated with minimum-norm selection.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex with \(0\in C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The update is algebraically a zero-anchor Halpern step, but Tikhonov-regularized fixed-point iterations have multiple inequivalent formulations. A source is needed to justify this naming and formulation for the exact leaf.

children.title: Halpern Parameter Policies
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic, optimized, adaptive, horizon-free, and restarted parameter families.

children.title: Classical Vanishing-Anchor Schedules
children.top_down_role: Classical parameter families used in strong-convergence theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Vanishing-Anchor Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Halpern control conditions ensuring persistent but asymptotically vanishing anchoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\subset(0,1)\) is a classical vanishing-anchor schedule when
\[
\alpha_k\to0,
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty,
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty.
\]
The first condition makes anchoring asymptotically negligible, the second prevents its cumulative influence from being finite, and the third controls oscillation. Standard examples are \(\alpha_k=(k+2)^{-p}\) for \(0<p\leq1\); these sequences are decreasing, so their total variation is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anchor weights vanish, have divergent total mass, and have finite total variation; inverse-power schedules with exponent at most one are standard examples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule has vanishing weights, infinite cumulative weight, and finite total variation.

notation.meaning: Halpern anchor weight at iteration k

children.title: Worst-Case Optimized Halpern Schedules
children.top_down_role: Parameter families optimized for residual performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Optimized Halpern Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon schedule design for minimizing the normalized fixed-point residual of Halpern iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and fix an anchor \(u\in H\). For a horizon \(N\), a worst-case optimized Halpern schedule is any \(\alpha^*=(\alpha_0^*,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}^*)\in[0,1]^N\) satisfying
\[
\alpha^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in[0,1]^N}\ \sup_{T,u,x_0,x_*}\frac{\lVert x_N-Tx_N\rVert}{\lVert x_0-x_*\rVert+\lVert u-x_*\rVert},
\]
where \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\), \(x_*\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and the supremum ranges over all admissible instances with nonzero denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimized finite-horizon schedule minimizes the largest normalized residual attainable by any admissible nonexpansive fixed-point instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha^*\) minimizes the finite-horizon worst-case normalized residual within the prescribed schedule class.

children.title: Universal Adaptive Halpern Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies avoiding unavailable operator constants or advance horizon information.

children.title: Adaptive Halpern Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies adjusting anchoring parameters from observed iteration behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Halpern Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent selection of Halpern anchor weights from observed iterates and oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a set \(C\), an anchor \(u\in C\), an initial point \(x_0\in C\), and an oracle for \(T:C\to C\), define the history \(\mathcal H_k=(x_0,Tx_0,\ldots,x_k,Tx_k)\). An adaptive Halpern policy consists of maps \(\pi_k\) with \(\alpha_k=\pi_k(\mathcal H_k)\in[0,1]\), followed by
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k.
\]
The policy stops when a prescribed history-measurable test holds and outputs the current iterate or the iterate having the smallest observed residual \(\lVert x_j-Tx_j\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive policy chooses each anchor weight from information already observed, then performs the corresponding Halpern update.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex, so every displayed update remains in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\pi_k(\mathcal H_k)u+(1-\pi_k(\mathcal H_k))Tx_k\) is a causal Halpern iteration.

notation.meaning: oracle history available through iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The causal-history formulation is plausible and the algorithm kind fits, but no source establishes that this is the intended definition of adaptive Halpern policies or supports the proposed stopping and output rules.

children.title: Parameter-Free Halpern Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies avoiding unavailable operator constants or preset horizons.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Halpern Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern policies requiring no horizon or unknown quantitative problem constants as inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a class \(\mathfrak I\) of fixed-point instances, a Halpern policy is parameter-free relative to \(\mathfrak I\) if its initialization, weights, stopping tests, and output are determined solely by the iteration index and observed oracle history. Formally, there are fixed maps \(\pi_k\) such that
\[
\alpha_k=\pi_k(k,\mathcal H_k)\in[0,1],\qquad x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k,
\]
and neither \(\pi_k\) nor initialization takes as input a terminal horizon, contraction factor, error-bound constant, Lipschitz constant, or distance to \(\operatorname{Fix}T\) that is unknown on \(\mathfrak I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-free policy uses only the iteration count and observed oracle history, not an unknown horizon or problem constant.
assumptions_latex: A fixed instance class \(\mathfrak I\) specifies which quantities count as unknown.
The policy accesses \(T\) only through its stated oracle history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated weights and iterates are invariant under changes to unprovided horizon and problem-constant metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Parameter-free terminology depends on which horizon and problem data are excluded. An authoritative locator is needed to validate this particular definition and its list of unavailable constants.

children.title: Unknown-Horizon Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern scheduling when the iteration horizon is not fixed in advance.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Horizon Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime Halpern policies whose first iterations do not depend on a terminal horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family of horizon-indexed Halpern schedules \(\{\alpha_k^{(N)}:0\leq k<N\}\) is horizon-oblivious if it is prefix-consistent:
\[
\alpha_k^{(N)}=\alpha_k^{(M)}\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad k<\min\{N,M\}.
\]
Equivalently, a single infinite sequence \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) generates every finite run through \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\). In an unknown-horizon regime, termination may occur at any finite stopping time determined by observed history, and the returned iterate must be defined without retroactively changing earlier weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unknown-horizon policy is prefix-consistent: extending or shortening the run never changes weights already used.
assumptions_latex: Every finite run uses the same anchor \(u\), operator \(T\), and initial point \(x_0\).
Termination uses only information available when it occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each finite run is a prefix of one horizon-independent Halpern trajectory.

notation.meaning: weight used at step k by an N-horizon schedule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Prefix consistency is mathematically coherent, but no source confirms that it exactly characterizes the intended unknown-horizon regime, especially when adaptive history-dependent policies and stopping times are allowed.

children.title: Unknown-Constant Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern scheduling without reliable operator constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Constant Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policies independent of unavailable regularity constants while retaining a stated uniform guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{\mathfrak I_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) be fixed-point instance classes indexed by an unknown quantitative constant \(\theta\), such as a contraction factor or error-bound modulus. A Halpern policy operates in the unknown-constant regime if the same causal maps \(\pi_k\) are used for every \(\theta\):
\[
\alpha_k=\pi_k(\mathcal H_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k,
\]
with no direct access to \(\theta\). Any claimed residual guarantee must therefore hold simultaneously for every \(\theta\in\Theta\), although its evaluated bound may depend on the true instance constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same history-based policy is used for every unknown regularity constant, and its guarantee must hold uniformly over all admissible values.
assumptions_latex: The value of \(\theta\) is unavailable to the policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameter-selection maps are independent of \(\theta\), while any guarantee is quantified over all \(\theta\in\Theta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the asserted simultaneous guarantee and its dependence on the true constant require a cited formulation specifying the instance classes and quantifiers.

children.title: Restarted Halpern Policies
children.top_down_role: Restart families exploiting stronger regularity or contractivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Restarted Halpern Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phasewise Halpern iteration with anchors reset to exploit stronger residual regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose phase lengths \(m_s\geq1\) and within-phase weights \(\alpha_{s,j}\in[0,1]\). Initialize \(z_0=x_0\). In phase \(s\), set the new anchor and starting point to \(u_s=y_{s,0}=z_s\), then compute
\[
y_{s,j+1}=\alpha_{s,j}u_s+(1-\alpha_{s,j})Ty_{s,j},\qquad 0\leq j<m_s.
\]
Set \(z_{s+1}=y_{s,m_s}\) and begin the next phase. Stop after a prescribed number of phases or when \(\lVert z_s-Tz_s\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and output that \(z_s\). Phase lengths may be fixed or selected causally from observed residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting divides Halpern iteration into phases and makes each phase endpoint the next phase’s anchor and starting point.
assumptions_latex: All phase lengths are positive integers and all weights lie in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The phase endpoints \((z_s)\) form the restarted Halpern trajectory, with each phase anchored at its initial endpoint.

children.title: Halpern Geometric Regimes
children.top_down_role: Space and operator classes governing convergence, selection, and residual optimality.

children.title: Hilbert-Space Nonexpansive Regime
children.top_down_role: The principal strong-convergence and tight residual-analysis setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Nonexpansive Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence of classical Halpern iteration for a nonexpansive Hilbert-space mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and let \(u,x_0\in C\). Suppose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\), \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\). Then the Halpern iterates
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k
\]
converge strongly to \(P_Fu\), the metric projection of the anchor onto the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard vanishing, nonsummable, bounded-variation weights, Hilbert-space Halpern iterates converge in norm to the fixed point nearest the anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive with \(F\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: metric projection of u onto F

children.title: Extended Normed-Space Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometry-dependent extensions beyond Hilbert spaces.

children.title: Banach-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern iteration in complete normed spaces with geometry-dependent behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Banach-Space Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric hypotheses under which Banach-space Halpern convergence can replace Hilbert projection arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, \(C\subset X\) nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(T:C\to C\) nonexpansive with nonempty fixed-point set \(F\). A Banach-space Halpern regime supporting strong selection requires geometric assumptions ensuring a single-valued, sufficiently regular normalized duality map and a well-defined sunny nonexpansive retraction \(Q_F:C\to F\). With weights satisfying \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), and an appropriate regularity condition on successive weights, the intended selected limit is \(Q_Fu\), not generally a Hilbert metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Banach-space convergence requires additional smoothness or convexity geometry, and the selected fixed point is expressed through a sunny nonexpansive retraction.
assumptions_latex: The geometry of \(X\) makes the relevant duality map and sunny retraction well defined.
The anchor weights are vanishing, nonsummable, and suitably regular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Banach-space target selected by Halpern iteration is formulated as \(Q_Fu\) under the stated geometric hypotheses.

notation.meaning: normalized duality map of the Banach space
sunny nonexpansive retraction onto the fixed-point set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement uses indefinite conditions such as “sufficiently regular” and “appropriate regularity,” so it does not specify a checkable Banach-space regime. A source is needed to select exact geometric, retraction, and weight hypotheses.

children.title: General Normed-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Extensions formulated beyond Hilbert geometry in normed spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: General Normed-Space Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of transferring Hilbert-space Halpern selection and residual arguments to arbitrary normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In an arbitrary normed space \(X\), nonexpansiveness of \(T:C\to C\) and the scalar conditions \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\) do not by themselves supply the Hilbert identities used in strong-selection analyses. In particular, the identity
\[
\lVert x+y\rVert^2+\lVert x-y\rVert^2=2\lVert x\rVert^2+2\lVert y\rVert^2
\]
holds for every \(x,y\in X\) exactly when the norm is induced by an inner product. Without replacement assumptions controlling norm geometry, Hilbert projection and squared-distance arguments cannot be invoked for Halpern iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonexpansiveness and scalar weight conditions alone do not justify Hilbert projection arguments in a general normed space; additional geometry is necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space not assumed to be Hilbert.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hilbert-specific squared-norm and metric-projection arguments require additional geometric hypotheses on \(X\).

children.title: Hilbert-Geometry Departure
children.top_down_role: Analytical changes arising when Hilbert-space structure is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Geometry Departure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of the Hilbert parallelogram identity in non-Euclidean finite-dimensional Banach geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(\mathbb R^2,\lVert\cdot\rVert_p)\) with \(1\leq p<\infty\) and \(p\neq2\). For \(x=(1,0)\) and \(y=(0,1)\),
\[
\lVert x+y\rVert_p^2+\lVert x-y\rVert_p^2=2^{1+2/p},
\qquad
2\lVert x\rVert_p^2+2\lVert y\rVert_p^2=4.
\]
These quantities are unequal because \(p\neq2\). Thus even a two-dimensional complete normed space can lack the Hilbert squared-norm identity, so any Halpern residual derivation using that identity does not transfer verbatim to this geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In two-dimensional ℓp space with p unequal to 2, the parallelogram identity fails, blocking verbatim use of Hilbert squared-distance analyses.
