children.title: Horizon-Free Doubling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies avoiding a prescribed terminal iteration.

children.title: Adaptive-Horizon Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that select or extend the terminal horizon during execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Horizon Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A certificate-driven wrapper that chooses successive horizons without knowing the required terminal horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be a mapping on a Hilbert space, let \(r(x)=\lVert x-Tx\rVert\), and let \(\mathcal A(N;x)\) return a candidate after at most \(N\) evaluations of \(T\). Given \(x_0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and an increasing integer sequence \((N_j)_{j\geq 0}\), set \(j=0\). At phase \(j\), compute \(y_j=\mathcal A(N_j;x_0)\) and evaluate \(r(y_j)\). If \(r(y_j)\leq\varepsilon\), stop and output \(y_j\); otherwise choose \(N_{j+1}>N_j\) from the observed candidates and certificates and continue. Correctness requires only that some tested horizon produces residual at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run increasing finite-horizon accelerations and stop at the first candidate whose directly evaluated fixed-point residual meets the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) can be evaluated.
For some tested horizon, the base routine returns a candidate with residual at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: base routine run with horizon N from x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic interface and certificate-based stopping rule fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this adaptive-horizon policy or its assumptions.

children.title: Doubling Policies
children.top_down_role: Geometric horizon schedules for operation without a prescribed terminal iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Doubling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric horizon search using powers of two and direct residual certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\), \(r(x)=\lVert x-Tx\rVert\), and let \(\mathcal A(N;x_0)\) be a finite-horizon fixed-point routine. Given \(x_0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and initial horizon \(N_0\in\mathbb N\), define \(N_j=2^jN_0\). For \(j=0,1,2,\ldots\), compute \(y_j=\mathcal A(N_j;x_0)\), evaluate \(r(y_j)\), and stop at the first index \(J\) satisfying \(r(y_J)\leq\varepsilon\). Output \(y_J\). Each phase is restarted from \(x_0\), so the finite-horizon guarantee of \(\mathcal A\) applies independently at every tested horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test horizons N₀, 2N₀, 4N₀, and so on, restarting the base routine and stopping when the measured residual is small enough.
assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) and its residual are evaluable.
\(\mathcal A(N;x_0)\) is defined for every positive integer horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy terminates at some finite \(J\) and outputs \(y_J\) with \(r(y_J)\leq\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The doubling algorithm is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but the record provides no citation for the wrapper, restart convention, or termination premise.

children.title: Horizon-Overhead Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Complexity overhead attributable to online horizon selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Overhead Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle overhead of geometric horizon search relative to the first successful horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the doubling policy tests \(N_j=2^jN_0\) and stops at the first successful phase \(J\). If a run of \(\mathcal A(N;x_0)\), including its terminal residual test, costs at most \(cN+d\) oracle operations, then the cumulative cost is at most \(c\sum_{j=0}^{J}N_j+d(J+1)<2cN_J+d\bigl(1+\log_2(N_J/N_0)\bigr)\). If \(N_\star\) is the least sufficient integer horizon and \(N_0\leq N_\star\), then \(N_J<2N_\star\); consequently the iterative work is less than \(4cN_\star\), with only logarithmically many terminal certificate evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Doubling spends less than twice the final tested horizon, hence less than four times the least sufficient horizon, plus logarithmically many certificate checks.
assumptions_latex: Phase cost is at most \(cN+d\), with \(c,d\geq0\).
Success is monotone in the horizon and \(N_0\leq N_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The total cost is less than \(4cN_\star+d\bigl(2+\log_2(N_\star/N_0)\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional geometric-sum bound is coherent and complexity_bound is the correct kind, but the overhead guarantee has no supporting source.

children.title: Universal Unknown-Constant Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies robust to unavailable regularity or Lipschitz information.

children.title: Unknown-Constant Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies operating without unavailable Lipschitz, contraction, or regularity constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Constant Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric search over an unknown positive constant appearing in a residual guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a base routine \(\mathcal A(N,c;x_0)\) is valid whenever its supplied estimate satisfies \(c\geq C_\star>0\), where \(C_\star\) is unknown, and that its output residual is directly evaluable. Given \(c_0>0\), \(N\in\mathbb N\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(c_j=2^jc_0\). For \(j=0,1,2,\ldots\), compute \(y_j=\mathcal A(N,c_j;x_0)\) and evaluate \(r(y_j)=\lVert y_j-Ty_j\rVert\). Stop and output the first \(y_j\) satisfying \(r(y_j)\leq\varepsilon\). If the chosen \(N\) guarantees this inequality whenever \(c_j\geq C_\star\), termination occurs by the first such index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double the guessed problem constant until the resulting candidate passes a directly checkable residual test.
assumptions_latex: The base guarantee applies whenever \(c\geq C_\star\).
The chosen horizon is sufficient under every valid estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy returns an \(\varepsilon\)-residual point after at most \(1+\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(C_\star/c_0)\rceil\}\) trials.

notation.meaning: constant estimate tested at trial j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The geometric unknown-constant search fits the algorithm leaf and its trial bound is internally consistent, but no source supports the policy or fixed-horizon sufficiency premise.

children.title: Universal Residual Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies designed to retain guarantees across multiple regularity regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Residual Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certification converts parameter search into a universally correct stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathcal A_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}\) be fixed-point routines indexed by tuning parameters, and let a policy generate trials \((\theta_j,N_j)\) without knowing the valid parameter set \(\Theta_\star\subseteq\Theta\). For each trial, form \(y_j=\mathcal A_{\theta_j}(N_j;x_0)\) and accept only when the observable residual satisfies \(\lVert y_j-Ty_j\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). Then every accepted output is an \(\varepsilon\)-residual point, irrespective of whether earlier parameter guesses were valid. If some finite trial belongs to \(\Theta_\star\) and uses a sufficient horizon, the policy terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search over tuning parameters and horizons, but accept only a directly certified residual; incorrect guesses can delay termination but cannot invalidate the output.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and the residual \(\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) are evaluable.
The trial schedule eventually reaches a valid parameter and sufficient horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance implies \(\lVert y_j-Ty_j\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), and the stated coverage assumption implies finite termination.

notation.meaning: parameters for which the base guarantee is valid
parameter and horizon used at trial j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-certification principle is precise and appropriately conditional on schedule coverage, but it lacks an authoritative source.

children.title: Universality Overhead
children.top_down_role: Costs incurred when a policy adapts across unknown problem scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Universality Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of geometric search over one unknown positive tuning constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_\star>0\) be unknown and suppose a run using any estimate \(c\geq C_\star\) achieves the target residual at cost at most \(K(c)\), where \(K\) is nondecreasing. Test \(c_j=2^jc_0\) and let \(J\) be the first index with \(c_J\geq C_\star\). If trial \(j\) costs at most \(a c_j^p+b\) for constants \(a>0\), \(b\geq0\), and \(p>0\), then total cost through trial \(J\) is at most \(a c_J^p/(1-2^{-p})+b(J+1)\), with \(c_J<2C_\star\) and \(J+1\leq2+\max\{0,\log_2(C_\star/c_0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric search incurs a constant-factor overhead in power-law computational work and a logarithmic number of residual tests.
assumptions_latex: Trial cost is at most \(ac_j^p+b\) with \(p>0\).

notation.meaning: first trial with a sufficient estimate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The power-law geometric-search calculation fits a complexity-bound leaf, but no citation supports this universality-overhead formulation.

children.title: Regularity-Adaptive Restart Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies adapting to stronger local geometry detected during iteration.

children.title: Restart Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that reset acceleration histories or phases after progress tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epochwise restart of a finite-horizon accelerator using its latest certified candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\), let \(r(x)=\lVert x-Tx\rVert\), and let \(\mathcal A(m;z)\) denote an accelerated fixed-point routine run for \(m\) evaluations from anchor \(z\). Given \(z_0\), epoch lengths \((m_s)_{s\geq0}\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), compute \(z_{s+1}=\mathcal A(m_s;z_s)\) at epoch \(s\). Stop and output \(z_{s+1}\) when \(r(z_{s+1})\leq\varepsilon\); otherwise discard the accelerator's internal history and start the next epoch from \(z_{s+1}\). Thus only the certified endpoint, not momentum or extrapolation state, crosses an epoch boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run acceleration in epochs, carry the latest endpoint forward, erase internal acceleration history at each boundary, and stop when the residual certificate passes.
assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) and its residual are evaluable.
The finite-horizon routine accepts an arbitrary anchor.
The epoch schedule eventually produces an \(\varepsilon\)-residual endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever the policy stops, its output \(z_{s+1}\) satisfies \(\lVert z_{s+1}-Tz_{s+1}\rVert\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: anchor at the start of epoch s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epochwise restart interface and certified stopping conclusion fit the algorithm leaf, but no source supports the specific history-reset policy.

children.title: Regularity-Detection Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that infer stronger local geometry from observed progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Detection Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A verifiable endpoint test for detecting contraction compatible with local regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an epoch beginning at \(z_s\) and ending at \(y_s\), fix a target contraction factor \(q\in(0,1)\). The residual-contraction detection predicate is \[D_q(z_s,y_s)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lVert y_s-Ty_s\rVert\leq q\lVert z_s-Tz_s\rVert.\] Both residuals must be evaluated with the same mapping and norm. A positive detection certifies the observed contraction for that epoch; it does not, by itself, establish a neighborhood-wide error bound, metric subregularity, or future contraction. Repeated positive detections may therefore guide epoch selection without being interpreted as a proof of global regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declare detected contraction only when the endpoint residual is at most a fixed fraction of the starting residual; this certifies observed, not global, regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(T:H\to H\) is evaluable at both epoch endpoints.
The same residual norm is used at the start and end.
\(q\in(0,1)\) is fixed before evaluating the epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_q(z_s,y_s)=1\) certifies the checkable inequality \(r(y_s)\leq q r(z_s)\) for the observed epoch only.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predicate correctly certifies only observed residual contraction and condition is a suitable kind, but its use as a regularity-detection policy is unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Detection-Triggered Restarts
children.top_down_role: Restart regimes governed by evidence of local regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Detection-Triggered Restarts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restart timing controlled by an observed residual-contraction predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_s\) be the current anchor, choose \(q\in(0,1)\), and generate accelerated iterates \(x_{s,1},x_{s,2},\ldots\) from \(z_s\). At prescribed checkpoints \(k\in\mathcal K_s\), evaluate \(r(x_{s,k})=\lVert x_{s,k}-Tx_{s,k}\rVert\). At the first checkpoint \(k_s\) satisfying \(r(x_{s,k_s})\leq q r(z_s)\), set \(z_{s+1}=x_{s,k_s}\), erase the accelerator's history, and restart from \(z_{s+1}\). Stop instead if \(r(x_{s,k})\leq\varepsilon\). If no checkpoint triggers by a prescribed cap \(M_s\), enlarge or otherwise update the cap according to the declared horizon policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monitor residual contraction at checkpoints and restart acceleration immediately after a certified contraction; revise the epoch cap if no trigger occurs.
assumptions_latex: Residuals are evaluable at the anchor and checkpoints.
Each checkpoint set is contained in \(\{1,\ldots,M_s\}\).
The cap-update rule is fixed independently of unobserved regularity constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every triggered restart anchor satisfies \(r(z_{s+1})\leq q r(z_s)\), and any terminal output satisfies \(r(x)\leq\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The checkpoint-triggered restart algorithm is internally coherent and properly limits its conclusions, but no source supports the interface or cap-update framework.

children.title: Resolvent-Based Acceleration Transfer

children.title: Accelerated Proximal Point Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Anderson, Halpern, inertial, and extrapolation wrappers for proximal-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Proximal Point Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent fixed-point representation underlying accelerated proximal-point wrappers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). Define the resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\). The proximal-point step from \(x_k\) is \(p_k=J_{\lambda A}(x_k)\), equivalently \((x_k-p_k)/\lambda\in A(p_k)\). Moreover, \[0\in A(x_\star)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_\star=J_{\lambda A}(x_\star).\] Hence a fixed-point accelerator may use calls to \(J_{\lambda A}\) as its oracle and combine the history of pairs \((x_i,p_i)\), provided its wrapper preserves the domain and the convergence hypotheses required for that accelerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal-point step is a resolvent evaluation, and zeros of the monotone operator are exactly fixed points of the resolvent, enabling fixed-point acceleration wrappers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion \(0\in A(x_\star)\) is equivalent to \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}(J_{\lambda A})\).

children.title: Monotone-Inclusion Acceleration Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Acceleration wrappers for resolvent-based inclusion solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Inclusion Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a maximally monotone inclusion into a resolvent fixed-point problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in H\), set \(y=J_{\lambda A}(x)=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}x\). Then \[(x-y)/\lambda\in A(y),\qquad \operatorname{zer}(A)=\operatorname{Fix}(J_{\lambda A}).\] Thus an algorithm seeking \(0\in A(x)\) may expose the single-valued firmly nonexpansive mapping \(J_{\lambda A}:H\to H\) to a fixed-point acceleration wrapper. The computable fixed-point residual \(x-J_{\lambda A}x\) simultaneously yields the inclusion certificate \((x-J_{\lambda A}x)/\lambda\in A(J_{\lambda A}x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximally monotone inclusion becomes a firmly nonexpansive resolvent fixed-point problem, and its fixed-point residual provides an explicit graph element of the operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in A(x_\star)\) if and only if \(x_\star=J_{\lambda A}(x_\star)\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of the scaled monotone operator

children.title: Variational-Inequality Acceleration Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point reductions for accelerated variational-inequality solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and resolvent fixed-point reductions for constrained variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space, let \(F:C\to H\), and let \(N_C\) denote the normal-cone operator. A point \(x_\star\in C\) solves the variational inequality \(\langle F(x_\star),y-x_\star\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in C\) exactly when \[0\in F(x_\star)+N_C(x_\star).\] For any \(\gamma>0\), this is also equivalent to \[x_\star=P_C\bigl(x_\star-\gamma F(x_\star)\bigr).\] Consequently, whenever the mapping \(T_\gamma=P_C\circ(I-\gamma F)\) satisfies the regularity required by a chosen fixed-point accelerator, calls to \(T_\gamma\) provide an acceleration interface for the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained variational inequality is equivalent to a normal-cone inclusion and to a projected fixed-point equation, permitting acceleration when the projected map has suitable regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variational-inequality solution set equals \(\operatorname{Fix}\bigl(P_C\circ(I-\gamma F)\bigr)\).

children.title: Forward–Backward Acceleration Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Backward Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded accelerator wrapper for a deterministic forward–backward fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and choose \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). Define \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) and \(r=I-T\). Given \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), safeguards \(\eta_k\in[0,1]\), and a history-based accelerator \(\mathcal E_k\), form \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(x_0,Tx_0,\ldots,x_k,Tx_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) when \(\|r(y_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|r(x_k)\|\), and otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). Stop and return \(x_k\) when \(\|r(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\). Thus the accelerator requires only evaluations of the forward–backward map and its residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wrap the forward–backward map with any history-based proposal, accepting accelerated points only when their fixed-point residual satisfies a prescribed safeguard.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E_k\text{ is defined on the available finite history}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-safeguarded acceleration of the relaxed Douglas–Rachford state map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, choose \(\gamma>0\) and \(\lambda\in(0,2)\), and define \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\) and \(R_{\gamma B}=2J_{\gamma B}-I\). The relaxed Douglas–Rachford map is \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda/2)I+(\lambda/2)R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B}\). From \(z_0\in\mathcal H\), an accelerator proposes \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(z_0,T_\lambda z_0,\ldots,z_k,T_\lambda z_k)\). Accept \(z_{k+1}=y_k\) if \(\|y_k-T_\lambda y_k\|\leq\eta_k\|z_k-T_\lambda z_k\|\); otherwise take \(z_{k+1}=T_\lambda z_k\). Stop when the residual is at most \(\varepsilon\), and report the shadow \(J_{\gamma B}z_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerate the Douglas–Rachford state while safeguarding its residual; recover a primal candidate through the appropriate resolvent shadow.

children.title: ADMM Acceleration Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Acceleration transferred through fixed-point representations of ADMM iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: ADMM Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-state, residual-safeguarded acceleration of a deterministically selected exact two-block scaled ADMM map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Z,\mathcal Y\) be Hilbert spaces, let \(A:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) and \(B:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Y\) be bounded linear operators, let \(c\in\mathcal Y\), and consider \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X,z\in\mathcal Z}\{f(x)+g(z):Ax+Bz=c\}\). Fix \(\rho>0\) and deterministic selection rules for the two attained subproblems. Define \(T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}\) on the product Hilbert space \(\mathcal S=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Y\) by mapping \(s=(x,z,u)\) to \(s^+=(x^+,z^+,u^+)\), where \(x^+\) is the selected minimizer of \(f(\xi)+(\rho/2)\|A\xi+Bz-c+u\|_{\mathcal Y}^2\), \(z^+\) is the selected minimizer of \(g(\zeta)+(\rho/2)\|Ax^++B\zeta-c+u\|_{\mathcal Y}^2\), and \(u^+=u+Ax^++Bz^+-c\). Given \(s_0\in\mathcal S\), let \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(s_0,T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}s_0,\ldots,s_k,T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}s_k)\). For a fixed product-space norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal S}\), accept \(s_{k+1}=y_k\) when \(\|y_k-T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}y_k\|_{\mathcal S}\leq\eta_k\|s_k-T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}s_k\|_{\mathcal S}\); otherwise set \(s_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}s_k\). Stop and return \(s_k\) when \(\|s_k-T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}s_k\|_{\mathcal S}\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat deterministically selected exact two-block ADMM as a product-space fixed-point map and accept an accelerated full-state proposal only when it satisfies the prescribed ADMM-map residual safeguard.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ and }g:\mathcal Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}\).
\(A:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\text{ and }B:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Y\text{ are bounded and linear, }c\in\mathcal Y\text{, and }\rho>0\).
The two ADMM subproblems attain minimizers and fixed deterministic selection rules are used.

notation.meaning: ADMM product-state Hilbert space equipped with a fixed product norm
one deterministically selected exact ADMM sweep

children.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Equivalence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representation conditions governing transfer between the two acceleration interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Equivalence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between base-map conjugacy and valid transfer of an accelerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose exact two-block ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting on the associated dual inclusion admit corresponding states related by a bijective affine map \(L\), so that \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}L=LT_{\mathrm{ADMM}}\). Their unaccelerated trajectories correspond when their initial states are matched by \(L\). An accelerated wrapper transfers through this correspondence only if its history rule is equivariant: \(\mathcal E_k^{\mathrm{DR}}(Ls_0,\ldots,Ls_k)=L\mathcal E_k^{\mathrm{ADMM}}(s_0,\ldots,s_k)\). Base-map equivalence alone is insufficient. For example, with \(L=aI\), \(a\neq1\), coordinatewise clipping \(\mathcal E(v)=\max(-1,\min(1,v))\) satisfies \(\mathcal E(Lv)\neq L\mathcal E(v)\) for some \(v\); hence the accelerated trajectories need not correspond.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact ADMM–Douglas–Rachford conjugacy transfers an accelerator only when the history rule commutes with the state correspondence; nonlinear clipping provides a counterexample.
assumptions_latex: The underlying ADMM subproblems and Douglas–Rachford resolvents are evaluated exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Operator Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded acceleration of the Davis–Yin three-operator fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and choose \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). Define \(T=I-J_{\gamma B}+J_{\gamma A}(2J_{\gamma B}-I-\gamma C J_{\gamma B})\). Starting from \(z_0\), compute \(Tz_k\), and let a history rule propose \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(z_0,Tz_0,\ldots,z_k,Tz_k)\). Accept \(z_{k+1}=y_k\) when \(\|y_k-Ty_k\|\leq\eta_k\|z_k-Tz_k\|\); otherwise set \(z_{k+1}=Tz_k\). Stop when \(\|z_k-Tz_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output the shadow \(J_{\gamma B}z_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply acceleration to the Davis–Yin state map, safeguard the fixed-point residual, and recover the solution candidate from its resolvent shadow.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-aware acceleration wrapper for a coupled primal–dual splitting operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be Hilbert spaces, let \(P:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive, and let \(T_{\mathrm{PD}}:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\) be the averaged fixed-point operator of a specified convergent primal–dual splitting scheme in the \(P\)-metric. Given \(w_0=(x_0,y_0)\), form \(v_k=\mathcal E_k(w_0,T_{\mathrm{PD}}w_0,\ldots,w_k,T_{\mathrm{PD}}w_k)\). Accept \(w_{k+1}=v_k\) when \(\|v_k-T_{\mathrm{PD}}v_k\|_P\leq\eta_k\|w_k-T_{\mathrm{PD}}w_k\|_P\); otherwise set \(w_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{PD}}w_k\). Stop and return both components of \(w_k\) when \(\|w_k-T_{\mathrm{PD}}w_k\|_P\leq\varepsilon\). Any separately computed primal and dual proposals must together define a compatible element \(v_k\in\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\) to which this coupled residual test applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerate a coherent coupled primal–dual state in the splitting method's metric, accepting the proposal only through a product-space fixed-point-residual safeguard.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E_k\text{ returns an element of }\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\text{ from the available finite history}\).

children.title: Common Fixed-Point Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Acceleration interfaces for families of fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Fixed-Point Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-safeguarded acceleration for a finite family sharing a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_m:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be averaged nonexpansive maps with nonempty common fixed-point set \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Fix}T_i\). Choose a control sequence \(i_k\) in which every index occurs infinitely often. Given \(x_0\), let \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(x_0,T_{i_0}x_0,\ldots,x_k,T_{i_k}x_k)\). Define \(R(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\|x-T_ix\|\). Accept \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) when \(R(y_k)\leq\eta_kR(x_k)\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=T_{i_k}x_k\). Stop and output \(x_k\) when \(R(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\). Evaluating \(R\) requires access to every family member at each safeguard test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maps sharing fixed points, accelerate controlled fixed-point steps while safeguarding the maximum residual over the entire family.
assumptions_latex: Every index appears infinitely often in \((i_k)\).

children.title: Projection-Map Acceleration

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Map Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded acceleration of a metric projection map onto one convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(P_C\) be its metric projection. Starting from \(x_0\in\mathcal H\), compute \(p_k=P_Cx_k\), and let a history rule propose \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(x_0,p_0,\ldots,x_k,p_k)\). With \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\), accept \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) if \(d_C(y_k)\leq\eta_kd_C(x_k)\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=p_k\). Stop and output \(x_k\) when \(d_C(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\). Since \(P_Cx\in C\), an unsafeguarded base step reaches an exact fixed point; this wrapper is chiefly an interface for projection maps embedded in larger compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerate a projection-map history only when the candidate reduces distance to the set; a fallback projection is already an exact fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Process Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded acceleration of cyclic projections for consistent convex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space with \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\), and define the cyclic projection map \(T=P_{C_m}\cdots P_{C_1}\). From \(x_0\), let \(y_k=\mathcal E_k(x_0,Tx_0,\ldots,x_k,Tx_k)\), and define the feasibility violation \(V(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}d_{C_i}(x)\). Accept \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) if \(V(y_k)\leq\eta_kV(x_k)\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). Stop when \(V(x_k)\leq\varepsilon\) and return \(x_k\). The stopping test uses all individual sets rather than only the composition residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerate cyclic projections while safeguarding maximum distance to every constraint set; stop using feasibility violation, not merely the composition residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathcal H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for each }i\).

children.title: Inconsistent-Feasibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transfer limits when the represented feasibility problem lacks a common solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent-Feasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition fixed points need not certify feasibility when the sets do not intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}\) and \(D=\{(t,1):t\in\mathbb R\}\) in \(\mathbb R^2\). Then \(C\cap D=\varnothing\), while \(P_CP_D(t,s)=(t,0)\) for every \((t,s)\), so \(\operatorname{Fix}(P_CP_D)=C\neq\varnothing\). Consequently, a projection-process accelerator that stops solely when \(\|x-P_CP_Dx\|\leq\varepsilon\) can return residual zero although the original feasibility problem has no solution. In inconsistent feasibility, a composition fixed point may instead encode a best-approximation cycle; feasibility must be tested through individual-set violations or an explicit inconsistency model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two parallel lines have empty intersection but their alternating-projection composition has many fixed points, so zero composition residual does not certify feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Approximation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern-type interface selecting the fixed point nearest a prescribed anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be nonexpansive with nonempty closed convex fixed-point set \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\), and fix an anchor \(a\in\mathcal H\). Choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\) with \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\). From any \(x_0\), perform the anchored update \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_ka+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\). Under these conditions, \(x_k\) converges strongly to \(P_Fa\), the unique best approximation to \(a\) from \(F\). Stop computationally when both \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|\leq\varepsilon\), and return \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anchored Halpern iteration selects the fixed point closest to a prescribed anchor, under standard vanishing, nonsummable, bounded-variation weights.

notation.meaning: best approximation to the anchor from F

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-anchor Halpern interface selecting the minimum-norm common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be nonexpansive with nonempty closed convex fixed-point set \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\). Choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\) such that \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\). Starting from arbitrary \(x_0\), apply \(x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\), which is the anchored best-approximation interface with anchor \(0\). Then \(x_k\) converges strongly to \(P_F0\), the unique element of \(F\) having minimum Hilbert-space norm. A computational implementation may stop when both the fixed-point residual and successive-step norm are at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Setting the anchor to zero in Halpern iteration selects the unique minimum-norm fixed point under standard weight conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Anchored Selection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern anchoring for selecting the fixed point nearest a prescribed anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive with \(C=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and choose an anchor \(u\in H\) and \(x_0\in H\). For weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\) satisfying \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\), perform \[x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)T(x_k).\] The anchored interface outputs the strong limit \(x_k\to P_Cu\), thereby selecting the fixed point closest to \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Halpern iteration mixes each fixed-point step with a vanishing but persistent anchor weight and converges to the fixed point nearest the anchor.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Selection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing Tikhonov regularization selects the anchor-nearest fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive with \(C=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and fix \(u\in H\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), define \(x_\varepsilon\) as the unique fixed point of the contraction \[T_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}T(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}u.\] Equivalently, \(x_\varepsilon-T(x_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon-u)=0\). As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the regularized solutions converge strongly to \(P_Cu\). Thus the regularization parameter supplies a single-valued interface that resolves a nonunique fixed-point set by anchored best approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding vanishing Tikhonov regularization makes the fixed-point problem uniquely solvable, and its solutions approach the fixed point nearest the anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.

knowledge_statements.title: Anderson–Newton Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type-II Anderson acceleration as an inverse-multisecant Newton-like step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and define \(F(x)=x-G(x)\). From stored differences form \(X_k=[\Delta x_{k-m},\ldots,\Delta x_{k-1}]\) and \(Y_k=[\Delta F_{k-m},\ldots,\Delta F_{k-1}]\). If \(Y_k\) has full column rank, the type-II Anderson step admits the Newton-like representation \[x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k),\qquad H_k=I+(X_k-Y_k)(Y_k^{\mathsf T}Y_k)^{-1}Y_k^{\mathsf T}.\] The matrix satisfies the inverse multisecant equations \(H_kY_k=X_k\). Replacing or regularizing the Gram inverse yields the corresponding damped or regularized Anderson–Newton interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Type-II Anderson acceleration is an approximate inverse-Newton step whose inverse Jacobian model satisfies all stored secant equations.
assumptions_latex: Stored residual-difference columns in \(Y_k\) are linearly independent.

notation.meaning: stored iterate and residual difference matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inverse-multisecant formula is algebraically consistent with the stated residual convention and satisfies the claimed secant equations, but no source establishes that this is the intended type-II Anderson convention or supports the regularized-interface extension.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine fixed-point extrapolation represented as residual-based nonlinear solving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(F=I-T\), and select stored points \(x_{i_0},\ldots,x_{i_m}\). For coefficients \(\alpha_j\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\alpha_j=1\), define \(\bar x=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\alpha_jx_{i_j}\) and \(\bar F=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\alpha_jF(x_{i_j})\). The accelerated fixed-point candidate has the exact residual representation \[x^+=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\alpha_jT(x_{i_j})=\bar x-\bar F.\] Consequently, minimizing \(\|\bar F\|\) over affine coefficients transfers residual-minimizing extrapolation directly into a nonlinear-solver interface without changing the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any affine combination of stored fixed-point images equals the matching affine iterate combination minus its combined residual.

notation.meaning: same affine combination of stored residuals

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact identity follows by expanding F=I-T

children.title: Secant Solver Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections from accelerated residual histories to secant-style nonlinear solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Secant Solver Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-multisecant residual solver for a fixed-point equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(F=I-T\), choose \(x_0\), memory \(m\), and an initial inverse model \(H_0\). At iteration \(k\), assemble \(X_k\) and \(Y_k\) from at most \(m\) differences \(\Delta x_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\) and \(\Delta F_i=F(x_{i+1})-F(x_i)\). Choose a bounded matrix \(H_k\) satisfying or least-squares fitting \(H_kY_k=X_k\), optionally with regularization, and set \[x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k).\] Stop when \(\|F(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon\); output \(x_k\) as an \(\epsilon\)-residual fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface solves the fixed-point residual equation using an inverse model fitted to stored multisecant conditions.
assumptions_latex: The multisecant fit is solvable exactly or by a specified regularized least-squares rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed solver does not specify a unique exact or regularized multisecant fitting rule, and its stopping condition does not ensure that termination occurs. A source and a precise solver variant are needed before the mathematical algorithm can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Fixed-Point–Secant Representation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing when fixed-point acceleration admits a secant interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point–Secant Representation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which fixed-point extrapolation has an exact secant-solver interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic transfer between acceleration of \(x=T(x)\) and secant solution of \(F(x)=0\) is exact when \(F=I-T\), the history coefficients are affine, and the same residual norm and stored pairs are used. It need not persist after replacing \(F\) by a nonlinear left preconditioner \(M(x)F(x)\), projecting the accelerated candidate onto a constraint set, applying componentwise clipping, or evaluating unmatched iterate and residual histories. In these cases no common affine identity \(\sum_j\alpha_jT(x_j)=\bar x-\sum_j\alpha_jF(x_j)\) represents the modified update unless the modification is explicitly absorbed into a new fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-point–secant correspondence is exact for matched affine residual histories, but nonlinear safeguards, projections, or preconditioning generally break it.
assumptions_latex: Acceleration uses matched stored iterates and residuals with affine coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine correspondence holds before, but generally not after, nonlinear modification of the candidate or residual.

notation.meaning: residual associated with the fixed-point map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unmodified affine identity is algebraic but listed obstructions require literature support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unmodified affine identity is algebraically correct, but the asserted boundary for preconditioning, projection, clipping, and unmatched histories depends on how each modification defines its update. The broad claim that no common representation remains requires a precise formulation and supporting source.

children.title: Picard–Newton Representation Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between accelerating a fixed-point map and solving its residual equation.

knowledge_statements.title: Picard–Newton Representation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact distinction between Picard displacement and Newton correction for the fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable and set \(F(x)=x-T(x)\). A Picard step uses \(s_P=T(x)-x=-F(x)\), whereas a Newton step, when \(I-DT(x)\) is invertible, uses \[s_N=-[I-DT(x)]^{-1}F(x).\] The two corrections coincide at \(x\) exactly when \(DT(x)F(x)=0\). Thus Picard acceleration and Newton solution of the residual equation share their zeros but not generally their local models; equality is automatic at a fixed point and exceptional away from one. Any transfer of Newton convergence claims therefore requires control of \(I-DT(x)\), not merely of \(T(x)-x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard and Newton solve the same fixed-point equation but take equal off-solution steps only when the map derivative annihilates the residual.

notation.meaning: Newton correction for the residual equation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equivalence follows by multiplying the Newton equation by I-DT(x)

children.title: Fixed-Point Residual as a Stationarity Proxy
children.top_down_role: The transfer from operator residuals to nonconvex stationarity.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct substitution in the gradient fixed-point map
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stationarity certificate for the gradient-descent fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, choose \(\eta>0\), let \(\epsilon\geq0\), and define the gradient fixed-point map \(T_\eta(x)=x-\eta
abla f(x)\). Its residual is \[R_\eta(x)=x-T_\eta(x)=\eta
abla f(x).\] Hence \(x\) is a fixed point if and only if it is first-order stationary, and the computable inequality \(\|R_\eta(x)\|\leq\eta\epsilon\) certifies \(\|
abla f(x)\|\leq\epsilon\). This equivalence is independent of convexity; smoothness or descent assumptions are needed only when a method claims a rate for producing such a residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a gradient step and any nonnegative tolerance, the fixed-point residual is exactly the stepsize times the gradient, so residual tolerance directly certifies stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual as a Stationarity Proxy

children.title: Critical Residuals for Nonconvex Splitting
children.top_down_role: Certificates tailored to nonconvex proximal and splitting maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical Residuals for Nonconvex Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient residual certificate for composite nonconvex stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(\gamma>0\), define \(z=T_\gamma(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma
abla f(x))\) and \(G_\gamma(x)=(x-z)/\gamma\). Proximal optimality gives a vector \(v\in\partial g(z)\) satisfying \(G_\gamma(x)=
abla f(x)+v\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(z))\leq\|
abla f(z)+v\|\leq(1+\gamma L)\|G_\gamma(x)\|.\] Thus a small splitting residual at \(x\) certifies approximate criticality at the proximal point \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small proximal-gradient residual produces an explicit nearby subgradient certificate for composite nonconvex stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

children.title: Objective–Residual Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Regimes where residual reduction and objective progress separate.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective–Residual Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small fixed-point residual need not imply small objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), minimize \(f_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon x\) on \(C_\varepsilon=[0,1/\varepsilon]\), and let \(T_\varepsilon(x)=P_{C_\varepsilon}(x-\varepsilon)\) be the unit-stepsize projected-gradient map. At \(x_\varepsilon=1/\varepsilon\), \[\|x_\varepsilon-T_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)\|=\varepsilon,\qquad f_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)-\min_{x\in C_\varepsilon}f_\varepsilon(x)=1.\] Therefore the residual tends to zero while the objective gap remains constant. A residual-complexity guarantee alone cannot yield an objective-gap guarantee without additional error-bound, growth, compactness-scale, or gradient-dominance information linking residual magnitude to objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected-gradient residual can vanish across a problem family while the objective gap stays fixed, so residual rates need not imply value rates.

notation.meaning: right endpoint of the feasible interval

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: all residual and objective values are directly computable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-iterate residual complexity of constant-step gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and satisfy \(f(x)\geq f_\star\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(0<\eta<2/L\), generate \(x_{k+1}=T_\eta(x_k)=x_k-\eta\nabla f(x_k)\), and set \(R_\eta=I-T_\eta\). For every integer \(K\geq1\), \[\min_{0\leq k<K}\|R_\eta(x_k)\|^2\leq\frac{2\eta\bigl(f(x_0)-f_\star\bigr)}{(2-L\eta)K}.\] Consequently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), an iterate satisfying \(\|R_\eta(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon\) is obtained within \(O(\epsilon^{-2})\) gradient evaluations when \(\eta\), \(L\), and \(f(x_0)-f_\star\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive tolerance ε, gradient descent finds an ε fixed-point residual in order ε⁻² gradient evaluations for a smooth lower-bounded nonconvex objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Fixed-Point Complexity

children.top_down_role: Residual-complexity families for proximal composite maps.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and may be nonconvex, while \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

notation.meaning: finite lower bound on the composite objective

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: constant follows from the proximal-gradient descent inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient residual complexity for a nonconvex smooth-plus-convex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) satisfy \(F(x)\geq F_\star\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and may be nonconvex, while \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and \(0<\gamma<1/L\), generate \(x_{k+1}=T_\gamma(x_k)=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x_k-\gamma\nabla f(x_k))\), and define \(G_\gamma(x)=(x-T_\gamma(x))/\gamma\). Then, for every integer \(K\geq1\), \[\min_{0\leq k<K}\|G_\gamma(x_k)\|^2\leq\frac{2\bigl(F(x_0)-F_\star\bigr)}{\gamma(1-\gamma L)K}.\] Consequently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), an iterate satisfying \(\|G_\gamma(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon\) is obtained within \(O(\epsilon^{-2})\) gradient and proximal evaluations when \(\gamma\), \(L\), and \(F(x_0)-F_\star\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a point with finite composite objective, proximal gradient reaches any positive ε residual in order ε⁻² gradient and proximal evaluations for a lower-bounded smooth-nonconvex plus convex-composite objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonconvex Fixed-Point Complexity

children.title: Nonconvex Splitting Residual Complexity
children.top_down_role: Residual-complexity families for Douglas–Rachford, ADMM, and multi-operator maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Splitting Residual Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic best-iterate residual bound induced by a nonconvex splitting merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to X\) be the update map of a Douglas–Rachford, ADMM, or multi-operator splitting scheme, let \(z_{k+1}=Tz_k\), and define \(R(z)=z-Tz\). Suppose a merit function \(\Phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfies \(\inf\Phi> -\infty\) and \(\Phi(z_k)-\Phi(z_{k+1})\ge c\lVert R(z_k)\rVert^2\) for some \(c>0\). Then, for every \(K\ge1\), \[\min_{0\le k<K}\lVert R(z_k)\rVert^2\le\frac{\Phi(z_0)-\inf\Phi}{cK}.\] Consequently an iterate with \(\lVert R(z_k)\rVert\le\varepsilon\) is obtained within \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) map evaluations. The bound applies only after the method-specific merit descent inequality has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A merit decrease proportional to squared splitting residual gives a best-iterate squared-residual rate of order 1/K and residual complexity of order epsilon to the minus two.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The telescoping residual bound is mathematically sound and complexity_bound fits the leaf, but no source supports its asserted Douglas–Rachford, ADMM, and multi-operator scope.

children.title: Descent Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Frameworks organized around controlled decrease of an energy or merit quantity.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient-decrease condition used in abstract KL convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(\Phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x_k)\subset\operatorname{dom}\Phi\). A quadratic descent framework holds when there exists \(a>0\) such that \[\Phi(x_{k+1})+a\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert^2\le \Phi(x_k)\qquad(k\ge0).\] More generally, an inexact framework permits a nonnegative summable sequence \((\delta_k)\) on the right-hand side. In the exact case, \((\Phi(x_k))\) is nonincreasing and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert^2\le(\Phi(x_0)-\inf\Phi)/a\) whenever \(\Phi\) is bounded below along the sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each step must decrease the objective by at least a positive multiple of its squared length, possibly up to summable errors.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(\Phi\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(x_{k+1})+a\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert^2\le\Phi(x_k)\), implying square-summable steps in the exact case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact sufficient-descent condition is standard and condition fits the leaf, but the KL framework and summable-error variant have no cited source; the inexact inequality is also not stated explicitly.

children.title: Relative-Error Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Frameworks relating residual information to local accuracy or stationarity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient relative-error condition coupled to successive iterate displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(\Phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x_k)\subset\operatorname{dom}\partial\Phi\). A relative-error framework holds if there exist \(b>0\), vectors \(w_{k+1}\in\partial\Phi(x_{k+1})\), and nonnegative errors \(\eta_{k+1}\) such that \[\lVert w_{k+1}\rVert\le b\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert+\eta_{k+1}\qquad(k\ge0).\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\Phi(x_{k+1}))\) obeys the same upper bound. The exact framework takes \(\eta_k=0\); an inexact KL analysis commonly requires \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient at the new iterate is controlled by the latest step length plus an optional summable error.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(\Phi\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\eta_k\ge0\), with summability required in the inexact framework.

notation.meaning: limiting subdifferential of the Lyapunov function
selected subgradient at the new iterate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-error condition is appropriate, but its limiting-subdifferential convention and inexact KL summability requirement require an authoritative source.

children.title: Descent–Error Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility regimes linking energy control to relative-error information.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent–Error Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility principle aligning sufficient descent, stationarity error, and KL geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. Suppose a bounded sequence \((x_k)\) satisfies sufficient descent with constant \(a>0\), relative error with constant \(b>0\), and has a cluster point \(\bar x\) for which \(\Phi(x_{k_j})\to\Phi(\bar x)\) along some convergent subsequence. If \(\Phi\) has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property on the cluster set, then the shared displacement \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\) links objective decrease to stationarity: the sequence has finite length, converges to a single point \(x_\star\), and \(0\in\partial\Phi(x_\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When descent and subgradient error use the same step measure, KL geometry converts them into finite length and convergence to one critical point.
assumptions_latex: \((x_k)\) is bounded and \(\Phi\) has the KL property on its cluster set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle matches the compatibility leaf and resembles a standard abstract KL convergence theorem, but the uniformized KL argument and cluster-value hypothesis are unsupported.

children.title: KL Rate Stratification
children.top_down_role: Local convergence regimes organized by KL geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Rate Stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-length KL rates under quadratic descent and relative error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the descent–error compatibility hypotheses hold and \(x_k\to x_\star\). Let \(s_k=\Phi(x_k)-\Phi(x_\star)\), and suppose the KL inequality near \(x_\star\) admits \(\varphi(s)=c s^{1-\theta}\) with \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in[0,1)\). Then: if \(\theta=0\), the sequence terminates finitely; if \(0<\theta\le\tfrac12\), both \(s_k\) and \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert\) converge at least geometrically; if \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\), then \[s_k=O\!\left(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\right),\qquad \lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert=O\!\left(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL exponent separates finite termination, geometric convergence, and polynomial convergence, with explicit objective-gap and iterate-distance exponents.
assumptions_latex: The compatible descent and relative-error conditions hold near \(x_\star\).
\(\varphi(s)=cs^{1-\theta}\) is a KL desingularizing function with \(\theta\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rates are finite for \(\theta=0\), geometric for \(0<\theta\le1/2\), and polynomial with the displayed exponents for \(1/2<\theta<1\).

notation.meaning: KL exponent under the stated convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated rate stratification is standard under the declared exponent convention and theorem fits the leaf, but the convention and displayed objective/iterate rates require a specific theorem source.

children.title: KL Acceleration Limits
children.top_down_role: The boundary between establishing convergence and establishing genuine acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: KL Acceleration Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL geometry alone does not compare an accelerated method with its baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KL property is a local inequality relating a function-value gap to a stationarity measure; it contains no comparison between two update maps. Consequently, knowing only that a baseline sequence and a modified sequence satisfy compatible descent–error conditions for the same KL function and exponent \(\theta\) does not imply that the modified sequence has a smaller asymptotic constant, fewer iterations, or a better rate exponent. A genuine acceleration claim additionally requires method-dependent quantitative information, such as sharper descent and error constants, a contraction-factor comparison, a local linearization or spectral estimate, or an oracle-complexity lower-and-upper-bound comparison. Thus KL convergence certification is not by itself an acceleration certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KL exponent can classify convergence but cannot alone prove that one fixed-point method is faster than another.
assumptions_latex: Both methods satisfy abstract KL-compatible descent and relative-error hypotheses.
Only the common KL function and exponent are specified.
No method-dependent contraction, spectral, or oracle comparison is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KL hypotheses alone imply no strict acceleration comparison between the two methods.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits exactly and the distinction between KL convergence certification and acceleration is reasonable, but the nonimplication claim lacks a formal comparison result or counterexample source.

children.title: Noisy-History Anderson Variants
children.top_down_role: Anderson variants designed for noisy histories.

children.title: Stochastic Anderson Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Anderson variants operating with stochastic residual or operator histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained least-squares Anderson mixing using noisy operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), memory \(m\ge1\), and stochastic evaluations \(g_k=\widehat T_k(x_k)\), set \(f_k=g_k-x_k\). At iteration \(k\), let \(m_k=\min\{m,k\}\), form \(F_k=[f_{k-m_k},\ldots,f_k]\), and compute \[\alpha^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf1^\top\alpha=1}\lVert F_k\alpha\rVert_2^2.\] Update \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{i=0}^{m_k}\alpha_i^k g_{k-m_k+i}\). Stop when a prescribed stochastic residual estimate or iteration budget is met, and return the latest iterate. Because noisy residual columns can be ill-conditioned, this unregularized rule requires an independent coefficient safeguard or stability hypothesis for convergence claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic Anderson acceleration mixes recent noisy operator values using coefficients that minimize their combined residual subject to affine consistency.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\widehat T_k(x_k)\) is an available stochastic evaluation of the target map.
The constrained least-squares problem is solved or assigned a specified minimizer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine least-squares update is a coherent Anderson algorithm, but no source establishes this stochastic-history variant or identifies the noise model and safeguard needed for convergence claims.

children.title: Noise-Regularized Anderson Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Anderson variants using regularization to stabilize noisy histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Regularized Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ridge-regularized Anderson mixing for noisy residual histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given recent noisy evaluations \(g_i=\widehat T_i(x_i)\) and residuals \(f_i=g_i-x_i\), form \(F_k=[f_{k-m_k},\ldots,f_k]\), where \(m_k=\min\{m,k\}\). For a regularization parameter \(\lambda_k>0\), compute \[\alpha^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf1^\top\alpha=1}\bigl\{\lVert F_k\alpha\rVert_2^2+\lambda_k\lVert\alpha\rVert_2^2\bigr\},\] and set \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{i=0}^{m_k}\alpha_i^k g_{k-m_k+i}\). The positive ridge term makes the coefficient problem uniquely solvable and suppresses amplification caused by nearly dependent noisy residual columns. Stop using a prescribed residual estimator or budget and return the latest iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive ridge penalty stabilizes Anderson coefficients when noisy residual histories are nearly linearly dependent.
assumptions_latex: A finite residual history \(F_k\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coefficient subproblem has a unique minimizer, which defines the regularized mixed update \(x_{k+1}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive ridge term does make the constrained coefficient problem uniquely solvable, and algorithm fits the leaf, but the proposed noisy Anderson variant and regularization policy lack a source.

children.title: Noisy-History Stability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes governing useful extrapolation under persistent history noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-History Stability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-amplification condition for contractive maps with noisy Anderson histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) have fixed point \(x_\star\) and satisfy \(\lVert T(x)-x_\star\rVert\le q\lVert x-x_\star\rVert\) with \(0\le q<1\). Suppose a noisy-history update is \(x_{k+1}=\sum_i\alpha_{k,i}(T(x_i)+\xi_i)\), where \(\sum_i\alpha_{k,i}=1\) and \(\lVert\alpha_k\rVert_1\le C\). Then \[\lVert x_{k+1}-x_\star\rVert\le qC\max_i\lVert x_i-x_\star\rVert+C\max_i\lVert\xi_i\rVert.\] Hence the history mixing is uniformly input-to-state stable when \(qC<1\); bounded noise produces a bounded error floor, while vanishing noise permits convergence under the associated delayed-recursion conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a contractive map, bounded coefficient one-norm controls noise amplification; stability requires contraction factor times that bound to be below one.
assumptions_latex: The history window is finite and the perturbations \(\xi_i\) are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(qC<1\), the mixed iteration obeys the displayed stable error recursion.

children.title: Stochastic Halpern Iterations
children.top_down_role: Anchored fixed-point methods under stochastic operator evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Halpern Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anchored Halpern iteration with minibatched stochastic operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, let \(u,x_0\in C\), and let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive. Given weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\), obtain a stochastic estimate \(\widehat T_k(x_k)=T(x_k)+\xi_k\), optionally project it onto \(C\), and update \[x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)\widehat T_k(x_k).\] Stop when a prescribed residual estimate or iteration budget is met and return the latest iterate. The classical anchoring regime requires \(\alpha_k\to0\) and \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\); stochastic convergence additionally requires a noise condition compatible with these weights, typically enforced through increasing batches or variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic Halpern step averages a fixed anchor with a noisy evaluation of a nonexpansive map using a vanishing but nonsummable anchor weight.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex, and \(T:C\to C\) is nonexpansive.
The stochastic evaluations and any projection rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)\widehat T_k(x_k)\) defines the anchored stochastic iteration.

children.title: Minibatch Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Sampling interfaces based on fixed or adaptive minibatch sizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Minibatch Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance representation for averaged stochastic fixed-point oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x,\zeta)\) be an unbiased stochastic evaluation of \(T(x)\) with \(\mathbb E[G(x,\zeta)\mid x]=T(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert G(x,\zeta)-T(x)\rVert^2\mid x]\le\sigma^2\). For conditionally independent samples \(\zeta_{k,1},\ldots,\zeta_{k,b_k}\), define \[\widehat T_k(x_k)=\frac1{b_k}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(x_k,\zeta_{k,j}).\] Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat T_k(x_k)\mid x_k]=T(x_k)\) and \[\mathbb E[\lVert\widehat T_k(x_k)-T(x_k)\rVert^2\mid x_k]\le\frac{\sigma^2}{b_k}.\] Thus the batch size enters a stochastic fixed-point analysis through inverse variance scaling, at a cost of \(b_k\) oracle calls per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging b independent unbiased operator samples preserves unbiasedness and reduces conditional variance by a factor of b, while using b oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: Its conditional second moment about \(T(x)\) is at most \(\sigma^2\).
Samples within each batch are conditionally independent.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Control Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summable effective-noise condition for stochastic quasi-Fejér fixed-point recursions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal F_k)\) be the iteration filtration and let \(V_k\ge0\) be an adapted error measure satisfying \[\mathbb E[V_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le V_k-a_kR_k+b_k
u_k,\] where \(a_k,R_k,b_k,
u_k\ge0\), and \(
u_k\) bounds the conditional variance of the stochastic operator error. A variance-control interface requires \(\sum_k b_k
u_k<\infty\). Under this condition, the accumulated noise perturbation is finite; the stochastic quasi-Fejér or supermartingale argument yields almost-sure convergence of \((V_k)\) and \(\sum_k a_kR_k<\infty\). For a minibatch oracle with \(
u_k\le\sigma^2/B_k\), it suffices that \(\sum_k b_k/B_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variance is compatible with stochastic convergence when its weighted contribution to the error recursion is summable; increasing batches can enforce this condition.
assumptions_latex: \(V_k\) is nonnegative and adapted to \(\mathcal F_k\).
The displayed conditional recursion holds with nonnegative coefficients.

children.title: Batch–Variance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between sampling effort, history quality, and acceleration stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch–Variance Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-minibatch tradeoff for a linearly contracting stochastic accelerated iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the expected error satisfies \(u_{k+1}\leq \rho u_k+a/b\), where \(0<\rho<1\), \(a>0\), and each iteration averages \(b\) independent samples. Then \[u_K\leq \rho^K u_0+\frac{a(1-\rho^K)}{(1-\rho)b},\qquad \limsup_{K\to\infty}u_K\leq\frac{a}{(1-\rho)b}.\] To ensure \(u_K\leq\varepsilon\), it suffices to take \(b\geq 2a/((1-\rho)\varepsilon)\) and \(K\geq \log(2u_0/\varepsilon)/(-\log\rho)\), using \(Kb\) samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger batches lower the variance floor inversely with batch size, while reaching accuracy ε with a fixed batch uses order ε⁻¹ log(ε⁻¹) samples.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration uses a constant batch size \(b\in\mathbb{N}\).

notation.meaning: Expected nonnegative error after iteration k.
Number of independent samples averaged per iteration.
Single-sample variance contribution in the error recursion.

children.title: Stochastic Noise Floors
children.top_down_role: Residual accuracy limits caused by persistent stochastic error.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Noise Floors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent additive variance prevents convergence below a positive mean-error floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_{k+1}=\rho u_k+a v\), where \(u_0\geq0\), \(0<\rho<1\), \(a>0\), and \(v>0\). Then \[u_k=\rho^k u_0+\frac{av(1-\rho^k)}{1-\rho},\qquad \lim_{k\to\infty}u_k=\frac{av}{1-\rho}>0.\] Thus contraction of the deterministic component cannot drive this error measure to zero while the additive stochastic forcing remains nonzero. Changing \(\rho\) alone can alter the floor but cannot eliminate it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent positive variance term produces a positive limiting error. Changing only the deterministic contraction factor can alter, but cannot eliminate, this stochastic floor.
assumptions_latex: The additive noise contribution is constant across iterations.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative error measure at iteration k.
Persistent variance or mean-square noise level.

children.title: Stochastic Sample-Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sampling limits for attaining prescribed residual levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Sample-Complexity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizon-dependent batching removes the extra logarithm incurred by constant batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(u_{k+1}\leq\rho u_k+a/b_k\) with \(0<\rho<1\). Choose \(K\) so that \(\rho^K u_0\leq\varepsilon/2\), set \(S_K=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\rho^{(K-1-j)/2}\), and take \[b_j=\left\lceil\frac{2aS_K}{\varepsilon}\rho^{(K-1-j)/2}\right\rceil.\] Then \(u_K\leq\varepsilon\) and \[\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}b_j\leq K+\frac{2a}{\varepsilon(1-\sqrt{\rho})^2}.\] Hence the sample complexity is \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon)+a/\varepsilon)\) for fixed \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocating larger batches near the target horizon attains ε error with order ε⁻¹ samples, plus logarithmically many outer iterations.
assumptions_latex: Batch sizes are positive integers and samples within each batch are independent.

notation.meaning: Batch size used at outer iteration j.
Sum of square roots of the horizon weights.

children.title: Noise-Floor Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where increasing sample effort can move residual accuracy below an initial noise floor.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Floor Escape Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing stochastic forcing is the boundary for escaping an additive noise floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\rho<1\), let \((v_k)_{k\geq0}\) be a bounded nonnegative sequence and define \[g_K=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\rho^{K-1-j}v_j.\] Then \(g_K\to0\) if and only if \(v_k\to0\). Consequently, every recursion \(u_{k+1}\leq\rho u_k+a v_k\), with \(u_0\geq0\) and \(a>0\), satisfies \(u_k\to0\) whenever \(v_k\to0\). For \(v_k=\sigma^2/b_k\), where \(\sigma^2>0\) is fixed and \(b_k\in\mathbb{N}\), one has \(v_k\to0\) if and only if \(b_k\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometrically accumulated stochastic forcing vanishes exactly when its per-iteration level vanishes. With fixed positive single-sample variance, batch sizes tending to infinity therefore escape the fixed-batch floor.
assumptions_latex: For the minibatch specialization, \(\sigma^2>0\) is fixed and \(b_k\in\mathbb{N}\).

notation.meaning: Positive integer batch size at iteration k.

children.title: Summable-Error Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Acceleration under diminishing deterministic evaluation errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Summable-Error Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of contractive accelerated maps under absolutely summable evaluation errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(x^\star\in X\), and let maps \(A_k:X\to X\) satisfy \(A_kx^\star=x^\star\) and \(\|A_kx-x^\star\|\leq\rho\|x-x^\star\|\) for a common \(0<\rho<1\). If \[x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+e_k,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|e_k\|<\infty,\] then \[\|x_k-x^\star\|\leq\rho^k\|x_0-x^\star\|+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\rho^{k-1-j}\|e_j\|\longrightarrow0.\] Thus summable deterministic evaluation errors preserve convergence of the accelerated outer iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly contractive accelerated maps still converge to their common fixed point when deterministic evaluation errors have a finite total magnitude.

notation.meaning: Exact accelerated outer map at iteration k.

children.title: Relative-Accuracy Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Accuracy Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative map-evaluation accuracy sufficient to retain a strict contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to X\) have fixed point \(x^\star\) and satisfy \(\|Ax-x^\star\|\leq\rho\|x-x^\star\|\), where \(0<\rho<1\). An inexact evaluation \(y\) satisfies the relative-accuracy interface at \(x\) when \[\|y-Ax\|\leq\eta\|x-Ax\|.\] Since \(\|x-Ax\|\leq(1+\rho)\|x-x^\star\|\), one has \[\|y-x^\star\|\leq\bigl(\rho+(1+\rho)\eta\bigr)\|x-x^\star\|.\] Strict contraction is retained whenever \(0\leq\eta<(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounding inner error relative to the exact fixed-point residual preserves contraction when the relative tolerance is below the stated threshold.

notation.meaning: Inexact value returned in place of the exact map value.

children.title: Adaptive Inner-Solve Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that vary inner-solve effort as acceleration progresses.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Inner-Solve Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certified adaptive stopping for an inner solver evaluating the outer accelerated map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\), an exact outer map \(A_k\), a tolerance \(0<\eta_k<1\), and an inner solver producing pairs \((y_{k,m},\Delta_{k,m})\) with \(\Delta_{k,m}\geq\|y_{k,m}-A_kx_k\|\), initialize \(m=0\) and refine until \[\Delta_{k,m}\leq\eta_k\|x_k-y_{k,m}\|.\] Set \(x_{k+1}=y_{k,m}\). If \(A_k\) contracts toward a common fixed point by \(\rho\), then the accepted iterate obeys \[\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|\leq\frac{\rho+\eta_k}{1-\eta_k}\|x_k-x^\star\|.\] Stop the outer iteration when its prescribed residual test holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine the inner solve until its certified error is small relative to the computed outer step, then accept the result.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta_{k,m}\) is a computable upper bound for \(\|y_{k,m}-A_kx_k\|\).
The inner refinement eventually satisfies the stopping test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=y_{k,m_k}\), where \(m_k\) is the first accepted inner index.

notation.meaning: Inner approximation after m refinement steps.
Certified upper bound on the inner evaluation error.

children.title: Outer–Inner Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between outer acceleration progress and inner computational effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer–Inner Accuracy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-logarithmic inner work under geometrically tightened inner tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(u_{k+1}\leq\rho u_k+\tau_k\), where \(0<\rho<\theta<1\), and choose \(\tau_k=\tau_0\theta^k\). Then \[u_K\leq\rho^K u_0+\tau_0\frac{\theta^K-\rho^K}{\theta-\rho}=O(\theta^K).\] Hence \(K=O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) outer iterations suffice for \(u_K\leq\varepsilon\). If producing tolerance \(\tau\) costs at most \(c_0+c_1\log(\tau_0/\tau)\) inner iterations, then total inner work through iteration \(K-1\) is \[Kc_0+\frac{c_1K(K-1)}{2}\log(1/\theta)=O(\log^2(1/\varepsilon)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometrically tightening inner tolerances preserves linear outer convergence but yields order log²(ε⁻¹) total inner work for logarithmic-cost inner solvers.
assumptions_latex: Inner cost at tolerance \(\tau\) is at most \(c_0+c_1\log(\tau_0/\tau)\).

notation.meaning: Absolute inner evaluation tolerance at outer iteration k.

children.title: Nonstationary Acceleration

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracking property for uniformly contractive accelerated maps with moving fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_k:X\to X\) satisfy \(A_kx_k^\star=x_k^\star\) and \(\|A_kx-A_ky\|\leq\rho\|x-y\|\) for a uniform \(0<\rho<1\). For the nonstationary iteration \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k\), define \(d_k=\|x_{k+1}^\star-x_k^\star\|\). Then \[\|x_{k+1}-x_{k+1}^\star\|\leq\rho\|x_k-x_k^\star\|+d_k,\] and therefore \[\|x_K-x_K^\star\|\leq\rho^K\|x_0-x_0^\star\|+\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\rho^{K-1-j}d_j.\] In particular, \(d_k\to0\) implies asymptotically vanishing tracking error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly contractive sequence of accelerated maps tracks moving fixed points up to a geometrically weighted sum of their drift.

notation.meaning: Fixed point of the map used at iteration k.
