children.title: Variable-Map Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Acceleration across histories generated by members of a changing map family.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Map Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded residual extrapolation using history residuals recomputed under the current map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given maps \(T_k:X\to X\), a history length \(m\in\mathbb{N}_0\), a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), a safeguard parameter \(0<\kappa<1\), and an initial point \(x_0\), first return \(x_k\) if \(\|T_k(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\). Otherwise let \(I_k=\{\max(0,k-m),\ldots,k\}\). For every \(i\in I_k\), recompute \(r_i^{(k)}=T_k(x_i)-x_i\), choose \[\alpha^{(k)}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i=1}\left\|\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i r_i^{(k)}\right\|,\] and form \(y_k=\sum_{i\in I_k}\alpha_i^{(k)}T_k(x_i)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) if \(\|T_k(y_k)-y_k\|\leq\kappa\|T_k(x_k)-x_k\|\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=T_k(x_k)\). Repeat the procedure at the next iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, stop if the current-map residual meets the prescribed tolerance. Otherwise recompute retained residuals with the current map, form a constrained least-residual extrapolation, and reject it unless it passes the residual safeguard.
assumptions_latex: Current-map evaluations \(T_k(x_i)\) are available for retained history points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the stopping test is reached, the returned iterate \(x_k\) satisfies \(\|T_k(x_k)-x_k\|\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Indices retained in the acceleration history.
Residual of history point i under the current map.

children.title: Map-Drift Stability
children.top_down_role: Limits on historical relevance under operator drift.

knowledge_statements.title: Map-Drift Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of accelerated fixed-point iteration under uniformly bounded map drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to X\) have fixed point \(x^\star\) and satisfy \(\|Ax-x^\star\|\leq\rho\|x-x^\star\|\) for \(0<\rho<1\). Suppose evolving maps \(A_k\) obey \(\|A_kx-Ax\|\leq\delta_k\) on the orbit, and set \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k\). Then \[\|x_K-x^\star\|\leq\rho^K\|x_0-x^\star\|+\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\rho^{K-1-j}\delta_j.\] Consequently, \(\delta_k\to0\) implies \(x_k\to x^\star\), while \(\sup_k\delta_k\leq\bar\delta\) gives \(\limsup_k\|x_k-x^\star\|\leq\bar\delta/(1-\rho)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map drift enters the accelerated error as geometrically filtered forcing; vanishing drift preserves convergence, while persistent drift creates a bounded tracking neighborhood.

notation.meaning: Evolving map used at iteration k.
Current map's deviation from the reference map on the orbit.

children.title: Cross-Map History Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where information from different effective maps remains usable.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Map History Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A singular-value criterion ensuring stored residual history remains usable after map changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For retained points \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let the current-map residual matrix be \(R_k=[T_k(x_i)-x_i]_{i=1}^m\) and the stored cross-map matrix be \(\widetilde R_k=[T_i(x_i)-x_i]_{i=1}^m\). The history is \(\gamma\)-compatible with \(T_k\) when \[\|\widetilde R_k-R_k\|_2\leq\gamma\sigma_{\min}(R_k),\qquad 0\leq\gamma<1.\] If \(R_k\) has full column rank, then \(\widetilde R_k\) also has full column rank and \[\|\widetilde R_k^\dagger\|_2\leq\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)\sigma_{\min}(R_k)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stored residuals are compatible when map drift is smaller than the current residual matrix's least singular value; this preserves rank and controls least-squares conditioning.

notation.meaning: History residual matrix recomputed with the current map.
Residual matrix assembled from historically stored maps.

children.title: Stale-History Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure of history-based models when the effective map drifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-History Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Drift boundary for multisecant acceleration of a sequence of fixed-point maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_k:X\to X\) act on a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(r_k(x)=T_k(x)-x\). A history pair formed at iteration \(i<k\) is stale at iteration \(k\) when
\[
\delta_{k,i}:=\|r_k(x_i)-r_i(x_i)\|\geq \eta\,\|r_i(x_i)-r_i(x_{i-1})\|,
\]
where \(\eta>0\) is the admissible relative-drift threshold. If this holds for any pair used by the multisecant model, stationary-map secant relations no longer approximate the current residual reliably; the affected pair must be discarded, downweighted, or recomputed before an accelerated proposal is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: History becomes stale when map drift at a stored point is comparable to its recorded residual change, invalidating the stationary-map secant model.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and every stored residual is well defined.
\(\eta>0\) is fixed by the acceleration safeguard.

notation.meaning: Residual of the iteration map used at iteration k.
Change in a stored residual caused solely by map drift.

children.title: Energy Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Globalization safeguards based on objective or merit-energy progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient-decrease acceptance test for an accelerated fixed-point proposal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be an energy bounded below, let \(R:X\to X\) be a residual map, and let \(y_k\) be an accelerated proposal from \(x_k\). For \(c>0\), the energy safeguard accepts \(y_k\) only if
\[
E(y_k)\leq E(x_k)-c\|R(x_k)\|^2.
\]
If the inequality fails or \(E(y_k)=+\infty\), the proposal is rejected and a prescribed safe baseline point is used. Thus every accepted accelerated step produces energy decrease proportional to the squared current residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an accelerated proposal only when it decreases a lower-bounded energy by at least a fixed multiple of the squared residual.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is bounded below on the generated level set.
review_flags: needs an authoritative nonconvex fixed-point globalization source for the stated sufficient-decrease test

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Energy Safeguards leaf, but no source supports this particular residual-squared sufficient-decrease test and fallback rule.

children.title: Envelope Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Globalization safeguards based on smooth or regularized envelope progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance through a smooth envelope representing the underlying nonsmooth objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex on a Hilbert space, and let \(\lambda>0\). Define its Moreau envelope by
\[
f_\lambda(x)=\inf_{z\in X}\left\{f(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|z-x\|^2\right\}.
\]
Given an accelerated proposal \(y_k\), a reference value \(M_k\), and \(c>0\), the envelope safeguard accepts only when \(f_\lambda(y_k)\leq M_k-c\|y_k-x_k\|^2\). Otherwise it rejects the proposal in favor of a designated safe step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate accelerated proposals with a Moreau envelope and accept only candidates satisfying a prescribed envelope decrease test.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of f with parameter lambda.

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

review_flags: the source supports the envelope definition; the acceleration acceptance test needs direct confirmation

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Beck's cited section supports the Moreau-envelope definition, not the proposed accelerated-candidate acceptance rule, reference sequence, or fallback consequence.

children.title: Energy–Envelope Acceptance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where energy tests and envelope tests support comparable acceptance decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy–Envelope Acceptance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjunctive, disjunctive, and switching combinations of energy and envelope tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_k^E\) denote the predicate \(E(y_k)\leq E_k^{\mathrm{ref}}-c_E\|R(x_k)\|^2\), and let \(A_k^V\) denote \(V(y_k)\leq V_k^{\mathrm{ref}}-c_V\|y_k-x_k\|^2\), where \(c_E,c_V>0\). Three well-defined acceptance regimes are: conjunctive, \(A_k^E\land A_k^V\); disjunctive, \(A_k^E\lor A_k^V\); and switching, \(A_k^E\) when a prescribed predicate \(S_k\) holds and \(A_k^V\) otherwise. The selected regime must be fixed before evaluating \(y_k\); rejection invokes the baseline safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combine energy and envelope tests by a fixed conjunctive, disjunctive, or state-dependent switching rule, with rejection sent to the baseline step.
assumptions_latex: Both merit quantities and their reference levels are finite at the test point.
The switching predicate \(S_k\), if used, is determined before acceptance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate is accepted exactly when the predicate of the selected regime is true.

notation.meaning: Predicate selecting the active merit test.

review_flags: needs a direct source for combined energy-envelope acceptance regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the leaf, but the claim that conjunctive, disjunctive, and switching rules constitute established energy–envelope acceptance regimes requires a direct source.

children.title: Nonmonotone Line-Search Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Controlled nonmonotonicity for accelerated proposals.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Line-Search Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed sufficient-decrease globalization of an accelerated search direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), direction \(d_k\), merit function \(\Phi\), memory length \(q\geq1\), \(c>0\), and \(\beta\in(0,1)\), set
\[
M_k=\max_{\max\{0,k-q+1\}\leq i\leq k}\Phi(x_i).
\]
Choose the least integer \(j_k\geq0\) for which, with \(t_k=\beta^{j_k}\),
\[
\Phi(x_k+t_kd_k)\leq M_k-c t_k\|d_k\|^2.
\]
Accept \(x_{k+1}=x_k+t_kd_k\). If no acceptable trial is found within the prescribed search budget, reject the accelerated direction and invoke the baseline fallback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtrack an accelerated direction against the largest recent merit value, permitting controlled increases while requiring sufficient decrease relative to that reference.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi(x_i)\) is finite for the stored reference window.
Trial points and merit values can be evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted point satisfies \(\Phi(x_{k+1})\leq M_k-c t_k\|d_k\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Maximum merit value over the recent window.

source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals
source_refs.locator: 3.1 General Structure of a Line-Search p. 71

review_flags: direct support for the finite-window nonmonotone reference rule remains to be checked

source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals
source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 General Structure of a Line-Search p. 71

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic line-search citation does not establish the finite-window maximum reference, the stated decrease term, or its use for accelerated proposals. A direct nonmonotone line-search source is required.

children.title: Fallback-Restart Recovery Interface
children.top_down_role: Recovery families for rejected or unstable accelerated proposals.

children.title: Baseline Fallback
children.top_down_role: Recovery through a trusted unaccelerated or safeguarded baseline map.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Fallback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe fixed-point update used after rejection of an accelerated proposal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to X\) be the baseline fixed-point map and let \(y_k\) be an accelerated proposal from \(x_k\). Compute \(b_k=T(x_k)\) and evaluate a prescribed Boolean safeguard \(A_k(y_k)\). Set
\[
x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}y_k,&A_k(y_k)=\mathrm{true},\\ b_k,&A_k(y_k)=\mathrm{false}.
\end{cases}
\]
The output is therefore always either the accepted accelerated candidate or one complete baseline iteration. If baseline evaluation itself fails, the algorithm terminates with failure rather than silently accepting \(y_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an accelerated candidate fails its safeguard, replace it with one evaluable step of the underlying fixed-point method.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x_k)\) is defined whenever fallback is invoked.
The acceptance predicate \(A_k\) is fixed before testing \(y_k\).

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

review_flags: fallback interface should be checked against a safeguarded acceleration source

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited material supports baseline fixed-point iteration generally but does not directly support this safeguarded acceleration interface or its failure-handling rule.

children.title: Acceleration Restart
children.top_down_role: Recovery through clearing or shortening unstable acceleration histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Restart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reset of all history-dependent acceleration state while preserving the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a restart index \(k\), retain the current point \(x_k\) and erase all stored displacement, residual-difference, and extrapolation-coefficient data. Set the effective history length to \(m_k=0\), compute the next point by the baseline rule \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), and begin rebuilding history only from pairs generated after index \(k\). No pre-restart pair may enter a subsequent accelerated model unless it is explicitly revalidated for the current map and metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart acceleration by clearing its history, taking a baseline step, and rebuilding the model solely from post-restart information.
assumptions_latex: The baseline map \(T\) is defined at \(x_k\).
The acceleration state can be separated from the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After restart, \(m_k=0\), \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), and subsequent history is post-restart history.

notation.meaning: Effective number of stored history pairs.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_refs.locator: 12 Acceleration p. 255; 12.3 When does an acceleration accelerate? p. 260

review_flags: exact restart state and revalidation rule need direct source confirmation

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_witnesses.locator: 12 Acceleration p. 255; 12.3 When does an acceleration accelerate? p. 260

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precise restart semantics—clearing every history component, forcing a baseline step, and excluding all pre-restart pairs absent revalidation—need direct support from a restart or safeguarded-acceleration source.

children.title: Fallback-Triggered Restart
children.top_down_role: Recovery regimes combining rejected proposals with history resets.

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback-Triggered Restart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled recovery rule that resets acceleration whenever fallback is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_k\) be an accelerated proposal, \(b_k=T(x_k)\) the baseline point, and \(A_k(y_k)\) the safeguard predicate. If \(A_k(y_k)\) is true, set \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) and retain eligible history. If it is false, set \(x_{k+1}=b_k\), clear every history-dependent acceleration variable, and set the next effective history length to zero. Hence each fallback event is also a restart event, preventing the rejected model from influencing the next proposal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treat every rejected accelerated proposal as both a baseline fallback and a complete reset of the acceleration history.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x_k)\) exists whenever the safeguard rejects the proposal.
The acceptance predicate is evaluated before the acceleration state is updated.

notation.meaning: History length available to the next acceleration model.

review_flags: needs a direct safeguarded-acceleration source coupling fallback to mandatory restart

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf, but no source establishes that every fallback event must trigger a complete acceleration restart.

children.title: Algebraic Instability
children.top_down_role: Instabilities caused by dependent, ill-conditioned, or finite-precision history information.

children.title: History Rank Deficiency
children.top_down_role: Degenerate secant and extrapolation histories.

knowledge_statements.title: History Rank Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic degeneracy of multisecant residual or displacement histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_k=[h_{k-m},\ldots,h_{k-1}]\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) be the history matrix used in a multisecant or extrapolation subproblem. The history is rank deficient exactly when
\[
\operatorname{rank}(H_k)<m,
\]
equivalently when its smallest singular value is zero. Then the Gram matrix \(H_k^{\mathsf T}H_k\) is singular, unconstrained normal-equation coefficients are not uniquely determined, and coefficient sensitivity is unbounded under arbitrarily small perturbations. A stable implementation must truncate, regularize, or restart rather than invert the Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history matrix with dependent columns has a singular Gram matrix, nonunique least-squares coefficients, and unbounded perturbation sensitivity.
assumptions_latex: \(H_k\) has \(m\) stored columns in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
Coefficients are computed through the associated least-squares or Gram system.

notation.meaning: Stored secant, displacement, or residual-difference matrix.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary singular-value and Gram-matrix characterization
requires an acceleration-specific source for the operational truncation or restart consequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gram-matrix implication is standard, but no citation is supplied. Moreover, equivalence with a zero smallest singular value needs either m≤n or an explicit convention including the zero eigenvalues of H_k^T H_k; the sensitivity and mandatory-response claims also need support.

children.title: Extrapolation-Coefficient Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Numerical sensitivity from large extrapolation coefficients.

children.title: Extrapolation-Coefficient Growth
children.top_down_role: Numerical sensitivity caused by large acceleration coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Extrapolation-Coefficient Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient blow-up caused by nearly dependent residual histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For residual columns \(R=[r_1,\ldots,r_m]\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), consider affine extrapolation coefficients
\[
\alpha\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}a=1}\|Ra\|_2.
\]
Let \(Q\) have orthonormal columns spanning \(\mathbf1^\perp\), and write \(a=m^{-1}\mathbf1+Qz\). If \(\sigma_{\min}(RQ)\downarrow0\) while the component of \(Rm^{-1}\mathbf1\) along the corresponding left singular direction remains nonzero, then every minimizing correction has \(\|z\|_2\to\infty\). Thus near dependence of the affine residual model can force unbounded extrapolation coefficients despite a small fitted residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly dependent residual histories can make affine least-squares extrapolation coefficients diverge even while the fitted residual remains small.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is an orthonormal basis matrix for \(\mathbf1^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated nonvanishing alignment, \(\sigma_{\min}(RQ)\to0\) implies \(\|\alpha\|_2\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis for the zero-sum coefficient subspace.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: constrained least-squares sensitivity under vanishing restricted singular value
needs a direct source for the precise coefficient-growth statement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precise coefficient-growth conclusion is not reliable as stated: a merely nonzero singular-direction component need not dominate the vanishing singular value, and alpha is set-valued without a minimizer-selection convention. A sourced formulation should specify a sequence, quantitative alignment, and treatment of nonunique minimizers.

children.title: Finite-Precision Cancellation
children.top_down_role: Loss of numerical information when large extrapolated terms nearly cancel.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Cancellation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-error amplification in signed extrapolated combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i z_i\) be evaluated by sequential floating-point multiply-add operations with unit roundoff \(u\), assuming no overflow or underflow and \((2m-1)u<1\). Then the computed vector \(\widehat y\) satisfies a componentwise forward-error bound implying
\[
\|\widehat y-y\|\leq\gamma_{2m-1}\sum_{i=1}^m|\alpha_i|\,\|z_i\|,
\qquad
\gamma_p=\frac{pu}{1-pu}.
\]
Consequently, if cancellation makes \(\|y\|\ll\sum_i|\alpha_i|\|z_i\|\), the relative error can be arbitrarily large even though each arithmetic operation is backward stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large signed extrapolation terms may cancel in exact arithmetic, making the relative floating-point error arbitrarily large despite small per-operation errors.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic has unit roundoff \(u\) and introduces no overflow or underflow.
The sum is evaluated sequentially and \((2m-1)u<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widehat y-y\|\leq\gamma_{2m-1}\sum_i|\alpha_i|\|z_i\|\), so severe cancellation destroys a uniform relative-error bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical floating-point summation error model
requires an authoritative numerical-analysis locator supporting the exact operation count and bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cancellation phenomenon is standard, but an authoritative numerical-analysis locator is required for the exact gamma_{2m-1} bound. The vector norm and componentwise-to-norm error model must also be specified.

children.title: Coefficient-Growth Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Ranges where coefficient magnitudes undermine reliable residual improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Growth Stability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform forward-stability boundary for affine extrapolation in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider affine extrapolates \(y_k=\sum_{i=1}^{m_k}\alpha_{k,i}z_{k,i}\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_{k,i}=1\), computed in floating-point arithmetic of unit roundoff \(u\), where \(m_k\leq m_{\max}\) and \(\|z_{k,i}\|\leq Z\). If \(\|\alpha_k\|_1\leq C\) uniformly, then
\[
\|\widehat y_k-y_k\|\leq\gamma_{2m_{\max}-1}CZ.
\]
If \(\|\alpha_k\|_1\) is unbounded, no iteration-uniform forward-error bound depending only on \(u\), \(m_{\max}\), and \(Z\) follows. Thus a coefficient cap or regularization threshold defines the finite-precision stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly bounded coefficient one-norms give a uniform absolute rounding-error bound; unbounded coefficient growth removes that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(m_k\leq m_{\max}\), \(\|z_{k,i}\|\leq Z\), and no overflow or underflow occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform bound \(\|\alpha_k\|_1\leq C\) yields uniform forward stability, whereas unbounded \(\|\alpha_k\|_1\) precludes this bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of the classical floating-point linear-combination bound
needs an acceleration-specific source validating coefficient clipping or regularization as the stated boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated absolute error estimate is a plausible consequence of a floating-point linear-combination bound, but no source supports the exact bound or the acceleration-specific clipping/regularization boundary. Calling it uniform forward stability is stronger than merely obtaining a uniform absolute-error bound.

children.title: Finite-Precision Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Loss of useful residual progress through rounding and ill-conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational stagnation threshold for a floating-point fixed-point accelerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to X\), let \(r(x)=T(x)-x\), and let \(\widehat x_k\) and \(\widehat r_k=\operatorname{fl}(T(\widehat x_k)-\widehat x_k)\) be computed in unit roundoff \(u\). Suppose \(\|\widehat r_k-r(\widehat x_k)\|\leq \eta_k\), where \(\eta_k=c_k u\kappa_k\) represents accumulated rounding amplified by conditioning. Finite-precision stagnation occurs once \(\|r(\widehat x_k)\|\lesssim\eta_k\): residual changes are then indistinguishable from evaluation error, and extrapolation coefficients computed from residual differences may cease to yield reliable progress even when \(r(\widehat x_k)\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagnation begins when the exact residual is no larger than its rounding-error floor, so computed residual improvements and extrapolation steps are no longer reliable.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and its residual are evaluated in floating-point arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|r(\widehat x_k)\|\lesssim c_k u\kappa_k\) is the finite-precision stagnation boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the error model and scale c_k u kappa_k require a finite-precision source and explicit interpretation of the amplification factors.

children.title: Dynamical Instability
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by aggressive extrapolation interacting with nonlinear dynamics.

children.title: Accelerated Motion Instability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Unstable motion around fixed points or solution manifolds.

children.title: Acceleration Overshoot
children.top_down_role: Accelerated proposals that move beyond a locally productive region.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Overshoot
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-mode overshoot event relative to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real inner-product space, let \(x_\star=T(x_\star)\), and let \(A_k:X\times X\to X\) define the accelerated iteration \(x_{k+1}=A_k(x_k,x_{k-1})\). For a nonzero direction \(v\in X\), define \(s_k=\langle v,x_k-x_\star\rangle\). An acceleration overshoot across the target hyperplane occurs at iteration \(k+1\) when \(s_ks_{k+1}<0\). It is an amplifying overshoot when additionally \(|s_{k+1}|>|s_k|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overshoot occurs when a monitored error component changes sign; it is amplifying when its magnitude also increases after crossing the target hyperplane.

notation.meaning: Signed error along the monitored direction.

children.title: Persistent Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Repeated motion around fixed points or solution manifolds without stable progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonvanishing alternating motion around a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_\star\) be a fixed point and let \((x_k)\) be generated by an accelerated iteration. The trajectory has persistent oscillation in a nonzero direction \(v\) if there exist \(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(k\geq K\), \(\langle v,x_k-x_\star\rangle\langle v,x_{k+1}-x_\star\rangle<0\) and \(|\langle v,x_k-x_\star\rangle|\geq\varepsilon\). The sign alternation therefore does not decay to the fixed point in that mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent oscillation is indefinite sign alternation of an error component whose amplitude remains bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v,x_k-x_\star\rangle\) alternates sign and has magnitude at least \(\varepsilon\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

notation.meaning: Positive lower bound on oscillation amplitude.

children.title: Overshoot-to-Oscillation Transition
children.top_down_role: Regimes where isolated excursions develop into sustained oscillatory behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Overshoot-to-Oscillation Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Modal real-root-to-oscillatory-root transition for constant-inertia acceleration of a linear fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a real invariant scalar eigenmode of a linear map \(T\), with real eigenvalue \(\lambda\), under \(y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\) and \(x_{k+1}=T(y_k)\), where \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) and \(\lambda\beta>0\). Its modal error satisfies \(e_{k+1}=\lambda(1+\beta)e_k-\lambda\beta e_{k-1}\), and the characteristic discriminant is \(\Delta=\lambda^2(1+\beta)^2-4\lambda\beta\). The boundary \(\Delta=0\) separates two real characteristic roots from a complex-conjugate pair. For \(\Delta<0\), every nonzero modal solution has an oscillatory sinusoidal form with an envelope that decays, remains constant, or grows according as the common root modulus is below, equal to, or above one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this real linear inertial mode, zero discriminant marks the transition from real characteristic roots to complex-conjugate roots and oscillatory modal behavior; real-root behavior need not itself constitute overshoot.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is linear on a real invariant scalar eigenmode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=0\) is the real-root-to-complex-root boundary, while \(\Delta<0\) yields oscillatory modal solutions.

notation.meaning: Real eigenvalue of the base fixed-point map on the mode.

children.title: Basin-Escape Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Accelerated iterates leaving a locally convergent region.

children.title: Basin-Escape Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Accelerated iterates leaving a region where the baseline dynamics are locally convergent.

knowledge_statements.title: Basin-Escape Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a local convergence guarantee after extrapolation leaves its basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subset X\) be a basin on which the unaccelerated map \(T\) is invariant and converges to \(x_\star\). For an extrapolated update \(y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1})\), \(x_{k+1}=T(y_k)\), a basin-escape event occurs when \(x_{k-1},x_k\in B\) but \(y_k\notin B\) or \(T(y_k)\notin B\). At that event the local invariance-based convergence guarantee no longer applies; subsequent iterates may enter another basin, cycle, encounter an undefined update, or diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration escapes a protected basin when extrapolation or its image leaves that basin, invalidating the local convergence guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Unaccelerated iterations starting in \(B\) converge to \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_k\notin B\) or \(T(y_k)\notin B\) is the basin-escape failure boundary for the local guarantee.

notation.meaning: Invariant convergence basin of the base map.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and failure-boundary kind match, but the nonlinear basin-escape formulation lacks a source. Under T(B) subseteq B, T(y_k) outside B cannot occur when y_k is in B, so the alternatives also require clarification.

children.title: Acceleration Divergence
children.top_down_role: Unbounded or nonconvergent trajectories caused by unstable acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral boundary for loss of local stability of a finite-dimensional accelerated state map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^{2n}\) be the lifted state map of a two-step accelerated iteration, let \(z_\star=(x_\star,x_\star)\) satisfy \(G(z_\star)=z_\star\), and suppose \(G\) is continuously differentiable near \(z_\star\). Write \(M=DG(z_\star)\). If \(\rho(M)>1\), then \(z_\star\) is locally unstable: there exist initial lifted states arbitrarily close to \(z_\star\) whose iterates leave a fixed neighborhood of \(z_\star\). Thus \(\rho(M)=1\) is the linearized spectral boundary between the sufficient stability regime \(\rho(M)<1\) and linearized instability when \(\rho(M)>1\); this conclusion concerns loss of local convergence and does not alone imply divergence to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the lifted accelerated map has a linearization with spectral radius above one, the fixed point is locally unstable, although this fact alone does not imply that trajectories diverge to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(G:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^{2n}\) is continuously differentiable near \(z_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(M)>1\) implies local instability of \(z_\star\), while \(\rho(M)=1\) is the linearized spectral boundary.

notation.meaning: Lifted fixed point of the accelerated state map.
Jacobian of the lifted map at its fixed point.

children.title: Post-Escape Recovery Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions separating recoverable basin excursions from irreversible divergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Escape Recovery Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient recovery condition based on re-entry followed by the invariant base contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subset X\) contain \(x_\star\), satisfy \(T(R)\subseteq R\), and obey \(\|T(x)-x_\star\|\leq q\|x-x_\star\|\) for every \(x\in R\), where \(0\leq q<1\). After an accelerated basin escape, suppose a safeguard produces an index \(K\) with \(x_K\in R\) and then disables acceleration so that \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) for every \(k\geq K\). Then \(x_k\in R\) for every \(k\geq K\) and \(\|x_k-x_\star\|\leq q^{k-K}\|x_K-x_\star\|\), hence \(x_k\to x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery is guaranteed once a safeguard returns the iterate to an invariant contraction region and subsequently uses the base contraction without acceleration.
assumptions_latex: \(\|T(x)-x_\star\|\leq q\|x-x_\star\|\) for every \(x\in R\), with \(0\leq q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\in R\) and \(\|x_k-x_\star\|\leq q^{k-K}\|x_K-x_\star\|\) for every \(k\geq K\), so \(x_k\to x_\star\).

notation.meaning: Contraction factor on the recovery region.
Index at which protected re-entry occurs.

children.title: Accelerated Attractor Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Persistent cycles and competing attractors under accelerated dynamics.

children.title: Accelerated Cycling
children.top_down_role: Persistent periodic or near-periodic trajectories under accelerated dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic attractor of the lifted accelerated dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a stationary two-step accelerator by a lifted map \(F:X\times X\to X\times X\), so that \(z_{k+1}=F(z_k)\). An accelerated cycle of prime period \(p\geq2\) is a collection of distinct states \(z_0,\ldots,z_{p-1}\) satisfying \(F(z_i)=z_{(i+1)\bmod p}\). It is an attracting cycle if some neighborhood \(U\) of the cycle satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(F^k(z),\{z_0,\ldots,z_{p-1}\})\to0\) for every \(z\in U\). Such a trajectory does not converge to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated cycling is convergence of the lifted iteration to an attracting periodic orbit of prime period at least two.
assumptions_latex: The accelerator induces a stationary lifted map \(F\) on \(X\times X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^p(z_i)=z_i\) with prime period \(p\geq2\), and attraction holds when nearby lifted states approach the cycle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the cycling leaf, but distance and neighborhood require a specified metric or normed state space, and no dynamical-systems source is supplied.

children.title: Accelerated Multistability
children.top_down_role: Coexistence of multiple attractors or limiting behaviors under acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Multistability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coexistence of multiple attracting invariant sets under one accelerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:Z\to Z\) be the lifted state map of a fixed accelerated iteration. The accelerator is multistable if there exist at least two distinct asymptotically stable compact invariant sets \(K_1,K_2\subset Z\) whose basins \(\mathcal B(K_i)=\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(F^k(z),K_i)\to0\}\) are both nonempty. The attractors may be fixed points, periodic cycles, or other compact invariant sets. Consequently, the asymptotic outcome is not determined by the algorithmic parameters alone but also by the initial lifted state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated multistability means that one accelerated map has multiple stable attractors with nonempty, distinct basins of attraction.
assumptions_latex: \(F:Z\to Z\) is a stationary accelerated state map.
The candidate attractors are compact and invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
There exist \(K_1
eq K_2\) with \(\mathcal B(K_1)
eq\varnothing\) and \(\mathcal B(K_2)
eq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Lifted state space of the accelerator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multistability role is appropriate, but distance on Z is undefined, and distinct invariant sets with merely nonempty convergence basins do not by themselves justify the plain-text claim that the basins are distinct.

children.title: Attractor-Selection Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of limiting behavior on initialization, perturbations, or acceleration history.

knowledge_statements.title: Attractor-Selection Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity near a boundary separating accelerated attractor basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:Z\to Z\) have distinct attractors \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) with basins \(\mathcal B(K_1)\) and \(\mathcal B(K_2)\). Attractor selection is sensitive at \(z\in\partial\mathcal B(K_1)\cap\partial\mathcal B(K_2)\): for every \(\delta>0\), there exist \(z_1,z_2\in Z\) such that \(\|z_i-z\|<\delta\), \(F^k(z_1)\) approaches \(K_1\), and \(F^k(z_2)\) approaches \(K_2\). Hence arbitrarily small initialization, rounding, or parameter-induced state perturbations can select different asymptotic attractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a shared basin boundary, arbitrarily close initial states can converge to different accelerated attractors.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has two distinct attractors with nonempty basins.
\(z\) lies on the boundary of both basins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every neighborhood of \(z\) contains initial states attracted to \(K_1\) and initial states attracted to \(K_2\).

notation.meaning: Boundary of the basin of attractor \(K_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared-basin-boundary formulation captures initialization sensitivity, but Z is not declared normed and the fixed-map hypotheses do not support the additional claim about parameter perturbations.

children.title: False or Mismeasured Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Cases where improvement in one surrogate measure does not reduce total solution cost.

children.title: Residual–Objective Decoupling
children.top_down_role: Residual improvement without comparable objective or stationarity progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Objective Decoupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scaled residual can be small while objective and stationarity errors remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), let \(T_\alpha(x)=(1-\alpha)x\) with \(0<\alpha<1\). Its unique fixed point and objective minimizer are \(x_\star=0\), while the fixed-point residual is \(r_\alpha(x)=T_\alpha(x)-x=-\alpha x\). At \(x=1\), \(\|r_\alpha(1)\|=\alpha\to0\) as \(\alpha\downarrow0\), but \(f(1)-f(x_\star)=\tfrac12\) and \(\|\nabla f(1)\|=1\). Thus an arbitrarily small raw residual need not imply comparable objective-gap or stationarity accuracy without an error bound uniform in the residual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling a fixed-point map can make its residual arbitrarily small while leaving the objective gap and gradient norm unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Residual accuracy is measured by the unnormalized norm \(\|T_\alpha(x)-x\|\).

children.title: Iteration–Work Decoupling
children.top_down_role: Reduced iteration counts offset by accelerator overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration–Work Decoupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-based criterion for whether iteration-count acceleration is genuine under an additive cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an accuracy tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Let \(N_b(\varepsilon),N_a(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb N_0\) be the baseline and accelerated iteration counts required to attain the same accuracy criterion. Let \(C_T>0\) be the baseline work per iteration, let \(m\in\mathbb N_0\) be the accelerator history length, let \(C_A(m)\geq0\) be its per-iteration overhead, and let \(C_0\geq0\) be its setup cost. Under additive accounting, \(W_b(\varepsilon)=N_b(\varepsilon)C_T\) and \(W_a(\varepsilon)=C_0+N_a(\varepsilon)(C_T+C_A(m))\). A lower accelerated iteration count constitutes work acceleration exactly when \(W_a(\varepsilon)<W_b(\varepsilon)\); the inequality \(N_a(\varepsilon)<N_b(\varepsilon)\) alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated additive cost model, fewer accelerated iterations give genuine work acceleration only when the total accelerated setup, baseline-step, and overhead costs are below the baseline total work.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) and both methods use the same accuracy criterion.
Work costs are additive under the stated accounting model.

notation.meaning: Accelerated and baseline iteration counts at tolerance epsilon.
Accelerator overhead per iteration at history length m.
Total accelerated and baseline work at tolerance epsilon.

children.title: Asymptotic–Transient Decoupling
children.top_down_role: Improved local behavior accompanied by poor transient performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic–Transient Decoupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates eventual local rate improvement from finite-tolerance performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two fixed-point schemes produce positive error sequences \(e_k^A\) and \(e_k^B\), and define \(K_M(\varepsilon)=\inf\{k:e_k^M\leq\varepsilon\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Asymptotic–transient decoupling occurs when \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{e_{k+1}^A}{e_k^A}<\liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{e_{k+1}^B}{e_k^B},\] while \(K_A(\varepsilon)>K_B(\varepsilon)\) throughout a nonempty operational tolerance interval. Thus scheme \(A\) has the better eventual contraction factor but requires more iterations at every tolerance actually evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method may have a better eventual convergence factor yet require more iterations over every practically tested tolerance because its transient phase is worse.
assumptions_latex: The displayed asymptotic ratios are well defined as extended real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is asymptotically faster although \(B\) is faster on the stated operational tolerance interval.

notation.meaning: error of method M after iteration k

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal acceleration-evaluation boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation fits the terminal container and is mathematically coherent, but no source or inspectable locator supports this formal asymptotic-versus-operational comparison.

children.title: Evaluation Biases
children.top_down_role: Apparent gains caused by favorable residual scaling or cost accounting.

children.title: Representation Bias
children.top_down_role: Apparent gains caused by favorable residual scaling or problem representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes rankings that depend on an arbitrary coordinate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let physical residuals \(r_A,r_B\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be represented after an invertible coordinate change by \(Sr_A,Sr_B\), where \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). A Euclidean-residual comparison exhibits representation bias if \[\|r_A\|_2<\|r_B\|_2\quad\text{but}\quad\|Sr_A\|_2>\|Sr_B\|_2.\] More generally, a reported ranking is representation-biased whenever it changes under an admissible reparameterization although the underlying physical states and algorithmic trajectories are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representation bias occurs when an admissible coordinate change reverses a method ranking even though the underlying states and trajectories are unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Both methods are evaluated at corresponding physical states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual-norm ranking is not invariant under the chosen representation.

notation.meaning: physical residual vectors for the compared methods

review_flags: The supplied sources do not contain a specific representation-bias criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly captures representation-dependent ranking reversal and fits the Evaluation Bias Taxonomy, but it has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Benchmark Bias
children.top_down_role: Apparent gains caused by instance selection, baselines, or evaluation conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines evaluation bias caused by a nonrepresentative problem distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_M(z)\) be the evaluation loss of method \(M\) on instance \(z\), let \(P\) be the target-instance distribution, and let \(Q\) be the benchmark distribution. Benchmark bias reverses the target ranking of methods \(A\) and \(B\) when \[\mathbb{E}_{z\sim Q}[L_A(z)]<\mathbb{E}_{z\sim Q}[L_B(z)]\quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{E}_{z\sim P}[L_A(z)]>\mathbb{E}_{z\sim P}[L_B(z)].\] The same definition applies to finite suites by taking \(Q\) as their empirical distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark bias occurs when performance averaged over the benchmark ranks two methods oppositely from performance over the intended problem population.
assumptions_latex: The displayed expectations exist and use the same loss definition.
Lower values of \(L_M\) indicate better performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark ranking does not represent the ranking under the target distribution.

notation.meaning: evaluation loss of method M on instance z

review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses benchmark-distribution bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional ranking-reversal condition matches Benchmark Bias and is internally precise, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Cost-Accounting Bias
children.top_down_role: Apparent acceleration caused by incomplete accounting of oracle, memory, or inner-solve costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Accounting Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detects ranking reversals between iteration counts and total computational work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For method \(M\), let \(K_M(\varepsilon)\) be the first iteration attaining a common tolerance and let \(c_{M,k}\geq0\) be the work charged to iteration \(k\). Define total work by \(C_M(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=0}^{K_M(\varepsilon)-1}c_{M,k}\). Iteration-only reporting has cost-accounting bias for methods \(A,B\) if \[K_A(\varepsilon)<K_B(\varepsilon)\quad\text{but}\quad C_A(\varepsilon)>C_B(\varepsilon).\] Relevant charges include base-operator evaluations, linear algebra, memory operations, rejected trials, and safeguard restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-accounting bias occurs when fewer reported iterations conceal greater total work under a common, inclusive accounting model.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same stopping tolerance and correctness test.
The per-iteration charges use a common resource model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iteration count alone reverses the ranking induced by total computational work.
review_flags: The source inventory lacks a locator establishing this inclusive accounting criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition appropriately distinguishes iteration count from total work and fits Cost-Accounting Bias, but the inclusive accounting criterion lacks supporting evidence with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Model-Mismatch Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by accelerator models incompatible with the active operator regime.

children.title: Noncontractive Local Models
children.top_down_role: Local models lacking the stability expected by an accelerator.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncontractive Local Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral obstruction to a locally contractive fixed-point model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be Fréchet differentiable at a fixed point \(x^\star\), and set \(J=DT(x^\star)\). If \(\rho(J)\geq1\), then no vector norm with its induced operator norm can satisfy \(\|J\|<1\). Consequently, the first-order model \(T(x^\star+h)=x^\star+Jh+o(\|h\|)\) cannot justify strict local contraction. Any accelerator whose stability argument requires such contraction is therefore outside that argument's validity regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the fixed-point Jacobian has spectral radius at least one, no induced norm makes its local linear model strictly contractive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(DT(x^\star))\geq1\) obstructs a strict local contraction model.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the fixed-point map at the fixed point

children.title: Nonsmooth Active-Set Changes
children.top_down_role: History information crossing incompatible local operator pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Active-Set Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multisecant histories become inconsistent when they cross incompatible operator pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a residual map be piecewise affine, with \(r(x)=J_i x+b_i\) on regions \(R_i\). For history points \(x_0,\ldots,x_m\), form \(\Delta x_j=x_j-x_{j-1}\) and \(\Delta r_j=r(x_j)-r(x_{j-1})\). If the history crosses active regions and no matrix \(J\) satisfies \(\Delta r_j=J\Delta x_j\) for every \(j\), then the history is incompatible with a single local affine model. An unsafeguarded multisecant extrapolation fitted to all these pairs consequently lacks a valid one-piece local-model interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When history points cross incompatible active regions, their secants may admit no common local linear model, invalidating unsafeguarded multisecant extrapolation.
assumptions_latex: The residual map is piecewise affine on the relevant neighborhood.
At least two stored points belong to distinct active regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of a common secant matrix certifies local-model mismatch across the stored history.

notation.meaning: linear part of the residual on region i

review_flags: No supplied source locator treats active-set changes in multisecant acceleration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional incompatibility criterion is mathematically sound and matches the active-set model-mismatch container, but no source locator supports its application to multisecant acceleration.

children.title: Noise-Dominated Histories
children.top_down_role: Extrapolation models fitting noise instead of useful dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Dominated Histories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when residual-history information is no larger than its perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose observed residual differences form \(\widehat R=R+E\), where \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) is the exact history matrix and \(E\) contains noise differences. The history is noise-dominated when \[\|E\|_2\geq\sigma_{\min}(R).\] At this boundary, an admissible perturbation of the observed magnitude can make the history rank deficient, so least-squares or multisecant coefficients based on \(\widehat R\) have no uniform relative-stability guarantee without regularization, truncation, or restarting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual history is noise-dominated when noise is at least as large as its smallest singular direction, allowing loss of rank and unstable extrapolation.
assumptions_latex: Noise is measured in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|E\|_2\geq\sigma_{\min}(R)\) permits noise to erase an informative history direction.
review_flags: The singular-value boundary is standard perturbation mathematics, but no supporting locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value threshold gives a coherent existential rank-loss boundary and the failure_boundary kind fits the container, but no perturbation-theory or acceleration source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Overacceleration of Fast Base Methods
children.top_down_role: Acceleration degrading superlinear, quadratic, or already accelerated base dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Overacceleration of Fast Base Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stale extrapolation can destroy an already superlinear scalar error law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p>1\), choose \(e_0\in(0,1)\), and define the base error by \(e_{k+1}=e_k^p\), which converges superlinearly to zero. Fix coefficients \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_m\) with \(m\geq1\), \(\alpha_m\neq0\), and define the accelerated candidate \(\widetilde e_{k+1}=\sum_{j=0}^m\alpha_j e_{k-j}\). Then \[|\widetilde e_{k+1}|\sim|\alpha_m|e_{k-m},\qquad \frac{|\widetilde e_{k+1}|}{e_{k+1}}\to+\infty.\] Thus retaining a fixed nonzero weight on the oldest state can degrade rather than accelerate the superlinear base dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a superlinear scalar recurrence, any fixed nonzero weight on the oldest stored error asymptotically overwhelms the new base error.
assumptions_latex: The extrapolation depth and coefficients are fixed, with \(\alpha_m\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extrapolated candidate is asymptotically much larger than the base method's next error.
review_flags: The counterexample is explicit, but the supplied inventory has no matching acceleration-failure source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit scalar construction is internally correct and counterexample is the proper content kind, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale satisfying the evidence contract.

children.title: Absent-Solution Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Behavior when exact fixed points do not exist or the represented problem is inconsistent.

children.title: Minimal-Displacement Behavior
children.top_down_role: Residual behavior in the absence of exact fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Displacement Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual lower bound determined by the minimal-displacement vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be a nonexpansive mapping on a real Hilbert space, and define its minimal-displacement vector by \[v=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}(0).\] For every \(x\in H\), \(x-Tx\in\operatorname{ran}(I-T)\), hence \(\|x-Tx\|\geq\|v\|\). In particular, if \(v\neq0\), then \(T\) has no fixed point and no sequence of iterates or accelerated candidates can have fixed-point residual converging to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal-displacement norm lower-bounds every fixed-point residual; if it is positive, exact fixed points and vanishing residuals are impossible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-Tx\|\geq\|v\|\) for every \(x\in H\), and \(v\neq0\) excludes fixed points.

notation.meaning: metric projection of zero onto the closed convex set C

children.title: Primal Failure Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Certificate interfaces exposed through accelerated splitting maps.

children.title: Infeasibility Certificate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Certificate interfaces exposing inconsistency through accelerated splitting maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificate Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic certificate interface for proving primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex cone. A vector \(y\) is an infeasibility certificate if \[A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\] Verification requires one adjoint multiplication, a dual-cone membership test, and a scalar sign test. If these conditions hold, no \(x\in K\) can satisfy \(Ax=b\), because feasibility would imply \(b^{\mathsf T}y=\langle A^{\mathsf T}y,x\rangle\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector certifies conic infeasibility when its adjoint image lies in the dual cone while its pairing with the right-hand side is negative.
assumptions_latex: The dual cone is \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \text{for all}\ x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of such a vector \(y\) certifies that \(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\).
review_flags: A direct conic alternative-theorem or infeasibility-certificate locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed dual-cone predicate is a correct infeasibility certificate and certificate is the correct content kind. However, no conic alternative-theorem locator is supplied, and the final explanatory clause contains proof text that should be removed once a source-backed replacement is prepared.

children.title: Unboundedness Certificate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Certificate interfaces exposing recession or unbounded behavior through splitting representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Certificate Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic recession-direction interface for certifying primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a convex cone. An unboundedness certificate consists of a feasible point \(\bar x\) and a direction \(d\) satisfying \[A\bar x=b,\quad \bar x\in K,\qquad Ad=0,\quad d\in K,\quad c^{\mathsf T}d<0.\] Then \(\bar x+td\) is feasible for every \(t\geq0\), while \(c^{\mathsf T}(\bar x+td)\to-\infty\). These displayed equalities, memberships, and inequalities form a directly checkable certificate interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point plus a cone-feasible null-space direction of negative cost certifies that a conic minimization problem is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The optimization problem is a minimization problem with linear objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible objective values are unbounded below.
review_flags: A direct conic unboundedness-certificate locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-point and negative-cost recession-direction interface correctly certifies unboundedness below and fits the certificate container. It lacks a direct source locator, and the sentence deriving the feasible ray and limiting objective is proof text.

children.title: Certificate-Outcome Separation
children.top_down_role: Diagnostic distinctions between infeasible and unbounded problem outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Outcome Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates algorithmic termination labels from independently verified mathematical certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic primal problem \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), an algorithmic status is not itself a mathematical certificate. The outcome \(\mathrm{infeasible}\) is certified only by data satisfying the infeasibility-certificate predicate, whereas \(\mathrm{unbounded}\) is certified only by a feasible base point and negative-cost recession direction satisfying the unboundedness predicate. A small fixed-point residual, residual stagnation, iteration-limit termination, or divergent iterates alone satisfies neither interface and therefore establishes neither outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver behavior or a termination label does not prove infeasibility or unboundedness; each outcome requires its own independently checkable certificate.
assumptions_latex: The certificate predicates use the same primal data \((A,b,c,K)\).
All cone-membership and numerical sign tests are interpreted at the declared verification tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only successful verification of the outcome-specific predicate justifies the corresponding failure classification.

notation.meaning: absence of any conic-feasible primal point
existence of feasible points with objective tending to negative infinity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation between solver behavior and outcome-specific certificates fits the terminal container, but no supporting source is supplied. The reference to verification tolerances also needs authoritative treatment because approximate numerical tests alone do not necessarily constitute an exact mathematical certificate.

children.title: Spurious Residual Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Apparent convergence caused by scaling, cancellation, or ill-conditioned residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Residual Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A translation map shows that an arbitrarily small, stagnant fixed-point residual need not indicate convergence or solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\), and define \(T_\varepsilon:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(T_\varepsilon(x)=x+\varepsilon\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\varepsilon)=\varnothing\), since \(x=T_\varepsilon(x)\) would imply \(\varepsilon=0\). Nevertheless, the fixed-point residual satisfies \[r_\varepsilon(x):=\lvert x-T_\varepsilon(x)\rvert=\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}.\] The iteration \(x_{k+1}=T_\varepsilon(x_k)\) therefore satisfies \(x_k=x_0+k\varepsilon\) for every integer \(k\ge 0\), while \(r_\varepsilon(x_k)=\varepsilon\) for every integer \(k\ge 0\). Because \(\varepsilon\) may be chosen arbitrarily small, residual smallness or stagnation alone cannot certify convergence or the existence of a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any positive translation size and any real initial point, the translation map has no fixed point and its iterates diverge, yet every iterate has the same residual, equal to the translation size. Since that size can be arbitrarily small, residual smallness or stagnation alone cannot certify convergence or solvability.
